# EQUALLY BY BIRTH AND VIRTUE
### To the Noble and Illustrious Lord REINHARD
### Count of Leiningen and Westerburg,
->Andreas Leennius sends greetings.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH no class of men is more worthy of a healthy—let alone a long—life than those devoted to letters <note>The "studiosi" or scholarly class</note>, since they prepare for themselves a rule for living well and wisely from the teachings of the best authors, and are able to pass it on, as if by hand, to others who will be future administrators of public affairs, instilling it into the minds of the youth: yet, I know not by what fate or error it happens that they are allotted a shorter life than others. Many who do survive live as chronic invalids; even more, through the neglect of their own health, are "hurled headlong to Hades" <note>original Greek: ἀΐδι προἰάπτα; a reference to the opening of Homer's Iliad</note>. I would more easily allow this to be blamed on ourselves than for the fault to be cast back upon the Gods, saying with Homer on their behalf:
> "Alas, how mortals now do blame the gods!
> For they say that evils come from us, yet they themselves
> suffer woes beyond their lot through their own reckless folly."
> <note>original Greek: Ω πόποι, οἷον δή νυ θεοὺς βροτοὶ αἰτιόωνται... A quote from the Odyssey, Book 1, where Zeus complains that humans blame the gods for disasters caused by their own choices.</note>

I remember you once telling me, noble Count, that this error could easily be remedied, and you first assigned me to this task then. Since you truly do not cease to urge me—and you wish me to undertake this duty not only in your name, but in the name of all scholars—come then, it has pleased me to comply with this useful command. And because you strive for this by every means,

<summary>In this dedication, Andreas Leennius addresses Count Reinhard of Leiningen, arguing that scholars often suffer poor health due to their own neglect rather than divine fate. He introduces his work as a response to the Count's request for a guide to maintaining scholarly health.</summary>
<keywords>Reinhard of Leiningen, Andreas Leennius, Homer, scholarly health, academic lifestyle, classical education, preventative medicine</keywords>

<meta>Continuity note: This page serves as the preface or dedicatory letter by Andreas Leennius, following the catchword "Is ce" from the preceding leaf.</meta>

# BY ANDREAS LEENNIUS

Since you wish it to be so, I am undertaking this task so that, with me as your guide, the well-being of students may be consulted. This labor has certainly occupied us long and sufficiently. Having finally shaken out the modest collection of books from our profession, I select for you these books by Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a celebrated Italian scholar and priest, central to the Florentine Renaissance and the revival of Neoplatonism.</note> titled *On the Threefold Life* <note>original: "De Vita triplici"; a famous medical and philosophical treatise on the health of scholars.</note>. The author truly seemed to me not unworthy of your sharp judgment, and highly suitable to be worn by the hands of many students, provided that, free from bookworms and moths, he might come forth into the light in a more corrected form. For the copies of this author that have been scattered in public until now are so filled with errors that there is almost no use for those things which were well written. The fair reader will easily perceive that we, on the contrary, have taken care to publish the meditations of such a great man free from "cancers" <note>A metaphor for textual corruptions or errors.</note>. In addition to the labor, exceptionally elegant typefaces have been added by Johann Bebel, the skillful printer <note>term: chalcographi (literally "copper-writer," a common Renaissance term for a printer or typographer)</note>. Wishing now to offer you a taste of these, he has provided those things which he is producing to be judged in public—as the saying goes, "judging the lion by its claws." Furthermore, there is no reason for us to be intensely anxious about winning you over to this work, since the narrowness of a letter does not allow for it, and the matter "plays its own flute" <note>original: "αὐτὴ σεαυτὴν αὐλεῖ"; a Greek proverb meaning the thing speaks for itself.</note>. According to the most ample judgment of Angelo Poliziano <note>A renowned Renaissance humanist and poet.</note>, he says that just as Orpheus's lyre recalled Eurydice, so has Ficino's lyre recalled Platonic wisdom from the underworld. Finally, he pursued his praises with this couplet:

> Character, genius, the Muses, and supreme wisdom—
> If you wish me to say them in one name: Marsilio.

<summary>In this preface, Andreas Leennius introduces a newly corrected edition of Marsilio Ficino's "On the Threefold Life," printed by Johann Bebel. He emphasizes the removal of textual errors found in previous editions and praises Ficino's role in reviving Platonic philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>Andreas Leennius, Marsilio Ficino, On the Threefold Life, Johann Bebel, Angelo Poliziano, Renaissance humanism, book printing, Platonic philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page serves as the dedicatory epistle (Epistola Nuncupatoria) for a medical treatise, establishing the author's intent and the work's structure.</meta>

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE
a 3

He has, through constant study of letters, relentless toil, and the wisdom and experience of a long life, attained these precepts of **Medicine** <note>Latin: *Medicinae*; here referring to the art of healing and clinical practice</note> which are most beneficial to students. He has joined and bound them together in this small volume so aptly that you would doubt—upon closer inspection—whether it could have been done with any greater skill. Providing for life in a threefold manner through these three small books, although each retains its own honor separately and without the other, yet each so takes up the defense of the other's parts that it would be safer *to fight against the triple-gated Geryon* <note>original: "διαμάχεσθαι γηρυόνῃ τριξαπύλῳ"; a Greek mythological reference to a three-bodied giant, emphasizing the unbreakable unity of the three books</note> than to dissolve the framework and the knot of their fellowship. *To these is added* <note>original: "τούτοις ἐπιγίνεται"</note> a Book on the diseases spreading everywhere, no less useful than the others for protecting good health. We decided this should be added as a supplement, fearing lest that which he brought forth for the benefit of the world with such great industry might be swallowed up by *time, the devourer of things* <note>original: "tempus edax rerum"; a famous phrase from Ovid's Metamorphoses</note>.

Truly, I refrain from saying how much labor and sleeplessness we have exhausted in restoring this author to his former dignity. He who compares our work with the old editions will easily perceive what *cancers and abscesses* <note>original: "carcinomatis atq; uomicis"; metaphorical language for textual corruptions and errors in previous manuscripts</note> we have covered with scars; let the judgment rest with him. Most Illustrious Count, you occurred to me not only as one worthy of having these small works dedicated to you, but you seemed plainly fit, as I have found that as soon as you obtain any leisure, you will gladly spend it all in reading of this kind. Indeed, you so excel in letters that if anyone favors more refined *humanity* <note>original: "humanitati"; referring to the 'studia humanitatis' or liberal arts and classical learning</note>, he should consider that you are truly to be congratulated—

<summary>This dedication introduces a three-part medical treatise, emphasizing its structural unity and the editor's efforts to "heal" the corrupted text from previous errors. It is addressed to an unnamed Illustrious Count praised for his devotion to the liberal arts and medical reading.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, medical education, textual criticism, Geryon, public health, humanism</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication of the work, addressing the patron directly in the traditional style of a Renaissance epistolary preface.</meta>

# DEDICATORY EPISTLE
<note>original: "EPIST. NVNCVPATORIA." — A formal letter at the beginning of a book dedicating the work to a patron.</note>

I would weave here a more extensive catalog of your virtues, were I not dealing with you, whom I know to be a despiser of immoderate praise, and who prefers to be good rather than merely to seem so. It is a pleasure to me, however, when I perceive myself to be held in such high esteem by you, that by your kindness <term>humanitate</term> <note>Refers to the refined culture and benevolence expected of a scholar-gentleman.</note> you not only give courage to one striving for higher things, but also aid with your magnificence one who has merited no such thing. I know indeed that there is nothing in me of such a kind that should have led a man of your nobility and dignity to seek out my friendship; nevertheless, I cannot fail to be greatly delighted by this testimony of either your benevolence or your judgment, and I give you immortal thanks for it. From this, I also easily understand how I may not live up to your expectation of me. To which, however, I hope enough will be done by us in whatever way possible, if I am able to uphold and maintain the praise of your testimony either by a perpetual memory of a grateful soul, or by any fruit of our studies. Farewell, happy Patron <term>Maecenas</term> <note>Gaius Maecenas was a Roman counselor and wealthy patron of the arts; his name became a standard title for any generous supporter of literature.</note> of Studies, and look with favor upon this little work of ours.

<vocab>Dedicatory Epistle, virtues, kindness, friendship, Patron, of studies</vocab>

<summary>The author concludes his dedication by praising the patron's humility and generosity, acknowledging that his own merits may not equal the patron's high regard but promising lifelong gratitude and scholarly effort.</summary>
<keywords>dedication, patronage, Maecenas, humility, friendship, academic studies</keywords>

->**To the Reader**<-

We wish to advise you, honest reader, <note>The Latin "candide lector" literally means "bright" or "fair" reader, a common greeting in Renaissance books to imply the reader is unbiased and well-intentioned.</note> that we have intentionally omitted the table of contents <note>original: "capita rerum," literally the "heads of things" or chapter headings.</note> for the matters contained within these books *On Life* by Marsilio Ficino. <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance, a priest and scholar who translated Plato and wrote extensively on how to balance physical health with intellectual labor.</note> This was done partly because the individual headings are already placed before each specific subject, and partly because the index itself—being much more comprehensive—will point out everything that might be read or sought after without causing any boredom.

<summary>An editorial note explaining that a formal table of contents was omitted because the detailed index and individual chapter headings provide a more efficient way to navigate Ficino's work.</summary>

# BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE
### A dedicatory letter for the book *On Life*, addressed to the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici, savior of his country.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'B' featuring classical foliage and a small figure or cherub within the frame.</image-desc>

Poets sing that BACCHUS, the supreme leader of priests, was born twice. Perhaps they mean that a future priest, once initiated, must be born again; or that the mind of a perfected priest, being utterly intoxicated by God, appears to have been reborn; or perhaps, in a humbler sense, that wine—the offspring of Bacchus—is generated once in the vine (as if from Semele <note>In mythology, Semele was the mother of Bacchus/Dionysus who died when Zeus revealed his true lightning-form; the "lightning" here refers to the heat of the sun ripening the grapes</note>) when the clusters mature under Phoebus <note>The sun god, Apollo</note>, and is regenerated again after the "lightning bolt" of the vintage as pure wine in its own vessel, just as if in the thigh of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, who finished Bacchus's gestation in his own thigh</note>. But we must not speak of sacred mysteries at present, when we are soon to assist the weary with physical aid instead. Nor should we proceed with a style enslaved to gravity, but rather one that is free and playful, since we have somehow begun immediately with Father Liber <note>original: "Libero patre" - a title for Bacchus emphasizing freedom and the "liberation" of the mind through wine</note>. And I say "somehow" rightly, for perhaps a more prudent man would have inaugurated a work of medicine with Phoebus, the first of physicians, rather than with Bacchus. But what of it? What if there is a favorable omen in my mouth now by chance uttering the name of Bacchus? For he heals perhaps more healthfully with a certain nourishing wine and a most joyful sense of security than that Phoebus does with his herbs and incantations. In whatever sense you take these things, let that leader of priests, Bacchus, be said to have had, as it were, two mothers.

<summary>Marsilio Ficino opens his treatise on health and longevity with a playful dedication to Lorenzo de' Medici, using the mythology of Bacchus's double birth to transition from spiritual mysteries to physical medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Lorenzo de' Medici, Bacchus, Dionysus, rebirth, medicine, wine, Phoebus Apollo, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# THE LETTERS OF MARSILIO FICINO

->**A Letter from Marsilio Ficino**<-

Now, that great high priest Melchizedek <note>A biblical figure representing a priest-king without a recorded genealogy; Ficino uses this to contrast his own "double" fatherhood.</note> had, it is said, but one mother and one father. I, however, the least of priests, have had two fathers: Ficino the physician and Cosimo de' Medici. From the former I was born; by the latter I was reborn. The first commended me to Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>, who was both a doctor and a Platonist; the second consecrated me to the divine Plato. Just as the first did, so the second destined Marsilio for the role of a physician. Galen is indeed a doctor of bodies, but Plato is the doctor of souls.

For a long time now, I have practiced the healing medicine of souls under Plato’s guidance. After translating all of his works, I soon composed eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness, thus satisfying the wishes of my "physician" father <note>Referring here to Cosimo, his spiritual/intellectual father.</note> to the best of my ability. Thinking it necessary next to satisfy my biological father, the physician, I composed a book *On Caring for the Health of Men of Letters* <term>De literatorum valetudine curanda: The first part of Ficino's "Three Books on Life," focusing on the physical ailments of scholars, such as melancholy.</term>. 

Furthermore, after these works, learned men desired not only to be well at certain times, but also to live a long life while remaining in good health. To these men, I then gave the book *On Long Life*. However, they lacked confidence in earthly medicines and remedies for such a great undertaking. I therefore added a book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, both robust and long <term>De vita coelitus comparanda: A controversial work on "natural magic" and astrology, explaining how to draw life-force from the stars.</term>, so that from the living body of the world itself, a more vigorous life might be propagated into our body—as if into a limb of the world—just as life spreads from a vine. 

I pray you, most indulgent Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent," Ficino's patron and the grandson of Cosimo.</note>, forgive these books of medicine if, while I wish to be a physician, I somehow become—even against my will—an occasional poet, though perhaps not a good one. For even Phoebus <note>Apollo, the Greek god of both healing and poetry.</note> himself...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains his dual lineage from his biological father and his patron Cosimo de' Medici, justifying his transition from writing on the soul's immortality to writing practical and astrological medical treatises for scholars.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, Cosimo de' Medici, Lorenzo de' Medici, Galen, Plato, Three Books on Life, immortality of the soul, medical astrology, Neoplatonism</keywords>

# THE EPISTLE OF MARSILIO FICINO

->is the discoverer of medicine and the master of poetry; he bestows his life upon us not so much through herbs as through the lute and song. Furthermore, even Venus, according to the Astrologers <note>Ficino refers here to the planetary influence of Venus, which was thought to govern harmony and the arts</note>, produces both the Musician and the Physician alike. But thus far, while I consult the lives of scholars and fellow citizens with great care, I neglect the safety of my own books as long as I allow them to remain separated from one another. Therefore, showing them devotion for the first time, I now join them together into a single body. Now that its limbs have been knit into one form, let life be present within it immediately. However, this physical work—this "body" of mine, as it were—cannot receive life unless it be my own. Indeed, a life of that kind depends solely upon my soul. But for a long time now, O magnanimous Lorenzo, my patron, this soul of mine has lived in your keeping, especially in that part of your most noble house where, together with Plato, that work of ours concerning the immortality of souls <note>original: "de animorum immortalitate"; referring to Ficino's major work, the Platonic Theology</note> is preserved, having long ago been dedicated to your name. Yet this soul of mine, even if it leads a life in a certain blessed homeland in your presence, is nevertheless restless in the meantime (as the Theologians maintain) until it receives this physical work as its own body. Receive, therefore, best Lorenzo, after those books concerning the Soul, these books also *Concerning the Body* <note>original: "De corpore"; likely referring to his medical and natural philosophy writings, such as "De vita libri tres"</note>, and breathe upon these with the same inspiration with which you long ago successfully favored those others. For in this way, this body shall live through its own soul under your spirit, and our soul, in turn, shall find rest within your household now that it is joined with its own body.</summary>

### On the nine guides of Scholars. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring intricate foliate and vine patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

Whoever enters upon that rough, arduous, and long journey—which indeed, with constant labor, finally leads to the high temple of the nine Muses—seems to stand in need of exactly nine guides for this journey. Of these, the first three lead us in the heavens, the following three in the soul, and the last three on the earth. In the beginning, in the heavens, Mercury <note>The Roman god of communication and intellect, associated with the planet Mercury</note> either impels or exhorts us to undertake the investigation of the Muses' path. Indeed, the duty of all investigation is attributed to Mercury. Next, Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun god, representing clarity and light</note> himself so illuminates both the seeking minds and the things sought with the most abundant splendor, that what was being sought may be clearly found by us. Then comes most graceful Venus, the mother of the Graces, and with nourishing and entirely joyful...

# MARSILIUS FICINUS ON THE HEALTH OF SCHOLARS
<note>Original title: Marsilius Ficinus de Studiosorum Sanitate Tuenda. Ficinus was a leading figure of the Italian Renaissance who sought to harmonize Platonic philosophy with medicine.</note>

->with his own graces, he so seasons and adorns the entire matter that whatever was sought through the prompting of Mercury, and whatever had already been discovered through the showing of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, now being bathed in a certain wonderful and health-giving loveliness of Venus, it might always delight and be of benefit. There follow three guides of this journey within the soul: namely, an ardent and stable will, sharpness of intellect, and a tenacious memory. There are three final guides on earth: the most prudent head of a household, the most esteemed teacher, and the most skilled physician. Without these nine guides, no one has ever been able, or will ever be able, to reach the very temple of the nine Muses. Indeed, Almighty God and Nature granted us the former guides from our beginning, but our own diligence must provide the final three. However, many ancient and wise men have treated the precepts and duties pertaining to the head of the household and the teacher regarding literary studies—especially our Plato, both elsewhere and most diligently in his books *On the Republic* and *On the Laws*. Then Aristotle in his *Politics*; Plutarch and Quintilian also did so excellently. Yet, until now, the only thing lacking for students of literature is a physician to stretch out a hand to those on the journey, and to aid with health-giving counsel and medicines those whom neither the heavens, nor the soul, nor the head of the household, nor the teacher has abandoned. I, therefore, pitying the most laborious lot of those who travel the difficult path of Minerva <note>Goddess of wisdom; here referring to the "nerve-diminishing" strain of deep study</note> which weakens the nerves, stand forth as the first physician for the infirm

# ON PRESERVING HEALTH. BOOK I.
A 2

And I am here for the sickly, but would that my ability were as complete as my favorable will. Arise now, youths, eager under the leadership of God. Arise, young men and adults, whom an over-ardent devotion to Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom; here representing intensive academic study</note> weakens too much. Approach the physician willingly, who, with God pointing the way and favoring the effort, bestows upon you healthy counsel and remedies for the perfection of your purpose.

### How diligent a care must be maintained for the brain, the heart, the stomach, and the spirit. Chapter II.

In the first place, as much care as runners are accustomed to take of their legs, athletes of their arms, and musicians of their voices, at least that much consideration ought students of literature to have for the brain, the heart, the liver, and the stomach. Indeed, even more so, as much as these organs are more excellent than those, and as these men use these organs more frequently and for more important things than those men use theirs. Furthermore, any skillful craftsman cares for his instruments most diligently: the painter his brushes, the blacksmith his hammers and anvils, the soldier his horses and arms, the hunter his dogs and birds, the lute-player his lute, and each similarly his own. Only truly the priests of the Muses <note>A metaphorical term for scholars and poets</note>, only the hunters of the highest good and truth, are so negligent (oh, the wickedness!) and so unfortunate, that they seem to utterly neglect that instrument by which they are able, in a certain way, to measure and grasp the entire universe. An instrument of this kind is the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to a subtle substance that connects the soul to the body</note>

<summary>The author calls upon scholars to prioritize their physical health, arguing that the brain and internal organs are the essential "tools" of the intellectual craft and deserve more care than a craftsman gives his physical tools.</summary>
<keywords>health of scholars, Minerva, Muses, medical philosophy, brain health, vital organs, spiritus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the physiological basis of thought, specifically focusing on the "spiritus" or subtle vapors of the blood as the bridge between the body and the mind.</meta>

# MARSILIUS FICINO: ON THE CARE OF SCHOLARS

It is this very thing which physicians define as a certain vapor of the blood—pure, subtle, hot, and clear. Generated from the more refined blood by the heat of the heart itself, it flies to the brain; there, the soul uses it continually to exercise both the internal and external senses.

<margin>Blood contributes the greatest part to intelligence. <note>original: "τὸ αἷμα πλεῖσον ξυμβάλλεται μέρος συνέσιος" - a quote attributed to Hippocrates.</note></margin>

For this reason, the blood serves the spirit, the spirit serves the senses, and finally, the senses serve the reason. Now, blood is produced by the natural power <note>The "natural power" refers to the metabolic functions of the liver and stomach in Renaissance medicine.</note> which flourishes in the liver and stomach. The thinnest part of the blood flows into the fountain of the heart, where the vital power flourishes. From there, the created spirits ascend to the brain and—if I may put it this way—to the citadels of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; Ficino uses this metaphor to describe the brain as the seat of intellect.</note>. In these citadels, the "animal" power—that is, the power of sensing and moving—holds dominion. Therefore, the quality of contemplation is almost always determined by the compliance of the senses themselves. The senses, in turn, are only as good as the spirit; and the spirit is only as good as the blood. Furthermore, those three powers we mentioned—namely the natural, the vital, and the animal—are only as good as the organs from which, through which, and in which the spirits themselves are conceived, born, and nourished.

---

->*That the learned are prone to phlegm and black bile.* Chapter III.<-

Indeed, those who are fond of letters must not only care for those organs, powers, and spirits with the greatest diligence, but they are also commanded to avoid phlegm <note>term: pituita (phlegm) - one of the four humors, associated with sluggishness.</note> and black bile <note>term: atra bilis (black bile/melancholy) - the humor associated with deep thought but also depression and madness.</note> as cautiously as sailors avoid Scylla and Charybdis <note>A classical metaphor for two equally dangerous hazards.</note>. For as much as...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino explains the physiological chain from blood to spirit to intellect, warning that scholars are particularly susceptible to imbalances of phlegm and black bile.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the health of scholars, specifically focusing on the physiological and astrological causes of their common ailments.</meta>

# ON PRESERVING HEALTH. BOOK I.

A 3

the rest of the body remains idle, they are busy only with the brain and the mind. From this, they are forced to produce <term>phlegm</term><note>original: "pituita," which the Greeks call "phlegma"</note>; and from that, <term>black bile</term><note>original: "atra bilis," which the same Greeks call "melancholia"</note>. The former often dulls and suffocates the intellect; the latter, however, if it should abound too much or become inflamed, vexes the soul with constant care and frequent delusions, and disturbs the judgment. Thus, it might not be undeservedly said that the lettered would be especially healthy, were it not for the trouble of phlegm; and they would be the most joyful and wisest of all, were they not forced by the vice of black bile to often mourn or sometimes lose their senses.

### Chapter IV. How many causes there are by which the lettered are, or become, melancholic.

There are three primary types of causes that make the lettered melancholic. The first is celestial, the second is natural, and the third is human. The celestial cause is because <term>Mercury</term><note>The planet associated with communication and investigation</note>, who invites us to investigate doctrines, and <term>Saturn</term><note>The planet associated with discipline and long-term memory</note>, who causes us to persevere in investigating those doctrines and to preserve what is found, are said by <term>astronomers</term> to be in a certain way cold and dry. Or, if by chance Mercury is not cold, he nevertheless often becomes very dry due to his proximity to the Sun. This is the same as the <term>melancholic nature</term> described by <term>physicians</term>; and Mercury and Saturn themselves impart this same nature to students of letters—their followers—from the beginning, and they preserve and increase it.

<summary>This page explores the physical and astrological origins of melancholy in scholars, attributing their mental distress to the buildup of phlegm and black bile influenced by the planets Mercury and Saturn.</summary>
<keywords>melancholy, phlegm, black bile, Mercury, Saturn, medical astrology, health of scholars, humoral theory</keywords>

daily. The natural cause seems to be that, in order to pursue sciences—especially the difficult ones—it is necessary for the mind to withdraw itself from external things to internal ones, as if moving from a circumference to the center; and while it contemplates, to remain most firmly fixed in what I might call the very center of man. Indeed, to collect oneself from the circumference to the center, and to be fixed in that center, is a property most characteristic of the Earth itself, to which black bile <note>original: "atra bilis," the humor associated with melancholy</note> is very similar. Therefore, black bile continually provokes the mind so that it may both collect itself into a unity and stand firm in that unity while it contemplates. And being similar to the center of the world, this humor compels one to investigate the center of individual things, and elevates the mind to comprehend the highest matters, since it is most congruent with Saturn, the highest of the planets.

In turn, constant contemplation itself, through a certain persistent concentration and a kind of compression, contracts a nature very similar to black bile. This is the human cause within us: since the frequent agitation of the mind vehemently dries out the brain. Therefore, when the moisture (which is the fuel of natural heat) is largely consumed, the heat also tends to be extinguished; from this, the nature of the brain becomes dry and cold, which is called the "earthy" or "melancholic" quality. Furthermore, because of the constant movement of inquiry, the spirits <term>spiritus: the subtle vapors that connect the soul to the physical body</term> are also continuously moved and dissipated. It is necessary for these dissipated spirits to be restored from the more subtle parts of the blood. For this reason, as the more subtle and clear parts [of the blood are consumed...]

# ON PRESERVING HEALTH. BOOK I.

<margin>Causes.</margin>
When the thinner parts of the blood are frequently consumed, the remaining blood necessarily becomes thick, dry, and black. Added to this is the fact that nature, when occupied in contemplation and focused entirely on the brain and heart, neglects the stomach and the liver. Therefore, when food—especially that which is either too abundant or too hard—is poorly digested, the resulting blood is made cold, thick, and black. Finally, due to the excessive idleness of the limbs, neither are superfluities excreted, nor are the sticky, clinging, and dark vapors exhaled. All these things are accustomed to produce a melancholic spirit and a sorrowful and fearful mind; for indeed, internal darkness occupies and terrifies the soul much more than external darkness.

But of all men of letters, those are most oppressed by black bile <note>original: "atra bile"; the humor associated with melancholy</note> who, being earnestly devoted to the study of philosophy, call the mind away from the body and bodily things and join it to the incorporeal. This is partly because a more difficult task requires a greater intention of the mind, and partly because the more they join the mind to incorporeal truth, the more they are compelled to disjoin it from the body. Hence, their body is sometimes rendered as if half-alive and melancholic. Our Plato signifies this in the *Timaeus* <note>A Socratic dialogue by Plato regarding the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>, saying that a soul contemplating divine things very often and very intensely grows so powerful on such nourishment that it surpasses its body more than the nature of the body can endure, and sometimes, by its more vehement agitations, it [dissolves] the body...

### Chapter V.

Up to this point, it must suffice to have shown—first by celestial, second by natural, and third by human reasons—why the priests of the Muses <note>Ficino refers to scholars and poets as "priests of the Muses" to emphasize the sacred nature of intellectual work</note> either are melancholic from the beginning or become so through their studies. Indeed, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Referring to the "Problemata," a work attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance</note> confirms this in his book of problems: *For he says that all men who have been outstanding in any faculty were melancholics.* In this matter, he confirmed that <term>Platonic</term> saying written in the book on knowledge: namely, that gifted men are usually very agitated and prone to frenzy. <term>Democritus</term> also says that there can never be any men great in genius except those who are stirred by a certain frenzy. Our <term>Plato</term> seems to approve of this in the <term>Phaedrus</term>, saying that the doors of poetry are knocked upon in vain without frenzy. Although he perhaps wishes divine frenzy <note>original: "divinum furorem"; the concept of "divine madness" or inspiration that elevates the soul</note> to be understood here, nevertheless, among physicians, frenzy of this kind is never incited in any others except melancholics. Next, however, we must assign the reasons why <term>Democritus</term>, <term>Plato</term>, and <term>Aristotle</term> assert that some melancholics sometimes so far excel everyone in genius that they seem not human, but rather divine.

Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle assert this without a doubt, yet they do not seem to sufficiently explain the reasoning behind such a great matter. Nevertheless, we must dare (with God as our guide) to investigate the causes. Melancholy <note>literally "black bile," from the Greek *melas* (black) and *chole* (bile)</note> is of two kinds: <margin>Two kinds of melancholy.</margin> One is called "natural" by physicians, while the other occurs through "combustion" <note>the process of humors becoming overheated or "burnt" in the body</note>. That natural kind is nothing other than a denser and drier part of the blood. The burnt kind, however, is divided into four types: it is conceived by the combustion of either natural melancholy, or of the purer blood, or of yellow bile, or of salty phlegm. Whichever type is born from combustion harms judgment and wisdom; indeed, while that humor is ignited and burning, it tends to make men agitated and raving—which the Greeks call *Mania* <note>original: "Maniam"</note> and we call fury. But when it is finally extinguished, and the finer and brighter parts have been dissolved, leaving only a foul soot behind, it renders men dull and stupid; this condition they properly call melancholy, as well as madness and folly. Therefore, only that black bile which we called "natural" contributes to our judgment and wisdom. Yet even this is not always the case. Truly, if it exists alone, it darkens the spirits with its excessively black and dense mass, terrifies the soul, and blunts the intellect. But if it is mixed with simple phlegm, since the cold blood stands against the heart, it brings on sluggishness <margin>Virgil, *Georgics* Book 2</margin> and torpor through a certain thick coldness; and as is the nature of all very dense matter, when melancholy of this kind...

Nor should it seem a wonder that black bile can be easily ignited, and once ignited, burns more violently. Melancholy <note>original: "melancholia"</note> has such great power toward either extreme, due to a certain unity of its stable and fixed nature. Because it is solid and very tenacious, once ignited it blazes for a very long time; because it is most powerful in the unity of its very tenacious dryness, it burns more violently...

### Five chief enemies of scholars: namely Phlegm, Black Bile, Sexual Intercourse, Overindulgence, and Morning Sleep. Chapter VII.

To return to the point from which we have now wandered quite far: the road that leads to truth and wisdom is very long, and full of heavy labors by both land and sea. Whoever undertakes this journey, as a certain poet might say, is often endangered on land and in the waves. For if they sail the sea, they are continually tossed between the tides—that is, between two humors, namely phlegm <term>pituita: one of the four bodily fluids, associated with coldness and sluggishness</term> and that harmful melancholy <term>atra bilis: literally "black bile," the humor thought to cause depression or genius</term>—as if caught between Scylla and Charybdis <note>A classical metaphor for being caught between two equally dangerous choices</note>. In the first place, three planets—as we were saying in the previous sections—greatly favor contemplation and eloquence: the Sun, Venus, and Mercury. However, after the rising of the sun, they are suddenly thrust into the twelfth region of the heaven, which is assigned by astronomers to "prison and darkness" <note>original: "carceri tenebrisque." On the contrary, when the sun recedes, all things are constricted, which by a certain natural order invites sleep, especially after the third or fourth part of the night. 

Whoever, therefore, slumbers in the morning when the sun and the world are waking up, but stays awake late into the night when nature commands us to sleep and rest from labors, undoubtedly fights against both the order of the universe and himself, while he is disturbed and distracted by contrary motions at the same time. Indeed, while he is being moved by the universe toward the outermost parts, he moves himself toward the innermost; and conversely, while he is drawn by the universe toward the innermost parts, he meanwhile withdraws himself toward the external. In the fifth place, we argue from the nature of the stomach in this manner: The stomach, by the long-lasting action of the daytime air, is greatly dilated as the pores are opened, and it is finally weakened significantly as the spirits fly out. <margin>B 2</margin>

It is with good reason, therefore, that those who unnaturally use the night for the day, and conversely, the day for the night, are like owls. Even against their will, they imitate owls in this respect: just as the eyes of those birds grow dim under the light of the sun, so too does the sharpness of these people's minds grow dim under the splendor of truth. 

Sixthly, the same point is proven by the <term>spirits</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that carried life and thought through the body; they were not "ghosts" but physiological vapors.</note> in this way. Through the fatigue of the day, all the most refined spirits are eventually dissipated. Therefore, at night, only a few thick and heavy spirits remain, which are entirely unfit for the study of letters. The intellect, relying on these crippled wings, can no more fly than can bats or horned owls. 

On the contrary, in the morning after sleep, the spirits are restored and the limbs are so strengthened that they require very little support from the spirits. Thus, many refined spirits are present to serve the brain; they can obey its commands more promptly because they are very little occupied with warming and governing the limbs. 

Finally, the seventh reason is derived from the nature of the <term>phantasy</term><note>The "phantasy" or imagination was considered a specific faculty of the brain that processed sensory images before they reached the higher intellect.</note>. The phantasy—whether it should be called imagination, thought, or by any other name—is distracted and disturbed during waking hours by many long and conflicting images, thoughts, and cares. This distraction and disturbance is utterly opposed to subsequent contemplation, which requires a completely tranquil and serene mind. Only through the quiet of the night is that agitation finally calmed and pacified. Therefore, as night approaches, the mind is always disturbed, but as it recedes, for the most part...

...we apply ourselves to our studies with a tranquil mind. For whoever attempts to judge matters while their mind is excessively agitated acts no differently than those suffering from vertigo; they believe all things are spinning (as Plato says) when it is they themselves who are turning. <note>original: "ut Plato inquit"; likely a reference to the Theaetetus or Republic regarding the stability of the soul.</note> For this reason, Aristotle wisely commands in his *Economics* to rise before dawn, asserting that this benefits both the health of the body and the study of philosophy to the highest degree. <note>The *Oeconomica* was a text attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance concerning the management of the household and self.</note> However, this must be understood with the condition that we most diligently avoid morning indigestion by eating a quick and modest supper the night before. Indeed, we ought to rise with our minds at that hour, and soon after with our bodies, provided that it can be done conveniently.

We ought to remember that at any given hour, the intense focus of the mind should be relaxed at least once for a short while. For since the spirits <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle substances that carried life and thought through the body</note> are dissipated because of such intense focus, you will deservedly become sluggish if you never cease to strain. While you labor with the mind, let the body rest in the meantime. Fatigue of the body is bad, that of the mind is worse, but fatigue of both at once is the worst of all, for it pulls a man apart with opposing movements and destroys his life. Finally, let meditation proceed no further than the point of pleasure—or rather, stop just short of it.

### Chapter 9. Precepts for Avoiding Phlegm.

It seems worthwhile to briefly repeat those things which we have said are harmful to the literate, and to apply remedies to each. Therefore, lest phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four humors believed to cause sluggishness and dullness if in excess</note> increase too much, one must engage in exercise twice daily when the stomach is nearly empty. However, this should never be laborious, lest the sharp spirits be dissolved; and waste products must be most diligently purged from all passages. Filth must be thoroughly wiped away from the skin of the whole body, and especially the head, both by washing and by rubbing. One must avoid foods that are excessively cold and—unless black bile <note>original: "atra bilis" or melancholy</note> prevents it—those that are damp, as well as everything that is fatty, rank, viscous, oily, and gluey, or those things which are prone to rot easily. If the stomach is cold either by nature or by age, the drinking of water should either be given up entirely or certainly diminished. Food ought to be moderate, but drink should be more moderate still. The dwelling should be high up, away from the heavy—

### On the Care of the Stomach. Chapter XI.

It follows that we must take diligent care of the stomach, so that overindulgence never brings about nausea or indigestion <note>original: "cruditatem"; literally "rawness," referring to undigested food in the stomach</note>, which might harm the head. Food should be taken twice daily, and it should be moderate and light, seasoned in moderation with cinnamon, mace, and nutmeg. However, dry food should always exceed soft nourishment and drink in weight, unless by chance we greatly fear the dryness of black bile. Food should wait for hunger, and drink for thirst (if this can be done conveniently). A desire for both should remain when leaving the table. <margin>Satiety is to be avoided.</margin> Loathing and over-fullness should be far away. One must abstain from those things which, on account of excessive moisture or a poisonous, greasy, and viscous nature, weaken the stomach by relaxing it.

### Remedies for Catarrh and Distillation, the Common Plague of Scholars. Chapter XIV.

When the head is overflowing with distillations <note>the "dripping" of excess fluids from the brain to the nose or throat</note> on account of phlegm, we will occasionally give some of the pills which we have just described at the hour of sleep. Furthermore, we shall order the patient to frequently chew Frankincense <note>original: "Thus"</note> at that hour and at others: for it wonderfully assists against distillations and aids all the senses and the memory. Again, nutmeg and theriac <note>a complex herbal "universal antidote" often containing dozens of ingredients</note> held in the mouth are approved; also Marjoram, which they call *amaracum*, or its water applied to or poured into the nostrils. After food, however, we shall restrain the vapors of the nutrients with coriander and quinces.

### On Restoring the Sense of Taste. Chapter XVII.

### *On the use of liquid medicines*
### Remedies. Chapter XXI.

One must remember that when the greatest danger of "drying out" <note>The author refers to the humoral theory where excessive dryness was seen as a cause of aging and illness, particularly melancholy.</note> is imminent, yet necessity forces a purging of the bowels, it is worthwhile to pause the use of pills. Instead, when it is time to purge, one should infuse into a syrup or a similar decoction made in Bugloss water <note>Bugloss (*Anchusa officinalis*) was traditionally used to "gladden the heart" and temper melancholy.</note> one ounce, or at least half an ounce, of *diasena*, *diacatholicon*, or *Persian triphera* <note>These were standard "electuaries" or medicinal pastes containing senna, rhubarb, and various spices used as laxatives.</note>. But if the body is more robust, or the bowels more constricted and hard, one should add one or two drams of the *Electuary of Hamech* <note>A stronger purgative specifically used to expel "black bile."</note>. Purified Cassia is also useful here, but Manna <note>A sweet resin from the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle laxative for children and the delicate.</note> is even more useful.

These remedies do not suit every type of melancholy, but especially that which is created by "combustion" <note>Known as *melancholia adusta*, thought to be caused by overheated humors becoming scorched and bitter.</note>. However, if it is "natural melancholy" <note>The innate cold and dry temperament of an individual.</note>, they are indeed suitable, but especially if a double or triple portion of polypody <note>A type of fern root.</note> is added to the syrup, along with similar amounts of liquorice, saffron, and raisins. Likewise, two ounces of liquid honey of roses should be added to the medicine.

We have stated in the previous sections how often the syrup should be taken. However, the medicine must be taken with the syrup for sixty days. But if no melancholic humor is actually present, and there is only a melancholic "complexion"—that is, a cold and dry quality of the limbs—remember that it is not at all expedient to purge the bowels or to perform bloodletting. Instead, perform only the remaining things which we have either already mentioned or will mention. Especially those things which pertain to—

### Rules for Bloodletting.
### Chapter XXII.

<margin>Signs of an abundance of blood.</margin>
There are some who are quite bold in the letting of blood, whom wise physicians greatly detest. For blood is the tempering force of black bile, the fuel of the spirit, and the treasury of life. Only when an abundance of blood is indicated—either by excessive laughter, great boldness and confidence, a ruddy color, or the swelling of the veins—should we draw blood from men of letters <term>literati: scholars and students whose sedentary work was thought to dry out the body</term> when the situation demands it. This should be done from the "spleen vein" of the left arm with a wide incision, taking four ounces in the morning and the same amount in the evening. ### Chapter XXIV.

### That we ought to be intent upon the protection of the spirits. Chapter XXVI.

**I**f men who are desirous of the truth ought to care for the corporeal spirit <note>original: "corporeum spiritum." In Renaissance medicine, this refers to the subtle substance that connects the soul to the body.</note> with such great medical diligence—lest, perhaps, if it is entirely neglected, it becomes an impediment or serves unsuitably for those seeking the truth—then without a doubt, it is fitting to cultivate the incorporeal spirit (that is, the intellect itself) much more diligently through the instructions of moral discipline. For by the intellect alone is truth itself grasped, since truth is incorporeal. Nor is it right to cultivate only the servant of the soul, which is the body, while neglecting the soul, which is the master and king of the body. This is especially true since it is the opinion of the Magi <note>Refers to ancient Persian priests or wise men often cited in Neoplatonic texts.</note> and of Plato that the entire body depends on the soul in such a way that unless the soul is well, the body cannot be well. For this reason, Apollo, the author of medicine, judged not Hippocrates—though he was born of Apollo's own lineage—but Socrates to be the wisest of men. This is because Socrates studied the healing of the soul as much as Hippocrates studied the healing of the body; although, what those men merely attempted, Christ alone has perfected. Therefore, we are commanded by Socrates to cultivate our minds with the best morals, so that we may more easily attain with a serene mind the light and truth sought by us through natural instinct; how much more so truth itself

# MARSILIO FICINO ON THE HEALTH OF SCHOLARS

*Is it not right, above all, to venerate the divine essence itself with holy devotion? The mind was created for the purpose of seeking and grasping this essence, just as the eye was created to perceive the light of the sun. And, as our Plato says <note>Ficino frequently refers to "our Plato," signaling his role as the leader of the Florentine Platonic Academy</note>, just as sight perceives nothing visible anywhere except in the splendor of the highest visible thing—that is, the sun itself—so too the human intellect apprehends nothing intelligible except in the light of the highest intelligible thing, which is God, who is always and everywhere present to us. In that light, I say, which illuminates every man coming into this world <note>original: "illuminat omnem hominem uenientem in hunc mundum" — a reference to the Gospel of John 1:9</note>. In the light of which David sings: In your light we shall see light <note>original: "In lumine tuo uidebimus lumen" — Psalm 36:9</note>. Surely, just as when the eyes are cleansed and look toward the light itself, its splendor is suddenly poured in, shining abundantly with the colors and shapes of things; so, as soon as the mind is purged of all bodily disturbances through moral discipline <term>moralis disciplina: the practice of virtue to calm the passions</term>, and is directed toward divine truth—that is, God himself—by a certain religious and most burning love, suddenly, as the divine Plato says, divine truth flows into the mind. It happily unfolds the true reasons contained within itself, by which all things consist; and by as much light as it surrounds the mind, by so much joy it simultaneously and blessedly drenches the will.*

Although our Plato lives by his own Genius <note>Ficino uses "Genius" in the classical sense of a guardian spirit or innate divine nature</note>, and will continue to live, I believe, as long as the world itself shall live; nevertheless, my own Genius always impels me that, after the worship of the Divine, I should look after the life of Plato above all else. For a long time now, the House of Medici <note>original: "Medica domus," a pun on the Medici family name and the Latin word for "medical"</note> has aspired toward this very goal for us more than any others. For this reason, I exhort and beseech you, my Valori, that with as much effort as you always favor the glory of Plato, you might with equal diligence read and observe these precepts of ours on prolonging life. By living long through these practices, you may be able to patronize the recently reborn discipline of Plato for a longer time, together with the magnanimous Lorenzo de' Medici.

Nor should they be spread among men dissolved in the ruinous lust for pleasures, who foolishly prefer a brief daily pleasure to a long life. Nor should they be opened to the wicked and the unjust, whose life is the death of the good. Rather, they are for prudent and temperate men alone, who will benefit the human race, whether privately or publicly, through the powers of a skillful mind.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON LIFE

### *That the vital heat is nourished by moisture, and that corruption or dissolution occurs through its excess or deficiency.*

-> Chapter II <-

Life indeed consists in natural heat, much like a flame. The fuel for this heat is a vaporous and fatty moisture, acting like oil. Therefore, if this moisture should happen to fail, or if it should excessively overflow or become tainted, the natural heat is immediately weakened, and once weakened, it is eventually extinguished. If the heat is weakened and lost through a lack of moisture, death occurs by "resolution" <note>original: "resolutione"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the body's vital substances dissipating or evaporating away</note>. <margin>Imbalance breeds disease. <note>original Greek: "Αμετρία νόσας τίκτει"</note></margin> If, instead, the heat is overwhelmed by an excess or vice of moisture, life perishes by "suffocation." This suffocation happens through the overflowing or rotting of any moisture, especially when phlegm <term>pituita: one of the four bodily humors, associated with coldness and moisture</term> either increases or becomes putrid in some way; thus, Phlegm has not undeservedly been called "the seeker of life" <note>A play on words: "Pituita petens uitam." Ficino suggests phlegm "hunts" or attacks the vital force</note>. Therefore, the precepts most necessary for prolonging life equally avoid resolution on one hand, and suffocation and putrefaction on the other. Equally, I say, by common reason. For if they happen to be treating a man who is quite hot or dry, and whose passages are open, while his fluids and spirits are subtle, they run a greater risk of resolution. But if they treat a body affected by the opposite condition, they must instead come to the aid of suffocation. They should be especially diligent in either case if the location or the season inclines toward one of these two extremes.

<summary>Ficino explains that life is a "natural heat" fueled by bodily moisture, warning that death occurs either when this fuel runs dry (resolution) or when it overwhelms the flame (suffocation).</summary>
<keywords>vital heat, humors, phlegm, resolution, suffocation, Marsilio Ficino, Renaissance medicine, longevity</keywords>

Let us learn from the lamp: oil must be constantly supplied to the flame, with such care that we do not overwhelm the light with a sudden flood. Nor, on the other hand, should we withhold a drink from the thirsty flame. We believe these two points have been sufficiently discussed in the preceding sections. Two others remain for us, one of which we seem to have touched upon lightly, and the other scarcely at all. In touching upon Pallas <note>The goddess of wisdom, often associated with the olive tree and its oil</note> in the meantime, we do so in such a way that she, who is never accustomed to laugh, might smile upon us.

What then? First, we shall consider that even a tiny flame is utterly devouring; therefore, that lamp shines longer in which the small flame is so tempered to the wick <note>original: "ellychnium, id est lucinium"</note> that it does not gulp down the oil, but merely sips it. And so, in our entire regimen <term>dietary and lifestyle habits</term>, we shall take care lest at any time—especially in youth—the innate fire, which is voracious by its very nature, should grow too powerful. It will be enough then to keep away both overflowing moisture and piercing cold.

Next, we shall reflect that a lamp is frequently extinguished when the oil poured in is not pure, but (so to speak) full of dregs <note>original: "amurcosum," referring to the watery, bitter sediment of olive oil</note>. From these dregs, "fungi" <note>crusty carbon deposits on a wick</note> soon grow and extinguish the light. Now, we have received from Pallas a nourishing oil that is as airy and pure as possible, and firm through a certain natural tenacity. Therefore, whatever is supplied to replace this as it is gradually consumed must not only be equal to it, but similar. To be truly similar, it must not only be airy and fatty, but thoroughly separated from the dregs, that is—

->*The causes of the drying up of natural moisture and the overflowing of foreign moisture. And how necessary perfect digestion is for life.*<-

### Chapter IV.

The following things quickly dry out the natural moisture <note>original: "humorem naturalem"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to the "radical moisture" or vital fluid that sustains life and heat.</note>: An excessive flow of blood; violent loosening of the bowels; a long-lasting slippery stomach; profuse sweating; widely opened pores; sexual intercourse performed to the point of weakness; panting thirst; agonizing hunger; long periods of wakefulness; the use of things that are simultaneously very hot and dry; laborious movement of the mind and body; anxiety; anger; pain; air that is both drier and hotter, especially when heated by fire; and a wind that is dry, violent, and long-lasting. The opposites of these things increase moisture beyond measure. Frequent drunkenness does both: for by excessive heat it dries out the drunkard, and by excessive moisture it suffocates him. Nothing, however, is more harmful to both states than indigestion <note>original: "cruditas"; literally "rawness," referring to food that remains undigested in the stomach.</note>. ...is lost, because when it overflows, it overwhelms the natural heat. For this reason, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> says that the blood is corrupted when digestion itself is corrupted; and following Galen <note>The most famous Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>, he calls digestion the root of life. Therefore, the best and almost unique rule of Galen is this: to care for the digestion <term>concoction; the "cooking" of food within the stomach by natural heat</term> of food above all else. For even what seems to be the greatest precept—namely, to use healthy things—will be of no use unless you digest them. Indeed, a harmful humor flows from these healthy things almost as much as from their opposites if they flow into the limbs raw <note>undigested</note>. However, from foods that are often less praised by the medical art, a less evil nourishment is frequently received if they are more vigorously digested. 

<margin>The necessity of digestion for life.</margin>

Let us therefore most diligently avoid indigestion <note>original: "cruditatem," literally rawness or crudity</note> as a heavy cause of both the dissolution and suffocation of the spirit. We do this by using a quantity of food and drink suited to us: by quality, simplicity, preparation, thorough chewing, and by fasting until hunger returns. If necessary, we may even use external warmth for the stomach <note>fomentation; applying heat to the abdomen</note> and certain styptic <note>astringent substances used to "bind" the stomach</note> things taken internally after meals. 

And let us carefully beware lest drink exceeds the food, or that the food be too liquid or too hard; or that one or the other be extremely cold in its effect, or that the nourishments be of vastly different types, or that we add raw food upon raw. For these things greatly hinder digestion. Furthermore, let us most diligently beware of sexual intercourse immediately after food, or of midday sleep (unless frequently necessary), or of staying awake at night, or of any untimely labor of the mind or body, or...

By digestion, I mean not only the first, which occurs in the stomach: but also the second, which occurs in the liver <margin>The four digestions.</margin>: furthermore, the third which occurs in the veins: and finally the fourth, which is completed in the limbs. These require a certain long interval of time, and if any of them are hindered, nourishment is not supplied to the <term>humors</term><note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament.</note>. Bodily movement is necessary—as continuous, as tempered, and as varied as the movements of the heavens, the air, fire, and water—provided that the necessity of <term>concoction</term><note>The "cooking" or ripening of nutrients within the body through natural heat.</note> and sleep is observed. However, exhaustion and the weakening of the body's tone must be avoided. Furthermore, we contract decay and rot when situated in the shade. We live under the open sky and under the light. This is what my father, Ficino, a distinguished physician, frequently had in his mouth <note>original: "habebat in ore" - a common idiom meaning he spoke of it often.</note>. Sometimes one should also maintain a somewhat varied type of nourishment and lifestyle. That wise man often advised me of this. For those who live in every stage of life with a certain most elegant fastidiousness often live less safely. Those who did not accustom themselves as youths should at least do so as adults, attempting it however with more cautious steps and little by little.

### Chapter V.

All the Greeks <note>Ficino refers here to the classical Greek medical authorities like Galen and Hippocrates</note>, among the precepts most necessary for a long life, command that we be nourished by *euchymis* <term>euchymis: a Greek medical term for "good juices" or healthy digestive fluids</term>. We call those foods *euchyma* which are wholesome and provide good nourishment—that is, good blood. Indeed, we define "good blood" as being neither cold, nor dry, nor turbulent, but rather warm, moist, and clear. It should be warm, yet not with a sharp or stinging heat; moist, but not with a watery moisture; and clear, yet not excessively thin. 

For blood that is too fervent <note>original: "ferventior," meaning boiling or overly hot</note> both sharpens the natural heat and dries out the moisture; furthermore, whatever moisture or heat such blood introduces is rendered easily dissolved and fleeting. Moreover, blood that is too watery and prone to being liquid blunts the natural heat; it either weakens the natural moisture, causes it to melt away under heat, or suffocates the heat with its excessive dampness. In general, if any portion of the natural moisture is drawn from watery blood, it both rots easily and quickly flows away and dissolves. 

From this it follows that those who eat soft fruits and herbs—unless perhaps they take them rarely as a medicine to soften the belly—will shortly fill their veins deep within with a raw juice that is liable to putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactionique obnoxio," referring to the medical theory that stagnant or "raw" fluids in the body lead to disease</note>. And lest that happen, it is safer...

Therefore, the blood should be neither fiery nor watery, but airy <note>The author follows the theory of the four humors, where blood is associated with the element of Air (warm and moist).</note>. It should not be like the thicker air, lest it be too prone to turn into water. Nor should it be like the most subtle air, lest it easily heat up into fire: but it should maintain a moderate substance, in which the middle air holds the greatest dominion. The other elements should be present only insofar as they are adapted to the command of the air.

<margin>The remaining qualities must be tempered to the Air.</margin>
Its substance should not be extremely subtle, lest it generate an unstable moisture and a volatile spirit <note>term: spiritus (spirit) — a vital, vaporous substance believed to circulate through the body to enable movement and thought</note> that is subject to dissolving. It should not be very thick; otherwise, it will not serve the intellect at all, and will hardly be transformed into natural moisture and spirit. It will obstruct the passages and provide an occasion for suffocation. And the spirit which is finally created from such thick blood is itself poorly suited for life due to its density; it suffocates the natural heat just as thick smoke immediately compresses and extinguishes a flame. I will omit the fact that it is at least so dark that it makes life sorrowful and worse than death. 

But above all, as it seems to me, it is expedient for a long life to have blood that—along with a very airy and not overly thick substance—possesses within itself a certain sticky and tenacious moisture. This is much like the quality found in olive oil (which combines subtlety with richness), or the moisture of a fat yet thin eel, or oil of turpentine <note>original: "olevm ex terebinthina"</note> drawn out by a certain sublimation. You, therefore, should choose foods and all other things which, according to their powers, [turn] the blood into moisture...

# THINGS TO BE PRODUCED. BOOK II.

By using onion, rose-sugar, and astringent substances, we will finally achieve that firmness of the blood and humor which we cannot safely attain here with overly sticky materials. We shall also lightly soothe the skin with oil of mastic and quinces, and meanwhile, we shall forbid those things which make the blood thin or boiling <note>overly agitated or hot</note>, unless perhaps we infuse a little saffron or cinnamon into the more tenacious meals, so that they may be both more easily digested and, once digested, transferred through the narrow passages to the limbs. Indeed, when you perform these, do so with softer hands. And remember to moisten the hands with a certain fragrant wine in which you have cooked chamomile, myrtle, and roses.

### *On the common rule of eating and drinking, and the quality of feasts. Chapter VI.*

But for the present, let us set aside those human bodies that are either extremely dull <note>original: "obtußißima," referring to a heavy or sluggish constitution</note> or extremely thin, and let us arrive at a common way of living, suited entirely to the common and middle habit of the body. Take care that by no means the passages of the body are either opened beyond measure or too greatly obstructed. For in the former, there is danger in the loosening of the spirit and injury inflicted from without; in the latter, however, there is danger in putrefaction <note>the breakdown of bodily fluids due to lack of circulation</note> and suffocation. And if I do not restrain you with the tightest bridle of rules—which Hippocrates <note>the famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> condemns—I nevertheless do not loosen the reins for you unto license.

Take moist herbs and fruits sparingly. Take milk and fish even more sparingly, and both of these with honey. Take mushrooms most sparingly of all, and only with aromatics and pear seeds. Likewise, drink pure water sparingly. Season those things which are more moist or fatty with aromatic and sharp spices; otherwise, they bring much foreign and rotten moisture into the limbs. Even if they provide some moisture necessary to nature, they offer it in a state subject to very rapid corruption. This is no different than how watery wine is quickly disturbed and spoiled. From this comes early gray hair, paleness, and the wrinkles of old age. Meat also, if eaten daily, or even if it approaches the weight of your bread, brings on rapid putrefaction. Whence Porphyry <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher who advocated for vegetarianism</note> says of the Pythagoreans and the ancients—

Everywhere, let the heat and moisture have something somewhat glutinous and styptic <note>term: styptic (an astringent quality that contracts tissues and tends to check bleeding or secretions)</note>, so that the moisture, having irrigated the limbs, may adhere more firmly and endure for a long time under the heat. 

Select wheat and select bread possess this quality in the highest degree. Next, a red and styptic wine that is only slightly sweet. Therefore, I cannot help but criticize those who criticize the wise Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet known for "Works and Days," a foundational text on farming and morality.</note> for omitting the use of manure in his writings on rural matters. In summary, we shall use sweet and somewhat warm scents. We should purge ourselves frequently and gently with properly prepared aloe. We say it is "properly prepared" if it has been washed with rose water or the juice of roses, or if it has been thoroughly mixed with fresh, crushed roses. Then, let myrobalan <note>A dried fruit used in medieval medicine, often sourced from India, thought to balance the humors.</note> and mastic <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree, used for digestion and breath.</note> be added to it, and perhaps more rose. Furthermore, we shall exercise the body and make use of a hearth at the appropriate time. We shall season our feasts with this powder: let there be a quarter-ounce portion of emblic myrobalans, a half-portion of sandalwood, a whole portion of cinnamon, and an eighth of saffron. Thus, with this powder and with sharp substances, we may perhaps be able to inhibit the corruption that threatens us from putrid food and locations. This wine, as we have said, when tempered, warms a cold bodily constitution, cools a heated one, moistens a dry one, and dries out one that is too moist; and (as Galen says) it restores the natural moisture, fosters heat, and balances both. However, it is more necessary to mix such wine with water for young people, less so for the elderly, and for cold-natured old men, not at all. For a cold and hard old age (as Plato says) is heated and softened by undiluted wine, just as iron is by fire, or lupin seeds by water. Know also that what we said about opposites being achieved and conflicting things being balanced through wine also occurs through licorice <note>original: "glycyrrhizã"</note>, though more weakly; it also occurs through rose oil, but when applied externally. Therefore, let these things be familiar to you. Nor should you doubt that whatever is balanced in quality and powerful in virtue can balance other things—just as cold things can make others cold—possessing this primarily through the temperament of Jupiter <note>In medical astrology, Jupiter represents the "Great Benefic," associated with warmth, moisture, and perfect balance</note>, by which things are also made most healthful. But these matters must be discussed elsewhere.

For it is most difficult (so to speak) to grow young again in body, unless you first become a child again in your character. Therefore, in every stage of life, it is greatly conducive to longevity to retain something of childhood and to always seek out various delights. However, long and profuse laughter is not advised: for it dilates the spirit too much toward the exterior. But let us return to the elderly.

### On gold, golden nourishment, and the restoration of the elderly. Chapter X.

All authorities approve of gold above all things, as it is the most balanced of all substances and the most resistant to decay. It is consecrated to the Sun because of its brilliance, and to Jupiter because of its temperate nature. Therefore, it is able to wonderfully balance natural heat with moisture, preserve the bodily fluids <note>original: "humores"</note> from corruption, and bring the power of the Sun and Jupiter into the spirits and limbs. 

However, it is necessary to make the extremely hard substance of gold finer and very easy to absorb. For those who study the heart <term>cordialia: medicines or foods that strengthen the heart</term> know that they best refresh the hidden power of the heart when nature labors the least in drawing them in. So that the body is not fatigued, these substances must be administered either after they have been made very fine, or alongside very fine materials. 

They think it would be best if "potable gold" <note>original: "aurum potabile," a legendary alchemical liquid gold believed to grant eternal youth</note> could be made without any foreign mixture. But if that is not possible, they wish for it to be taken crushed and reduced into leaves. You shall have (so to speak) a nearly drinkable gold in this way: Collect the flowers of borage, bugloss, and balm—which we call "lemon-balm" <note>original: "citrariam"</note>. When the Moon enters Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, and looks upon the Sun or Jupiter <note>This refers to favorable astrological alignments for gathering and preparing medicine</note>, cook them with white sugar dissolved in rose water. For every ounce, carefully insert three gold leaves. Take this while fasting with a certain "golden" wine. There is a certain common and ancient opinion that certain wise-women <note>original: "sagas," often implying sorceresses or folk-healers</note> (who are also called "shrieking owls" <note>original: "striges," a mythical bird-like spirit or witch said to prey on children</note> in the common tongue) suck the blood of infants so that they may grow young again as much as possible. Then, let them immediately take the same amount of sugar and wine; and they shall do this while hungry and thirsty during a waxing moon. Do not, therefore, doubt that youthful blood drunk by an old man can be drawn to the veins and limbs, and there be of the greatest benefit.

While walking among these green things, we shall meanwhile seek the cause for why the color green, above all others, nourishes the sight and delights it healthfully. We shall find at last that the nature of sight is luminous and a friend to light, yet volatile and easily scattered. For that reason, while it dilates itself through light as if through a friend, it is sometimes snatched away by an excessive surplus of light and dissolved by that vehement dilation. On the other hand, it flees darkness as a natural enemy, and thus withdraws its rays into a narrow space. 

<margin>
Why the color green, above all others, affects the sight with pleasure.
</margin>

Truly, the sight desires to enjoy the light in such a way that it is indeed amplified by this friend of its own, yet not scattered in the process. Now, in whatever color there is significantly more darkness or blackness than light, the ray of sight is not dilated, and therefore is not delighted according to its wish. Where, conversely, there is significantly more splendid color than black, the sight is spread too widely, distracted by a certain harmful pleasure. For this reason, the color green, most of all, tempers the black with the white and provides both, delighting and [preserving] equally...

->What business do you have with this Venus, who is always a young girl, you old men? What, in turn, does Venus have to do with serious discourse? Are not these discourses mine as much as yours? Is not my reason equal to your own? Listen to me, therefore, with the same attention you gave to her—and indeed with much greater attention than you gave to Venus. You know there are five senses: Sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Learn now that there are, in turn, five "reasons" (if I may call them that). For while the soul is daily steeped in information through the five senses, and from these it conceives the reasons of things, meanwhile five notions and habits for judging things result, acting as five modes of reasoning. Furthermore, just as there are five senses on one hand and five modes of reason on the other, so the course of life is arranged in five stages concerning sense and reason.<-

<margin>The five stages of life</margin>
From this, five ages are numbered. The first is drawn only by sense. The second is attracted much more by sense than it is led by reason. The third, after these, is driven equally by the alternating persuasions of reason and sense. The fourth is led by reason rather than by sense. The fifth, finally, ought to be ruled by reason alone. Therefore, let the first and second ages, as they are subject to Venus <note>Venus here represents physical desire and youthful passion</note>, listen to Venus speaking if they wish; but let the remaining ages listen to Mercury <note>Mercury represents the intellect, communication, and the transition to wisdom</note>. I, therefore, address all the rest of you, not only for myself, but also for this Diana whom you see to my left; for since she is speechless and I am "double-tongued" <note>original: "bilinguis"; likely referring to Mercury's role as an interpreter between the divine and human or his mastery of both logic and rhetoric</note>, I speak by right for her, whose tongue I...

He argues that while youth is the domain of Venus and the senses, the later stages of life must be governed by the intellect and the wisdom of Mercury and Diana.</summary>

This goddess <note>Referring to Venus, though the text uses the metaphor of a "prostitute" to describe her seductive nature</note> again (if it is permitted to say so) is like a prostitute who is not satisfied with just any one man. I, however, through the benefit of my father and brother, promise you five; I provide five that are pure, perpetual, and healthful, of which the lowest is in smell, the higher in hearing, and the most sublime in sight.
