### Chapter XVI.

Astrologers say that Venus and Saturn are enemies to one another. However, since in heaven—where all things are moved by love and where there is no defect—there can be no hatred, we interpret "enemies" to mean diverse in their effects. Let us set aside other matters for the present. Behold, Saturn has placed our pleasure in the center, while Venus has placed it in the circumference. Pleasure is, as it were, the bait of the spirits <note>In Ficino's philosophy, "spirit" is a subtle vapor that connects the soul to the body</note>. Therefore, from opposite sides, Venus and Saturn lie in wait for the flight of our spirit. She, through her pleasure, lures it toward external things; he, meanwhile, through his own pleasure, recalls it to the innermost things. They distract the spirit, therefore, if they move at nearly the same time, and they dissipate it. For this reason, nothing is more pestilential to a contemplator or a seeker of knowledge than the venereal act <note>sexual intercourse</note>; and conversely, nothing can be more foreign to one pursuing such acts than cares and contemplation. Indeed, for the contemplator

On a similar level, we consider anyone who is deeply pensive in their affairs and subject to heavy cares. From this it follows, in turn, that if we wish to relieve and otherwise console someone who is either too occupied with **Saturnine contemplation** <note>Saturn was traditionally associated with deep thought, melancholy, and old age</note> or weighed down by care, we would attempt this in vain and even with harm if we used **Venerean acts** <note>Activities associated with Venus, such as sex, luxury, or physical pleasure</note>, games, and jokes, as these are remedies too far removed from the condition. 

And conversely, if we wish to moderate someone who is either lost in Venerean work or loosened by games and jokes, we would not easily be able to correct them through **Saturnine severity**. Indeed, the best discipline is to use certain pursuits and similar remedies of **Phoebus and Jupiter** <note>The Sun and Jupiter, representing balance, vitality, and justice</note>—who are the mediators between Saturn and Venus—to call back to the middle path those men who are leaning toward one extreme or the other. 

But let us finally act as physicians. Just as a flame is commonly extinguished in two violent ways—either as if blown away by winds, or on the contrary, as if smothered by ashes—so do we either quickly dissipate the **spirit** <note>term: spiritus (the subtle substance connecting the soul and body)</note> through Venerean effect, or gradually suffocate it through the Saturnine, and often we squeeze it out by compressing it, and likewise dissolve it. Certainly, the spirit flying frequently to the outermost parts renders the innermost parts either empty or foreign to life. But when the spirit is often forced to the innermost parts, it renders the rest of the limbs less fit for life. Therefore, both Venus and Saturn bring on **old age**: Venus brings it to our interior parts, while Saturn brings it to our exterior. Venus does this especially when, from any of its movements, the body easily [becomes] **weak**...

# THINGS TO BE PRODUCED, BOOK II.

All those things which we have explained in the preceding sections, or at least indicated, all city-dwellers ought to diligently avoid: heat, frost, any cold following heat or occurring at night, mists, and winds—whether blowing from a marsh or bursting through a narrow passage. Likewise, they should avoid places where the air either moves too violently or does not move at all. They must shun any dwelling that is overly damp, as well as foul odors, sorrow, and lethargy. 

However, the <term>followers of Mercury<note>original: "Mercurij sectatores." This refers to scholars, writers, and merchants who were thought to be governed by the planet Mercury.</note></term> should be more diligent in these matters, and the elderly most diligent of all. Furthermore, after they have lightly rubbed the entire body in the morning, they should anoint it against the discomforts of the air and labor with warm oil or some slightly bitter wine, into which they have previously infused myrrh, rose, and myrtle. They should frequently carry sage in their mouths, as it is most friendly to the nerves and the teeth. 

And when, due to the failing of their teeth, they are forced to return to liquid nourishment like infants, they should avoid the softest foods <note>The author likely refers here to overly processed or "slimy" foods that lack nutritional vigor.</note>. Indeed, they should replace milk with a moderate amount of wine. They should use fire only as a medicine—specifically, as much as the necessity of expelling cold and arousing the <term>innate heat<note>original: "calor innatus." In ancient medicine, this was the vital warmth present in a living body from birth, which diminished with age.</note></term> demands; otherwise, fire acts as a consumer that will dry out the <term>natural moisture<note>original: "humor naturalis." The essential bodily fluids believed to sustain life and flexibility.</note></term>. 

They should follow the sun as if it were food, as long as it is pleasant, while avoiding <term>distillation<note>original: "destillatione." A medical term for the dripping of excess phlegm or catarrh, often thought to be triggered by improper exposure to the elements.</note></term> and similarly declining intense heat. They should love easy movements, which are quite necessary for exciting the heat. However, they should hate labors of the body, and much more those of the mind; nor should they less avoid long thirst, fasting, and wakefulness.

### On the nourishment of the spirit and the preservation of life through odors. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>As with the Mouthless People <note>original: "Astomos." A legendary race mentioned by Pliny the Elder who lived only on the scent of fruits and flowers.</note> in the East near the source of the Ganges.</margin> We read that in certain hot regions, which are fragrant everywhere with many scents, there are many people with slender bodies and weak stomachs who are nourished, as it were, by odors alone. This is perhaps because the very nature of the place reduces almost all the juices of herbs, fruits, and produce into scents, and likewise dissolves the humors of human bodies there into spirit <note>Ficino refers to the "spiritus," a thin, vaporous substance in the body that acts as the vehicle for the soul's powers.</note>. Since, therefore, both—namely the odor and the spirit—are a kind of vapor, and like is nourished by like, it is no wonder that both the spirit and the "spiritual" man <note>The scholar or person of refined temperament.</note> receive a great deal of nourishment from odors. Indeed, whatever kind of nourishment or warming comfort this may be, it is especially necessary for the elderly and the slender, so that we may somehow compensate for the lack of more solid and substantial food.

However, some people are accustomed to doubt whether the spirit is truly nourished by odors. But I am of the opinion that it is perhaps nourished by these alone; for unless thick foods are finally thinned into vapors by digestion, the spirit itself (which we have said is a vapor) would receive no nourishment from them. Therefore, wine full of fragrance immediately restores the spirit, which other things can barely refresh at last. We call that vapor into which cooked foods are finally transformed an "odor," because odor is everywhere a kind of vapor; and this vapor drawn inward from foods [would not be] pleasing to the spirit unless [it were endowed] with a certain fragrance... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "plas" suggests the next word is "placeat" (pleases).</note>

For the smell of honey is not to be despised. Indeed, honey exists as the flower of flowers; it nourishes not a little by its very sweetness, and by its quality it protects whole things from putrefaction for a long time. Wherever you fear a suffocation or an excessive compression of the spirits—which frequent sorrow and lethargy portend—cherish the use of surrounding fragrances. 

However, where you dread the flight of exhaling spirits, you should instead take in odors infused within your nourishment. And if you take any other scents externally, apply them only like a shield to the left ribs <note>The left side was associated with the heart, the seat of the vital spirits</note>. Do you not see how suddenly the womb <note>original: "matrix"; referring to the historical medical belief in the "wandering womb" that responded to scents</note> itself flings itself upward or downward toward odors? How swiftly the spirit flies to the mouth and nostrils, enticed by the bait of a sweet scent? 

Therefore, where the spirit is found to be either meager or very fleeting—which faint-heartedness and bodily weakness often declare, occurring frequently even from a small cause—allure the spirits, or rather feed and retain them, not so much by odors applied from without, but by those injected within. 

Choose the odor of wine above all others. For an odor exhaling from a substance that both nourishes the body most abundantly and swiftly, and affects the sense with pleasure, greatly nourishes the spirit. Such a wine, above all others, is warm, moist, fragrant, and clear. I would say that sugar is also such a thing, if it should take on a scent. Cinnamon is also similar, as are doronicum <note>Leopard's bane, used historically as a heart tonic</note>, anise, and sweet fennel <note>original: "marathrum"</note>, if they were to add a greater sweetness to their sharpness. But what temperament nature...

And so that I do not entice you here with smells alone, I instruct you to compose an electuary <note>term: electuarium; a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> to be tasted every day in the morning, sweet in smell and taste, and extremely beneficial to life. Crush them diligently. Add as much rose-sugar as satisfies the taste, and as much red sandalwood as is enough for color; likewise honey...

From this, he asserts that life has been known to be extended even for those who are almost at the point of death. In every *tryphera*, the myrobalan is the foundation, but they temper this with certain subtle and soft substances—especially when the myrobalan is drier—so that it may penetrate, not obstruct the passages, nor excessively dry out or constrict the bowels. Furthermore, we use it most conveniently with wine, but in a moderate amount, lest it be diluted too much. As for the composition of Peter which I just mentioned, if it is indeed useful, I judge it to be more beneficial by smell than by drink.

->The medicine of the Magi for the elderly.<-
### Chapter XIX.

The Magi, observers of the stars, came to Christ—the leader of life—under the guidance of a star. They offered a precious treasure of life: Gold, frankincense, and myrrh, dedicating three gifts representing the three lords of the Planets to the Lord of the stars. Gold was offered for the temperament of Jupiter <note>Ficino associates Jupiter with the "vital spirit" and perfect balance</note>, as it is the most balanced of all things. Frankincense was for the Sun, as it is especially burning with both Solar heat and fragrance. Finally, myrrh—which strengthens and preserves the body—was for Saturn, the most firm and enduring of all the Planets. Therefore, come here to the wise Magi, all you elderly people, bringing gifts that will also prolong your life, the same gifts with which they are said to have once worshipped the Author of life. Come, I say, you elderly who endure old age with difficulty. Come also, you whom the dread of approaching old age disturbs. Receive, I pray, these vital gifts with alacrity. Take two ounces of frankincense, one of myrrh, and half a drachm of gold beaten into leaves. Crush these three together, melt them, and mix them into pills with a certain golden, pure wine <note>original: "aureo quodam mero"</note>. Prepare this at the opportune time when Diana <note>The Moon</note> rejoices in a favorable aspect with Apollo <note>The Sun</note> or Jupiter. After this, take a small portion of this great treasure at every dawn, and wash it down with a small drink of pure wine, unless perhaps it is the heat of summer. For then it is better to drink rose water. If, however, any among you feels heat at any time—

### *On avoiding the dangers looming from every seventh year of life. Chapter XX.*

Since astronomers have distributed the individual hours of the day to the individual planets in order, and similarly the seven days of the week, and have even assigned the duties of the planets by months during the development of the fetus itself, why should we not also arrange these same things by years? Just as <term>Saturn</term> ruled the infant hiding in the womb in the first month, and the <term>Moon</term> in the last; so, once the child is born, the order is reversed: let the Moon lead in the first year of life; in the second, if you please, <term>Mercury</term>; in the third, <term>Venus</term>; in the fourth, the <term>Sun</term>; in the fifth, <term>Mars</term>; in the sixth, <term>Jupiter</term>; and in the seventh, Saturn. And thereafter, a similar order is repeated throughout life. Therefore, in every seventh year of life, a very great change occurs in the body, and it is for that reason most dangerous, since Saturn is generally a stranger to us <note>original: "peregrinus"; in astrology, a planet is "peregrine" when it has no essential dignity in its current position, often weakening its influence.</note> and the governance then returns immediately from that highest of planets down to the Moon, the lowest of the planets. The Greek astronomers call these the <term>Climacteric years</term><note>Critical periods or "turning points" in a person's life, believed to occur in multiples of seven or nine.</note>.

<margin>Judiciary years.</margin>
For this reason, every seventh year is called "Judiciary" <note>Also known as a climacteric year, believed to be a period of great change or danger.</note> for the same reason. The fourth year is also included, since it holds the middle position in the seven-year cycle. Therefore, if you desire to extend your life to old age, uninterrupted by any such "steps," consult an astrologer diligently whenever you approach any seventh year. Learn from where the danger threatens you; then, either visit a physician or summon your own prudence and temperance. For even Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> admits that the threats of the stars can be averted by these remedies. He even adds that the promises of the stars can be increased just as a farmer increases the fertility of the earth. Pietro d'Abano <note>A 13th-century physician and astrologer known for reconciling Greek and Arabic science with Christianity.</note> proves through many arguments and the testimony of Aristotle, Galen, and Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a 11th-century Arab astrologer.</note> that the natural end of life is not precisely determined from the beginning, but can be moved further away or brought closer. He asserts this based both on the stars and on physical matter. He concludes, by these authors and reasons, that even a natural death can be postponed, both by the mechanisms of astrology and the protections of physicians. Therefore, we do not labor over these precepts in vain. Do not be reluctant to inquire of physicians what your natural diet should be, and of astrologers which star favors your life. When that star is well-positioned, and the Moon is aligned with it, prepare those things you have learned will benefit you. Nor should you be ashamed to listen often to those who [succeed] not so much by fortune as by virtue...

# ON PROLONGING LIFE. BOOK II.

> To Phoebus and Bacchus belongs eternal youth,
> For unshorn hair befits both gods. <note>original: "Solis æterna eſt Phœbo Bacchoq; iuuentus, Nam decet intonſus crinis utrunq; deum." A reference to their perpetual vitality.</note>

Phoebus <note>Apollo, representing the Sun</note> and Bacchus <note>Dionysius, representing wine and life-force</note> are always inseparable brothers; both are almost the same. Phoebus is indeed the very soul of that celestial sphere. The sphere itself is Bacchus; or rather, Phoebus is the entire circuit of the sphere. Bacchus, however, is that flaming circle within this circuit; or better yet, Phoebus is the nourishing light in this flaming globe. Bacchus exists in that same place as the health-giving heat derived from the light. Therefore, they are always brothers and companions, almost always one and the same. What else? If the Sun in Springtime is indeed Phoebus, awakening the songs of birds with his own song, and again tempering the seasons with his lyre; then in Autumn, the same Sun exists as Bacchus, the author of wine.

# ON PROLONGING LIFE, BOOK II.

That father **Bacchus** <note>original: "Liber," an Italian deity identified with the Greek Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, who loves the hills, brings three things to us for the preservation of our youth. First, these very sunny hills. Second, upon these hills, the most delightful wine. Third, a lasting sense of security found within that wine. **Apollo** <note>original: "Phœbus"</note>, the brother of Bacchus, bestows three gifts with equal kindness. First, the light of day. Second, under the warmth of that light, sweet-smelling herbs. Third, in the shade of this light, the lyre and perennial song. With these tasks especially, and with these threads, **Clotho** <note>The Fate who spins the thread of life</note>—no longer a "Parca" <note>A play on words: "Parca" is the name for a Fate, but also means "sparing" or "stingy"</note> to us—will extend the long threads of our life. *Almost all poets sing of the three Fates. We too, though not poets, sing of three things. Indeed, a prudent moderation in all sustenance begins a long life for us. A constant moderation in undergoing cares also extends life. But a moderation that is negligent in enjoying the heavens cuts life short.* <note>The author uses "parcitas" (frugality/moderation) to contrast with the "Parcae" (Fates)</note> **Pythagoras celebrates three temperances above all things; we also celebrate three in this present moment. Maintain temperance in your emotions; maintain temperance in all your diet. Observe the temperance of the air.** For by this foresight, and with God’s favor, you will drive far away the imbalance of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to govern health</note>, which is the cause of rapid old age and untimely death. Moreover, the Author of Life will breathe upon you if you desire a long life only on the condition that you live longer for the sake of the human race, and especially that you live for Him, by whose inspiration the whole world lives.

# MARSILIO FICINO THE FLOREN-
### tine’s epistolary preface to the third book, *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, addressed to the most serene King of Pannonia <note>Matthias Corvinus, the King of Hungary and Bohemia, known as a great patron of the arts and sciences.</note>.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a classical figure (possibly a philosopher or deity) standing amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

The ancient philosophers, O most happy King of all, having most diligently scrutinized the powers of the heavenly bodies and the natures of inferior things, believed that a man is wise in vain who is not wise for his own benefit. They seem, therefore, to have rightly directed their entire investigation primarily toward obtaining life for themselves from the heavens. They judged (as I believe) that the elements and the things composed from them would be known to them in vain, and the movements and influences of the heavens observed with too much rashness, unless these things—known and joined together—should eventually lead them toward life and happiness. 

Furthermore, such contemplation seems to have benefited them first in this present life. For Pythagoras, Democritus, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>original: "Apollonius Theanaeus"; a Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the 1st century AD.</note>, and whoever else applied themselves chiefly to this study, achieved prosperous health and a long-lived life through the use of the things they had learned. It contributed, moreover, to their future life, both by spreading their glory among posterity and by enjoying the presence of God in eternity. Indeed, from the marvelous order of the entire world, they finally came to know its Ruler, and above all else, they loved Him once He was known. To you, indeed, glory shall remain through all ages, O magnanimous...

<summary>This preface introduces Book III of Ficino's "De Vita," arguing that ancient philosophers studied the heavens not for abstract knowledge, but to practically improve their health, longevity, and spiritual connection to the Divine.</summary>

I pray, most merciful King, that you embrace this Valor of ours. For your nature, virtue, and authority are so great that without you, even Valor himself cannot prevail.

July 10, 1489. Florence.

### AN EXHORTATION BY MARSILIO FICINO TO THE
### reader of the following book.

Greetings, talented guest. Greetings again, whoever you are that hungers for health <note>original: "salutis"; can mean both physical health and spiritual salvation</note> and makes your way toward our threshold. I pray you, eager guest, see first how hospitable I am: It was certainly the duty of the one entering to offer a greeting to the house immediately; yet I, anticipating your greeting, have bid you welcome as soon as you came into view. I have most gladly received you as you enter, even while you are yet unknown. To you who linger a while with me, I shall grant the promised health (if God breathes favor upon us). You have therefore found a lodging that is friendly to all, and now full of love toward you. If by chance you carry anything with you contrary to love, if you hold any hatred, I pray you lay it down before you touch these life-giving medicines. For love and the pleasure of your parents gave you life; in turn, hatred and pain take life away. Therefore, for the man whom hateful pain vexes, no place remains anywhere for life-giving Medicine. For this reason, I no longer address you merely as a guest, but as a friend. The workshop <term>officina: a laboratory or apothecary's shop where medicines are prepared</term> of your Marsilio is somewhat larger than can be confined merely by these boundaries you see here. For it is not circumscribed by this following book alone, but also by the two preceding ones. Indeed, the whole work in summary is a certain Medicine intended to assist life according to its powers, so that your life may be strong and long-lasting. And everywhere it strives for this by the help of physicians, aided from heaven. Truly, this workshop of ours offers various antidotes, drugs, heat-treatments, ointments, and remedies for

# EXHORTATION TO THE READER

...bears. If perhaps some things please you less, set those aside, but do not reject the rest on that account. Finally, if you do not approve of **astronomical images** <note>original: "imagines Astronomicas"; these were talismans or amulets engraved with celestial symbols intended to capture planetary power</note>, which were otherwise devised for the sake of mortal health—and which I myself do not so much approve of as describe—then by all means, with my permission and even my advice if you wish, leave them be. By this kind of diligence, he was seen to be restored to life by us—or rather by God—rather than merely saved; he has now completed nearly three years in good health. Now, if I were to recount more instances of this same kind, I would be speaking the truth. I offer these things not boastfully (which is entirely foreign to a philosopher) but rather by way of encouragement.

*In what, according to Plotinus, the power of attracting favor from the heavens consists: namely, in the fact that the Soul of the World <note>Latin: anima mundi; the vital spirit connecting the universe</note> and the souls of the stars and demons are easily enticed by forms of bodies that are made suitable to them.*

### CHAPTER ONE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring two figures in Renaissance-style clothing (green and red) seated and engaged in conversation or study within a garden or landscape setting.</image-desc>

If there were only these two things in the world—on one side the Intellect <note>The realm of pure divine thought</note> and on the other the body—but the Soul were absent: then neither would the Intellect be drawn to the body (for it is entirely motionless and lacks the impulse of motion, being as far distant from the body as possible), nor would the body be drawn to the Intellect, as it is by itself ineffective and unfit for motion, and far removed from the Intellect. But if a Soul is placed between them, being conformable to both, an attraction will easily occur from both sides toward the other. In the first place, the Soul itself is led most easily of all, since it is the primary thing capable of motion <note>Latin: primum mobile; the first moved mover</note>, and moves of its own accord and spontaneously...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces the concept of the World Soul as the essential intermediary that connects the divine Intellect to the physical body, allowing celestial influences to affect the material world. He argues that without the Soul, the spiritual and physical realms would remain entirely separate and unable to interact.</summary>

# ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS
### BY MARSILIO FICINO

->Page 518<-

Furthermore, since the Soul is (as I have said) the middle point of all things, it contains all things within itself in its own manner, and is closely related to both sides by its very nature. Therefore, it is reconciled to all things—even equally to those things which are distant from one another—because they are clearly not distant from the Soul itself. For besides the fact that it is on one side conformed to divine things, and on the other to perishable things, and inclines toward both by its affection, it is meanwhile entirely and simultaneously everywhere. Added to this is the fact that the World Soul possesses at least as many <term>seminal reasons</term><note>original: "rationes seminales"; these are the "seeds" or formative blueprints in the Soul that translate abstract Ideas into physical matter</note> of things by divine gift as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind. By these reasons, the Soul itself fashions just as many species in matter. 

Hence, every single species corresponds specifically to an Idea through its own seminal reason, and through this reason, it can often easily receive something from that higher source, since it was created from there by means of this very reason. Therefore, if at any time a thing should degenerate from its proper form, it can be formed again through this intermediary which is closest to it; and through that medium, it can be easily reformed from above. This is certainly the case if you rightly apply many things which are scattered, yet conform to the same Idea, to a certain species of thing or to an individual member of it. Soon, into this matter which has been so opportunely prepared, you will draw a singular gift from the Idea through the seminal reason of the Soul. 

<margin>
Each individual species is allotted its own Ideas.
</margin>

For it is not the Intellect itself that is properly drawn down, but the Soul. Therefore, let no one think that by certain worldly materials, specific divine powers <note>original: "numina"</note> are drawn down that are entirely segregated from matter; rather, it is <term>daemons</term><note>In the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or energies, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> that are drawn, or rather the gifts of the animate world and of the living stars. Again, let no one marvel that the Soul can be, as it were, enticed through material forms.

Indeed, the Soul itself has created the kinds of food suitable to it by which it might be enticed, and it always and willingly dwells within them. Nor is there anything found in the entire living world so deformed that it lacks a soul, or is devoid of the soul's function. Therefore, Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, often cited in the Renaissance as a source of "primeval" wisdom.</note> called these harmonies of forms—aligned with the principles of the World Soul—"divine lures," which Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and bishop known for his writings on dreams and magic.</note> also confirmed were magical enticements. Finally, let no one believe that all gifts are drawn from the Soul into a specific type of matter at a certain time; rather, as opportunity allows, only the gifts of the seed from which such a species sprouted, and the fellowship of those seeds, are drawn. Thus, a human being, by employing only human things, does not claim for himself the specific qualities of fish or birds, but rather human and similar qualities. However, by employing things that pertain to a particular star and its spirit <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or celestial intelligence, not necessarily evil</term>, one undergoes the specific influence <note>original: "influxum"</note> of that star and spirit, just as wood prepared with sulfur catches a flame that is present everywhere. And this happens not only through the rays of the star and spirit themselves, but also through the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> which is present everywhere, in which the principle of every star and spirit flourishes: partly as a "seminal" principle for generating, and partly as an "exemplary" principle for knowing. For according to the older Platonists, the Soul built figures in the heavens beyond the stars according to its own principles, and impressed properties upon all of them. In the stars, moreover, in the figures, the parts, and the properties...

In these [the heavens], all species of lower things and their properties are contained. He <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or an ancient authority previously cited</note> established forty-eight universal figures: namely, twelve in the zodiac,

<margin>The division of the Zodiac.</margin>

and thirty-six outside of it. Likewise, in the zodiac, there are thirty-six according to the number of the "faces" <note>A "face" or decan is a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note>. Again, in the same place, there are three hundred and sixty according to the number of degrees. For in every degree there are many stars, from which images are constructed there. Similarly, he divided the images outside the zodiac into many figures according to the number of their own faces and degrees. Finally, he established certain relationships and proportions from these universal images to other universal images, which themselves also exist there as images. Figures of this kind each have their own continuity from the rays of their stars cast into one another by a certain peculiar property. From these most highly ordered forms, the forms of lower things depend, being clearly ordered from that source. But even those celestial forms, though seemingly disjointed among themselves, proceed from the "reasons" <note>term: rationes (seminal reasons) — the spiritual blueprints or formative powers within the World Soul</note> of the Soul which are joined together, and being in a certain way changeable, they proceed from stable things. But these, insofar as they do not comprehend themselves, are referred back to the forms in the Mind—whether in the Soul's mind or a higher one—which do comprehend themselves; these, being manifold, are reduced to the most simple One and Good, just as the celestial figures are reduced to the pole. But let us return to the Soul. These are provided not so much by the aid of celestial forms and figures, but rather by the position of the stars, the nature of their motions, and the aspects of the planets, both among themselves and in relation to the stars higher than the planets. *Indeed, our own soul, beyond the specific powers of individual limbs, brings forth a common power of life everywhere within us. It does this especially through the heart, which acts as the source of the fire closest to the soul. Similarly, the World Soul, flourishing everywhere, unfolds its common power of life throughout the universe, primarily through the Sun. For this reason, some scholars place the soul—both in ourselves and in the world—entirely in every limb, yet principally in the heart and the Sun. Always remember, however, that just as the power of our soul is applied to our limbs through the <term>spirit<note>Latin: spiritus; in Renaissance medicine, this was a subtle vapor that linked the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note></term>, so the power of the World Soul is spread through all things by the <term>fifth essence<note>Latin: quinta essentia; also known as the ether or the quintessence, the pure substance of the heavens.</note></term>, which flourishes everywhere like a spirit within the body of the world. This power is infused most greatly into those things which have drawn in the most of this spirit. Furthermore, this fifth essence can be taken into ourselves more and more if one knows how to separate it when it is mixed with other elements, or at least if one frequently uses those things which abound in it—especially in its purer form. # MARSILIO FICINO: ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

### On the harmony of the world, and on the nature of man according to the stars. How an attraction is made from each individual star. Chapter II.

Indeed, no one ought to distrust that we, and all things which are around us, are able to claim for ourselves celestial things through certain preparations. For these things were made by the heavens and are continually ruled by them, and from that source they were primarily prepared for those celestial ends. And what is most important: the world is a living being <note>original: "animal"; Ficino refers to the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, a concept where the universe itself is alive and interconnected</note> that is more truly "one" within itself than any other living being, provided it is the most perfect of beings. 

Therefore, just as in us the quality and motion of any member—especially a principal one—pertains to the others, so the actions of the principal members in the world move all things; and the lower members easily receive from the highest ones, which are ready to give of their own accord. For the more powerful a cause is, the more ready it is to act, and therefore the more inclined it is to give. Thus, a small amount of preparation applied by us is sufficient for receiving the gifts of the heavens, provided that each person accommodates himself chiefly to that star to which he is primarily subject. 

But before considering the individual property of each of us, we must consider the property of the human species. The Arabian astrologers <note>Ficino frequently cites Arabic authorities like Al-Kindi or Albumasar, who preserved and expanded Greek astrological knowledge</note> agreed that this species is Solar. I judge this to be true from the erect and beautiful stature of man, from the subtle humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</note> and the clarity of the spirit, from the perspicuity of the imagination, and from the pursuit of truth and glory; truly...

<summary>Ficino argues that the universe is a single living organism (the World Soul), allowing humans to attract celestial influences through proper preparation, and identifies the human species as being primarily governed by the Sun.</summary>

...I conjecture these things to be so. Furthermore, I add to this a **Mercurial** <note>Referring to the qualities of the planet Mercury: agility, intellect, and communication</note> property, on account of the vigorous movement of a versatile mind. And since the human race is born naked, unarmed, and destitute of all things, it acquires all these necessities through its own industry, which is the specific characteristic of Mercury. I also add a **Jovial** <note>Referring to Jupiter: associated with law, temperance, and growth</note> property, on account of the tempered constitution of the body and the influence of laws. This is also because in the second month of gestation, over which Jupiter rules, we receive life; and we are born in the ninth month, when he again resumes his dominion. Therefore, the human species will finally be able to claim even more ample gifts from these three planets <note>The Sun, Mercury, and Jupiter</note> if it adapts itself more and more every day to them through Solar, Mercurial, and Jovial practices. 

But what of the remaining planets? **Saturn** does not easily signify the common quality and lot of the human race, but rather a man set apart from others—either divine or brutish, blessed or weighed down by extreme misery. **Mars**, the **Moon**, and **Venus** signify the passions and actions that humans share equally with all other living creatures. Let us therefore return to the Sun, Jupiter, and Mercury. We have already mentioned several Solar and Jovial things, but somehow we overlooked the Mercurial ones. They are of this sort: Tin <note>original: "Stannum"</note>, Silver, especially Quicksilver <note>Mercury/Liquid silver</note>, silver Marcasite <note>A brittle mineral with a metallic luster</note>, the Agate stone, Porphyritic glass, and things that mix saffron-yellow with green, such as emerald and lac <note>A resinous secretion used for dyes or varnishes</note>. Also, animals that are wise and ingenious as well as vigorous, such as monkeys and dogs; and men who are eloquent, sharp, and versatile—

# COMPARISONS BOOK III.

Do not doubt that Saturn possesses something of gold within himself. For it is believed he possesses it on account of his weight. Furthermore, gold is similar to the Sun; just as it exists in all metals, so the Sun exists in all Planets and stars. Now truly, if anyone should argue that Saturn and Mars are harmful by nature—which I for my part would never believe—nevertheless, these too must be utilized just as Physicians sometimes use poisons, which Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, an influential 2nd-century astronomer and astrologer</note> proves in his *Centiloquium* <note>original: "Centiloquio"; a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note>. Therefore, the power of Saturn, when taken cautiously, will occasionally be beneficial, just as Physicians use substances that bind and contain, or even those that induce stupor, such as Opium and Mandrake; likewise the power of Mars is used like spurge <note>original: "euphorbium"</note> and hellebore. 

The most cautious in this matter seem to have been the Magi, the Brahmans <note>original: "Brachmanes"; ancient Indian philosophers</note>, and the Pythagoreans. Since they feared the tyranny of Saturn due to their diligent pursuit of philosophy, they clothed themselves in white garments and daily employed Jovial <note>pertaining to Jupiter</note> or Phoebian <note>pertaining to the Sun/Apollo</note> sounds and songs, and lived mostly under the open sky. Truly, remember that everywhere, through the affection and pursuit

Through civil and ambitious business, through natural and common philosophy...

*...the medium within us, and then strengthened by the spirit of the world: from there, indeed, through the rays of the stars acting happily upon our spirit—which is similar in nature to those rays—it then fits itself to the heavenly things.*

->*Chapter III. That between the soul of the world and its body there is clearly its spirit, in whose power are the four elements: and that we can draw this in through our own spirit.*<-

Certainly, the worldly body—as is apparent from its motion and generation—is alive everywhere, which the Indian philosophers <note>Ficino likely refers to ancient accounts of Gymnosophists or general Eastern wisdom regarding spontaneous generation.</note> prove by the fact that it generates living things from itself in every place. Therefore, it lives through a soul that is present everywhere within it and is perfectly adapted to it. Thus, between the tangible and partially perishable body of the world, and its soul itself—whose nature is too distant from such a body—there exists everywhere a spirit, just as there is between the soul and the body in us; provided that life is everywhere and always communicated by the soul to the denser body. This breath is properly drawn in by a human being through their own spirit, which is by its very nature conformable to that world-spirit. This is especially true if the human spirit is rendered even more kindred by art—that is, if it becomes as celestial as possible.

<margin>

Indeed, the spirit becomes celestial if it is purged of filth, and entirely of those things which cling to it that are unlike the heavens. Such filth, if present not only within the internal organs but even in the mind, on the skin, in clothes, or in one's dwelling and the air, frequently infects the spirit. It will finally be made celestial if it creates its own orbits in imitation of the circular motion of the mind and body; if it glows red by more frequent gazing upon and contemplation of the light; and if things similar to the heavens are applied to it with that same diligence by which Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher (980–1037 AD)</note> cares for the spirit in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*. We also strove to provide such care in our book *On Caring for the Health of Scholars*. In that work, first, clouding vapors are separated from the spirit by purging medicines. Second, it is illuminated by shining things. Third, it is cultivated so that it is simultaneously refined and strengthened. Finally, it will become celestial to the highest degree—as far as present reason dictates—if the rays and influences of the Sun are applied to it above all...

From these three Graces of heaven <note>Ficino identifies the three Graces with the planets Venus, Sol (the Sun), and Jupiter</note>, and from stars of the same kind, astrologers both hope for and diligently seek out favors. They believe and arrange for these favors to be transmitted through Mercury and the Moon, acting as messengers; they believe this happens easily and commonly through the Moon. Indeed, they consider the Moon to be more fortunate when joined with Jupiter or Venus than if she views them through a sextile or trine aspect <note>A "sextile" is an astrological angle of 60 degrees, and a "trine" is 120 degrees; both are considered harmonious alignments</note>. The same applies if she is beheld by the Sun and received at the same time.

However, if we wished to run through all the powers and effects of these three and of similar stars one by one, we would be undertaking a long task, difficult to investigate and most difficult to observe. If we apply ourselves specifically to Venus, we do not easily have the Sun; if specifically to the Sun, we do not easily have Venus. Therefore, so that we may embrace the three Graces at once in one, we shall finally take refuge in Jupiter. He is the middle ground between the Sun and Venus in both nature and effect, being quite tempered in quality. Whatever is hoped for from Venus or from the Sun, he delivers in his own certain way—more magnificently and honorably than **Venus**, and more temperately than the **Sun**—and he is, in all things, most congruent with human nature. We shall therefore make use of Jupiter when both he and the Moon possess both natural and accidental dignity <note>In astrology, "dignity" refers to a planet's strength based on its position in the zodiac</note>, and when they are together or viewing each other favorably. It will truly be worthwhile to remember that the daily course of the Moon is divided into four quarters. In the first quarter, it ascends from the East to the middle of the sky <note>the midheaven or zenith</note>, and during this time it increases the <term>moisture and natural spirit</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" refers to the subtle fluids that carry life and sensation through the body.</note>. In the third, it goes from the West to the point below the middle of the sky <note>the nadir</note>, and again increases that spirit and moisture. In the fourth, it falls from there toward the East, and diminishes them in turn. This is most apparent on the shores of the ocean, where the sea visibly advances and recedes according to this course; in the same order, vigor fluctuates in the sick. It is also probable that the Sun, through its own identical quarters, increases or diminishes the natural heat and vital spirit—and the animal spirit as well, insofar as it has Mercury as its companion. Once these things are known, the physician will be able to observe the more opportune times for restoring moisture, natural heat, and any spirit whatsoever. 

But enough has been said of the Moon for now. Nor is it fitting to dismiss Jupiter, in whose second month we received life, and in whose other month we were commonly and more happily born. He is the one who stands between the Sun and Venus, and likewise between the Sun and the Moon, as a mediator in quality and effect, and therefore he embraces all things. Indeed, we consider it a wicked and dangerous thing to omit the Sun itself, the lord of the heavens—unless perhaps someone should say that he who possesses Jupiter...

However, although we observe the Moon especially in relation to the Sun when we greatly fear phlegm <term>pituitam: one of the four bodily humors associated with cold and moisture</term>, and in relation to Venus when we fear bile and similar dryness, nevertheless the direction of the Moon toward Jupiter contributes in some way to all these things. It is especially useful for expelling black bile <term>atra bilis: the humor associated with melancholy</term>, as well as for restoring and strengthening the general constitution <term>complexionem: the balance of the four humors in an individual</term> of men. 

For just as licorice <note>original: "glycyrrhiza"</note> and rose oil warm up colder things and cool down warmer things—and wine acts similarly, which moreover moistens dry things and dries out the more humid—so Jupiter is agreeable to human heat, like wine, rose oil, chamomile, and licorice. Therefore, when you hear Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer of the 9th century</note> saying: *There is no life for living things, besides God, except through the Sun and the Moon*, understand that as far as it regards the influence common to all things. However, the influence most proper and most suitable to man is from Jupiter. Furthermore, there are in the nature of the body powers of attracting, retaining, digesting, and expelling. All of these, therefore, Jupiter himself assists. Especially...

# MARSILIO FICINO: ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

Indeed, the power of cooking—or rather, digesting—as well as the power of generating, nourishing, and increasing all at once, is due to its <note>Jupiter's</note> airy and abundant moisture, and its ample heat which moderately dominates that same moisture. Truly, through the rays of Jupiter which are always diffused everywhere, the Sun's own light is greatly tempered for the health of mankind; meanwhile, the rays of Venus constantly contribute to the same end, with the Moon transferring these influences in a similar way. 

The rays of Venus and the Moon, being somewhat more humid, require a tempering agent, just as the rays of the Sun, being hotter, demand the temperament of something more moist. The rays of Jupiter, however, desire no tempering at all. For what else is Jupiter but a certain "Sun" that was tempered from the beginning specifically for the health of things, especially human affairs? What else is he, again, but a Moon and Venus made hotter and more powerful? 

Therefore, Astrologers look to Jupiter to herald a fertile, serene, and healthy year, and from him they hope for remedies against imminent diseases. And Empedocles, when he attributed specific gifts to each of the planets, named Jupiter alone as the prince of generation, imitating Orpheus. 

<margin>

</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII.

Astrologers <note>original: "Astrologi"</note> report that certain major stars discovered by Mercury possess the greatest authority. Such is the Navel of Andromeda <note>the star Mirach</note> at the 22nd degree of Aries, which partakes of the nature of Mercury and Venus. Likewise, at the 18th degree of Taurus is the Head of Algol, possessing the nature of Saturn and Jupiter. They believe the Diamond and Mugwort <note>original: "artemisiam"</note> are subject to this star, and that it grants boldness and victory. At the 22nd degree of the same sign are the Pleiades, a lunar and martial constellation. To this they subject Crystal, the herb *diacedon*, and Fennel seed. They believe these contribute to sharpening the eyesight. However, as for what some say regarding their usefulness for summoning demons, I judge that to be a fiction. Aldebaran, at the 1st or 3rd degree of Gemini, is of the nature of Mars and Venus. Capella <note>original: "Hircus," the Goat star</note>, at the 13th degree of the same sign, is of Jupiter and Saturn. To this they subject Sapphire, Chrysoprase, Mint, Mugwort, and Mandrake. They trust it helps in attaining dignity and the favor of princes, unless perhaps their opinion deceives them. To this star <note>referring to the influence of Sirius/Canis Major mentioned hereafter</note> they wish the Ruby, Spurge, and Honeysuckle to be subject, increasing riches and glory. In the 6th or 7th degree of Cancer, the Greater Dog Star <note>Sirius</note> is of the nature of Venus; it presides over Beryl, Savin, Mugwort, and Dragonwort. It grants favor. Likewise, at the 17th degree of the same sign is the Lesser Dog Star <note>Procyon</note>, of the nature of Mercury and Mars. Indeed, Iarchas <note>The leader of the Indian Brahmans in the life of Apollonius of Tyana</note> told Apollonius that his own grandfather, a philosopher, had lived for one hundred and thirty years, perhaps relying on a heavenly gift of this kind. However, as for the promise that these rings will be effective against demons or enemies, or for gaining the favor of princes, this is either a fiction or it is derived from the fact that they make the spirit fearless and firm, or even gentle, lovable in its obedience, and gracious. Now truly, if I were to say that celestial things—beyond physical health—contribute anything to one's natural talent, art, or fortune, I would not be in disagreement with our Thomas Aquinas <margin>Saint Thomas.</margin> <note>original: "Diuus Thomas"</note>, who proves in the third book of his work *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra Gentiles"</note> that something is imprinted upon our bodies by the celestial bodies. Jupiter holds a <term>triplicity</term><note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element.</note> in the fiery and airy signs. The Sun in the fiery only; Mercury in the airy only. Mars, Venus, and the Moon in the watery and earthy signs. For one must return to him once the number of planets has been completed. In Gemini, the first is of Jupiter, evidently following Saturn; the second of Mars, the third of the Sun in the same order, and so on similarly thereafter.

When a planet holds lordship in our revolution <note>The "solar return" or annual renewal of the birth chart</note> and birth, even planets like **Saturn** and **Mars**—which we would otherwise seek to suppress—must instead be elevated by us if they happen to be the significators <note>The specific planets that represent the individual's life or body</note> of our birth. We shall, however, perform a task especially worth the effort based on this reminder: whenever we intend to use the benefit of the **Moon**, **Venus**, and **Jupiter** in the preparation of medicines, we must take care that they do not reside within the "terms" <note>Specific degrees of a zodiac sign ruled by a particular planet</note> of **Saturn** or **Mars**. The exception is when we are compelled either to restrain a physical dissolution and repress a feverish heat through **Saturn**, or to warm the coldest things and rouse the sluggish through **Mars**. Otherwise, we shall choose the terms of **Jupiter** and **Venus**. We shall also accept the terms of **Mercury**, which are primarily beneficial to "Mercurial" men. Nor should it escape our notice that men who are strongly Mercurial—such as those who excel in talent, craftsmanship, and eloquence—are also Solar to no small degree. <margin>The establishment of the Houses.</margin>
The sign which rises from the East we call the first house, the house of life. That which follows into the ascent is the second; then the third, and the others likewise; so that the seventh house is the sign which, now descending in the West, is opposite the one ascending. The eighth follows this. The ninth falls away from the Midheaven <note>original: "medium coeli"</note>, which constitutes the tenth house. The eleventh follows this. But the twelfth falls away from the Ascendant. Therefore, for the Planets to be powerful, they must be held in the "angles" <note>The four most powerful points in a chart: East, West, Midheaven, and Lower Heaven</note> of either the East, the West, or the Midheaven at either end.

<margin>It is beneficial to take care to strengthen the spirits under their respective Planets.</margin>

The spirit <note>The 'spiritus' in Renaissance medicine was a thin vapor or fluid that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the material body</note> flows out, pours forth, and is transferred entirely in a Venereal <note>Influenced by the planet Venus</note> manner; it propagates offspring, expands itself toward the pleasure of any sense whatsoever, and flees from pain. In summary, however, insofar as the spirit contributes to the body for life, motion, and propagation, it is considered Jovial <note>Influenced by Jupiter</note>, Venereal, and Solar. Insofar as it serves the soul for sensation and imagination, it is judged to be Solar and Mercurial; indeed, it is Mercurial everywhere. Since it is so mobile and so easily convertible and formable, a healthy spirit commonly does not possess much of the nature of Saturn, Mars, or the Moon. Otherwise, from the former <insert>Saturn</insert> it would often become stupid; from the second <insert>Mars</insert> it would become furious; and from the latter <insert>the Moon</insert> it would be, in a certain way, dulled. For this reason, Lunar things—being thicker and at the same time more humid—are quite foreign to the subtle and volatile nature of the spirit. Those things which are greatly Saturnine, or excessively Martial, are like poisons, naturally hostile to the spirit: the former because of extreme coldness and dryness, the latter because of dryness and a consuming heat. Therefore, the nature of the spirit is judged to be Jovial and Solar first of all, then Mercurial, and in a certain way Venereal. 

By a specific distinction, the **natural spirit** <note>The spirit responsible for nutrition and growth, centered in the liver</note> is properly dedicated to Jupiter; the **vital spirit** <note>The spirit responsible for heat and life-force, centered in the heart</note> to the Sun; and the **animal spirit** <note>The spirit responsible for thought and sensation, centered in the brain</note> to Mercury. Therefore, when the situation requires helping one of these three spirits, you will not easily be able to assist the little "client" if its patron planet is unfortunate or weak. It is truly more difficult to help the animal spirit while Mercury is unhappily [situated]...

There is a similar reasoning and distinction regarding odors, for these are the brothers of tastes. A similar rule applies to colors. Truly, colors that are watery, white, green, somewhat saffron-colored, and similar to the colors of violets, roses, and lilies—as well as odors of that kind—reflect Venus, and the Moon, and Mercury. But colors of sapphire, which are also called airy; likewise fuller purples, and golds mixed with silver, and those that are perpetually green, reflect Jupiter. Burning saffron colors, pure golds, and the clearer purples reflect the Sun. Indeed, any colors, if they are vivid or at least silky, are more "stellar" in nature. They are also powerful in metals, stones, and glasses because of their celestial similarity. But to return to Jupiter: its taste and smell are like those found in a golden peach, a similar pear, or an orange, and in a lighter Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, fortified wine</note>, or a light Vernaccia. It is like the taste in green ginger, or cinnamon, or sweet fennel <note>original: "marathro"</note>, or leopard's bane <note>original: "doronico"</note>, if these are tasted when preserved with plenty of sugar. For these four, and fresh nutmeg, if they are alone, are rather of the Sun; the clove <note>original: "chariophylus"</note> and musk are also of the Sun, but in their scent, not in their taste or appearance. Saffron is Solar in all respects, even though its color and scent are dedicated by the Astrologers to all the Graces. Its flavor, however, belongs properly to the Sun. Finally, all things that are fragrant and aromatic—insofar as they bring a pleasing scent—belong to Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury as much as to the Sun; although among these, the sharper scents belong more to the Sun, while the more dull or faint scents belong rather to Venus and Mercury. To Jupiter belong those things that are properly tempered in smell, taste, hearing, sight, and touch. Furthermore, sounds and songs that are pleasing and gentle look toward all the Graces and Mercury; but those that are quite threatening or mournful display the influence of Mars and Saturn.

Do not wonder that we attribute so much to colors, odors, and voices. For while flavors belong chiefly to the *natural spirit* <note>The "natural spirit" was thought to govern digestion and metabolism, centered in the liver</note>, odors belong rather to the *vital* and *animal spirits*. Colors, shapes, and voices belong to the *animal spirit* <note>The "animal spirit" (from 'anima' or soul) was believed to be a fine substance in the brain responsible for sensation and movement</note>. Also, the movement of the mind—whether joyful, or sorrowful, or constant—vehemently agitates the spirit into its own likeness: first the animal spirit, through this the vital spirit, and through this moreover the natural spirit. 

Finally, because all spirit—on account of its nature being in a certain way fiery, airy, entirely luminous, and mobile—is similar to lights, and therefore to colors, airy voices, odors, and movements of the mind, it is therefore suddenly moved and shaped in either direction through these things. And whatever the spirit itself becomes, it in turn produces a similar affection in the mind and a general quality in the body. Lastly, as soon as through those things which are proper to the Graces, a favorable grace...

### That natural and even artificial things possess hidden virtues from the stars, through which they expose our spirit to those same stars. CHAPTER XII.

When we say that the spirit is exposed to favors through those things which belong to the favors <note>original: "gratijs... gratiarum"; here referring to the astrological "graces" or influences bestowed by the heavens</note>, we believe it is accommodated not only through qualities that are seen, heard, smelled, and tasted, but also through those that are touched. <margin>The individual degrees and their parts are allotted to specific Planets.</margin> Remember, therefore, that **Heat** in the first degree belongs to Jupiter; in the second, to the Sun with Jupiter; in the third, to Mars with the Sun; in the fourth, to Mars. **Cold** in the first degree belongs to Venus; in the second, to the Moon; in the third, to the Moon with Saturn; in the fourth, to Saturn. **Moisture** in the first degree belongs to Mercury with Jupiter; in the second, to Venus with the Moon; in the third, to the Moon with Venus; in the fourth, to the Moon when it is joined to Venus and Mercury. **Dryness** in the first degree belongs to Jupiter; in the second, to Mercury with the Sun; in the third, to the Sun with Mars; in the fourth, to Mars with Saturn. In summary, from the qualities of the Planets which Ptolemy describes in the *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "Quadripartito"; the famous four-part work on astrology by Claudius Ptolemy</note>, we gather that the harmony fused from all of them inclines toward heat and moisture. For the immense heat of Mars and the Sun, and the tempered heat of Jupiter, overcomes the immense coldness of Saturn and the slight coldness of Venus and the Moon, so that heat exceeds cold in that arrangement.

# MARSILIO FICINO: ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

Likewise, the moisture of the Moon and Venus—which is abundant, close to us, and tempered by Jupiter—overcomes the great dryness of Saturn and Mars, as well as the tempered dryness of the Sun. Therefore, heat and moisture dominate over cold and dryness, and similarly, heat dominates over moisture. This is just as it is in a man with a healthy body, tempered according to celestial harmony: from the heat and dryness of the heart, the heat and moisture of the liver, and again the cold and moisture of the brain, there grows together a certain <term>complexion</term><note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's physical and mental constitution.</note> tending toward heat and moisture, with heat reigning moderately. For the heat of the heart and liver overcomes the cold of the brain. Likewise, the moisture of the liver and brain exceeds the dryness of the heart.

Indeed, I would not wish us to overlook that there exists among all the fixed stars a common harmony, just as we have described among the planets. For astrologers consider these stars to be similar to the planets. To what end is all this? So that you may remember that our spirit and body—through a certain temperament tending toward heat and moisture, whether established by nature or sought through art—can be accommodated to the heavenly bodies and claim celestial gifts for itself. 

However, we do not say that our spirit is prepared for celestial things solely through the qualities of objects known to the senses, but also, and much more so, through certain <term>properties</term><note>Ficino distinguishes between "manifest qualities" (like hot or cold) and "occult properties," which are hidden powers inherent in things like herbs or stones that act directly on the soul or spirit.</note> implanted in things from heaven; these are hidden from our senses and barely known even to reason. For since such properties and their effects cannot consist of elementary power alone, it follows that they proceed in a unique way from the life and spirit of the world through the very rays of the stars.

<margin>L 5</margin>

...originate, and therefore the spirit is greatly and immediately affected by them, being vehemently exposed to heavenly influxes. For this reason, the emerald, hyacinth <note>likely a blue or orange zircon or sapphire</note>, sapphire, topaz, ruby, and unicorn horn—but especially the stone called *bezoar* <note>a mass found in the digestive system of goats, prized as an antidote</note> among the Arabs—are endowed with hidden properties of grace. Therefore, these substances do not only work when taken internally, but also if they touch the flesh; once warmed there, they bring forth their power and introduce a celestial force into the spirits, by which they defend themselves against the plague and poisons. That these and similar things perform such actions by celestial power is proven by the fact that even when taken in a tiny weight, they have no small importance in their effect. This is scarcely ever granted to an elementary quality, except perhaps to a highly celestial fire. For a material power requires much matter to act greatly; but a formal <note>referring to the "substantial form" or essential nature of a thing in Aristotelian philosophy</note> power is most effective even with the smallest amount of matter.

<margin>Peony heals the falling sickness.</margin>
By a similar power, the Peony—sacred to Apollo—arms the spirits against the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note> when it touches the flesh, by means of a vapor infused into them. Similarly, coral and chalcedony work against the illusions of black bile <note>melancholy or depression</note>, chiefly through the power of Jupiter and Venus; and other things act in a like manner. By a property of this kind, the myrobalan plums <note>an astringent fruit used in medieval medicine</note> preserve youth, sharpen the senses, and benefit the intellect and memory, primarily on account of Jupiter (the temperer of Saturn) and Mercury (the friend of the senses). Indeed, someone might perhaps think that this tree existed in Paradise for the purpose of prolonging life.

They consecrate the Agate stone to Mercury. For this reason, natural philosophers agree that it is effective for eloquence and vision, and acts against poisons. Frankincense supports the vital and animal spirits against dullness, forgetfulness, and fear. Truly, Sage and Mint, by the power of Jupiter—the former puts paralysis to flight, while the latter strengthens the mind even by its scent. By that same power, Cinquefoil <note>original: "Pentaphyllon," meaning five-leaved</note> resists poisons; one of its leaves drunk in wine twice daily cures a one-day fever; three leaves cure a tertian fever; four cure a quartan fever <note>referring to the cycles of malarial fevers</note>. Because of its purity, the ancient priests used this herb in their purification rites. Chasteberry <note>original: "Agnus castus"</note>, by the power of Saturn, halts sexual desire. Jasper, truly, stops the flow of blood. However, wonderful effects are accustomed to arise when a hidden property is served by an elemental property.

Furthermore, images made of wood perhaps possess little power. For wood is perhaps too hard to easily receive celestial influx <note>The flow of spiritual energy from the stars to the earth</note>, and if it does receive it, it is less tenacious in retaining it. Moreover, once it has been torn from the bowels of Mother Earth, it loses almost all the vigor of the world-life shortly thereafter and is easily transformed into another quality. 

However, small stones and metals—even if they seem harder for receiving a celestial gift—nevertheless retain it longer if they have received it, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and divine mysteries</note> confirms. Indeed, by their very hardness, they contain for a very long time after being extracted the traces and gifts of the world-life which they once possessed while clinging to the earth. For this reason at least, they are judged to be suitable materials for grasping and holding celestial things. It is also probable, as I said in the previous book, that things so beautiful <note>referring to precious gems and metals</note> cannot be forged under the earth except by a very great effort of the heavens, and that the virtue once impressed upon them by that effort endures within them.

For in the cooking and refining of these things, the heavens have labored for a very long time. But since you cannot easily assemble many things of this kind, you are compelled to seek out diligently which metal among the rest stands highest in the order of a particular star, or which stone is supreme in that order, so that at the very least, in one supreme example of a whole genus and order, you may grasp the remaining powers according to your ability; and by such a receptacle, you may borrow celestial qualities agreeable to it. 

For example, in the Solar order <note>original: "ordine Solari"</note>, beneath the Solar man <note>original: "homine Phœbeo"; referring to a person born under or embodying the qualities of Apollo/the Sun</note>, the Goshawk or the rooster holds the highest place among animals; among plants, balsam or the laurel; among metals, gold; among stones, the carbuncle <note>a glowing red gemstone, often associated with the ruby or garnet</note> or the *pantaura* <note>a mythical "all-bright" stone said to attract other stones, similar to a magnet but for solar light</note>; among the elements, the glowing air. For fire itself is judged to belong to Mars. However, when we say that the influence of the Sun, Jupiter, or Venus should be increased, we mean this in a general sense, and not for someone in whose birth chart <note>original: "geneſi"</note> one of these appears as a "killer" <note>a technical term in astrology for a planet that threatens life or health in a specific horoscope</note>.

->*Concerning the orders of things depending on the stars, such as Solar things and the like. And how a spirit becomes solar.* CHAPTER XIV.<-

I have indeed said elsewhere that from each and every star (to speak in the Platonic manner) a series of things proper to it hangs down even to the lowest extremes. Beneath the Heart of the Scorpion <note>the star Antares</note>, after the spirits <note>original: "dæmonas"; here meaning guiding spirits or celestial intelligences rather than evil beings</note> and men of that kind, and the animal the scorpion, we can also place the herb *Asterion*—that is, the "star-herb"—which is similar in shape to a star and shines at night, which...

Next, they place men of a similar nature and Solar beasts. Then follow Phoebian plants, as well as metals and gemstones, and glowing vapor and air. By a similar logic, they believe that from any star in the firmament, a woven chain of things descends step-by-step under that star's specific property through the mediation of a Planet.

If, therefore (as I was saying), you opportunely assemble all Solar things through any level of that order—namely, such men, or something belonging to such a man, as well as animals, plants, metals, gemstones, and whatever pertains to these—you will drink in the power of the Sun everywhere, and in a sense, the natural faculty of the Solar spirits. Consider the same to be said for the others. Solar men are indeed such as I have described before: those born when Leo is ascending and the Sun is either occupying or beholding <note>an astrological "aspect" or alignment</note> that sign, and likewise those born under Aries. The blood from the left side of such people, when they are in good health, is also Solar.

For the same reason, Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the "chains" of being connecting the divine to the material world.</note> says that a solar spirit <note>original: "Apollineum dæmonem"</note>, which sometimes appeared in the form of a lion, immediately vanished when a rooster was presented to it.

Truly, among these animals, the heart is the most Solar. I also believe that the seal <note>original: "marinum uitulum," literally "sea-calf"</note> is subject to the heart of the celestial Lion <note>The zodiac sign Leo</note>; for this very reason, its hide—when it cinches the bare skin with a buckle made from the same animal's bone—is said to deliver one from pain in the kidneys. For Astrologers are accustomed to using the influences of that constellation against such pain. By the same chance, it is said that this skin protects us from lightning. Among plants, the palm tree belongs to Apollo, and especially the laurel, which by its power repels both poison and lightning. The ash tree also keeps poisonous things at a distance by a similar faculty. That the lotus is solar is evidenced by its round leaves and fruit, and by the unfolding of its leaves by day and their closing by night. That the peony is solar is indicated not only by its power, but also by its name <note>The peony was named after Paeon, the physician of the Greek gods, often associated with Apollo.</note>. To this same category belong flowers and herbs that contract when the Sun departs and immediately unfold when it returns, turning continually toward the Sun. Furthermore, gold and the *Aetites* stone <note>The "Eagle-stone," believed to have golden rays or inclusions</note> imitate the Sun with golden rays. Likewise, the stone called the "Eye of the Sun" <note>likely a variety of tiger's eye or cat's eye chrysoberyl</note>, which has the shape of a pupil from which light flashes. Again, the Carbuncle <note>A deep red gemstone, often garnet or ruby</note> glowing in the night, or the *Pantaura* <note>A legendary "all-powerful" stone described in ancient texts as attracting other stones</note> which contains within itself all the powers of stones.

Likewise, we have discussed in the book *Against the Plague* which herbs possess miraculous powers against epidemics and poison through the influence of the Sun and Jupiter; among these is the **Perforated Herb** <note>Hypericum perforatum, commonly known today as St. John's Wort</note>, which has been called the **demon-flee** <note>original: "fugadæmon"</note>. # COMPARISONS. BOOK III.

<margin>The lodestone is moved toward the Great Bear <note>original: "Vrsam"; referring to Ursa Major, the constellation used to find the North Star</note></margin>
The lodestone is moved toward the Great Bear, for it is clearly drawn there by the power of the Magnet. Because the power of the Bear prevails in this stone, it is transferred from here into the iron, and the Bear draws both toward itself. Moreover, a power of this kind was both infused from the beginning and is continually nourished by the rays of the Bear. Perhaps Amber <note>original: "Succinum"</note> behaves in the same way toward the other pole and toward straws. But tell me meanwhile, why does the Magnet draw iron everywhere? Not because it is similar, otherwise a Magnet would draw a Magnet much more so, and iron would draw iron. Not because it is higher in the order of bodies; on the contrary, metal is superior to a small stone. What then?

Both are indeed enclosed in the order following the Bear. But the Magnet holds the higher rank in that specific property of the Bear, while iron holds the lower. In the same context of things, the superior draws that which is inferior and turns it toward itself, or agitates it in some other way, or affects it by a power previously infused. The inferior, in turn, is turned toward the superior by that same infusion, or is otherwise agitated, or utterly affected. 

Thus, in the series of the Sun <note>original: "Solis"</note>, the inferior man admires the superior. In the Jovian order <note>relating to Jupiter</note>, he venerates him. In the Martial <note>relating to Mars</note>, he fears him. In the Venerean <note>relating to Venus</note>, the inferior is snatched toward the superior by the heat of love and deserts himself. In the Mercurial, the one always learns from or is persuaded by the other. In the Lunar motion, the one more often begins from the other. In Saturnine rest <note>relating to Saturn</note>, the same occurs.

Indeed, the Persian Magi <note>original: "magos Persarum"; wise men or priests of ancient Persia known for their knowledge of astronomy and medicine</note> advised the King to engrave this image upon a Hematite stone <note>original: "Hæmatiti"; a reddish-black iron oxide stone believed to have blood-stanching properties</note>, which he should then enclose in a golden ring, provided that he inserted the root of the snakeweed <note>original: "serpentariæ"</note> between the small stone and the gold. Remember that small stones growing within animals that are not suffering from illness—such as in the dragon, the rooster, the swallow, and others—are generally as effective as stones growing in the earth, and they are attributed to the same stars to which these animals belong. Hence the Cock-stone <note>term: Alectorius; a small stone supposedly found in the gizzards of old roosters</note> extracted from the stomach of an old rooster is powerful with Solar authority; concerning this, Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note> says it has often been discovered that he who carries this stone in his mouth fights unconquered. He also says that the Swallow-stone <note>term: Chelidonium; a stone said to be found in the bellies of young swallows</note>, when dug out of a swallow and being of a reddish color, cures the melancholic and renders one lovable and fit for affairs. This stone indeed derives its power from Jupiter, through those principles we have discussed: namely, that everywhere beneath the Moon, things exist that are stellar in nature.

That deeply Platonic saying is strongly confirmed: that this machine of the world <note>original: "mundi machinam"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the structured universe</note> is so interconnected with itself that celestial things exist on earth in a terrestrial condition, and conversely, terrestrial things exist in heaven with celestial dignity; and in the hidden life and mind of the world—the queen of the world—celestial things are present, yet with a vital intellect.
