And there, as it pleases the <term>Pythagoreans and Platonists</term><note>Followers of Pythagoras and Plato who believed in a mathematical and spiritual order to the universe.</note>, these forces are strongest: both because they touch the center from every side in a straight line, and because they are all gathered into a narrow space. By their intensity, the dry matter of the earth there—being far removed from moisture—is utterly set on fire; once ignited, it is thinned out and dispersed through passages in every direction, breathing out flames and sulfur alike. But they think this fire is exceedingly dark, like a sort of conflagration devoid of light, just as in heaven there exists a light devoid of conflagration. However, the fire between the celestial and the infernal realms joins light together with heat. 

<margin>Temples of the goddess Vesta were built in the center of cities.</margin>

Furthermore, they think that the fire breathing out from the center is the <term>Vestal fire</term><note>Referring to Vesta, the Roman goddess of the hearth; Ficino links the geological heat of the earth's core to a divine vital spirit.</note>; for indeed, they used to think that Vesta was the life and divinity of the earth. For that reason, the ancients used to construct the temple of Vesta in the middle of cities, and they would place a perpetual fire in the center. But lest we wander too far afield, let us now conclude: if the rays of the stars penetrate the entire earth immediately, it cannot easily be denied that metal and small stones—when they are being carved with images—are suddenly penetrated by them, and that the rays impress upon them wonderful, or at least some kind of, gifts. 

For indeed, they also generate the most precious things in other parts of the earth. But who would deny that the rays penetrate through these? Since even the air and its qualities, and sound (which is less effective), pass through solid objects suddenly and affect them with a certain quality of their own. Now truly, if hardness were to obstruct the rays of light from penetrating, light would pass through air much more quickly than water, and through water much more quickly than glass, and through glass similarly more quickly than crystal.

that the stars are most greatly powerful: when they hold the four angles—or rather, the hinges <note>term: "cardines"; the four pivotal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</note>—of heaven, namely the East, the West, and the two midpoints of heaven <note>The points directly overhead and directly underneath</note>. Among their characters <note>Hieroglyphs or sacred symbols</note>, the cross was a distinguished one, signifying the "life to come" according to their custom; they even used to carve that figure upon the breast of **Serapis** <note>A Graeco-Egyptian deity representing abundance and resurrection</note>.

I, however, believe that the high regard for the cross among the Egyptians before Christ was not so much a testimony to the influence of the stars as it was a prophecy of the power it was destined to receive from Christ. Furthermore, I suspect that the astrologers who lived immediately after Christ—seeing wonders performed by Christians through the cross, yet being ignorant of or unwilling to attribute such great things to Jesus—ascribed this power to the heavens. They should have considered, however, that miracles are by no means performed through the cross itself without the name of Jesus. It is perhaps plausible that the cross is suited to <term>images</term><note>In this context, "images" refers to astrological talismans or amulets engraved with specific symbols to capture celestial influence.</note> because it represents the strength of the Planets and all the stars. Nevertheless, it does not possess its immense power for this reason alone. Yet, when joined with other necessary elements, it may perhaps contribute something toward the prosperous health of the body.

It would be a matter of curious reporting, and perhaps harmful, to describe what images they used to make, and in what manner, to join or separate souls from one another, in order to bring about happiness or inflict calamity upon an individual, a household, or a city. # MARSILIO FICINO ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

In his book *On Fate*, he <note>Ficino is referring to Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> also says that the constellations provide the order of being and of enduring, not only for natural things, but even for artificial ones; therefore, images are manufactured under certain constellations. But if anything wonderful should happen to us through them beyond the accustomed effects of natural things, he attributes this to demons, the seducers of men. This is clearly evident in his book *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "Contra Gentiles," a major work by Aquinas defending Christian doctrine</note>, and most especially in the short treatise *On the Hidden Works of Nature*, where he seems to place little value on the images themselves, however they are made. And I, too, shall hold them of no account, insofar as he himself has commanded.

Furthermore, to attribute certain wonderful effects of images to the deception of demons is not foreign to the Platonists. For even Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and the soul</note> says that those who, having neglected religion and the highest sanctity, trust only in images and hope for divine gifts from them, are very often deceived in this matter by evil demons, who present themselves under the pretext of being good spirits. Nevertheless, he does not deny that certain natural benefits can happen from images constructed by the legitimate method of Astrology.

Finally, I judge that it will be safer to entrust oneself to medicines rather than to images; and the reasons assigned by us concerning celestial power in favor of images can have efficacy in medicines rather than in figures. For it is probable that if images have any power, they do not acquire this so much through the figure recently added, as possess it by nature through the material being so affected. ### CHAPTER XIX.

But why indeed do we overlook the universal image—that is, the image of the universe itself? It is from this, after all, that people seem to hope for benefit from the entire cosmos. Therefore, a follower of those [ancient masters] will perhaps carve, if he is able, a certain archetypal form of the whole world in bronze. Then, at the opportune time, let him impress this onto a gilded silver plate. But when is the best time to impress it? When the Sun has reached the very first minute of Aries <note>The first point of Aries marks the Spring Equinox, considered the beginning of the astrological year and the moment of the world's symbolic rebirth.</note>.

<margin>Astrologers predict the quality of the year from the Sun's first entry into Aries.</margin>
For it is from this point that astrologers—as if from the revolution of its own birthday—divine the fortune of the world looming for at least that year. He shall, therefore, on this very birthday of the world, impress the figure of the entire world. But do you see how beautifully, in the midst of our discussion, the argument for the world having been born at some point occurs to us? Since it is reborn every year, do not astrologers, in a person's own birth chart <note>original: "genesi"</note>, measure first in which sign, which degree, and which minute the Sun was located? There they lay the foundation of the entire figure. And in each subsequent year, as soon as the Sun enters that same minute, they consider the person as if reborn, and from that they predict the year's fortune. Just as they would not be able to do this for a man unless he were, in a sense, reborn; and he could not be reborn unless he had been born at some time; so too one may infer that the world was born at some point, with the Sun then positioned under the first minute of Aries, since through that same position every year,

But since we have fallen into mention of the celestial temperament, it might perhaps be opportune to remember that there is no excess of elemental quality in the heavens—to speak in the <term>Peripatetic manner</term><note>Referring to the school of Aristotle, who taught that the heavens were made of a fifth element, distinct from the four earthly elements.</note>—otherwise, if it were so composed, it would have been dissolved after so many <margin>The heaven is devoid of all excess of qualities.</margin> ages; or even if it were a simple substance, it would have destroyed all other things by its sheer magnitude, power, and motion. For we see that composite things only then finally attain life when a perfect mingling of qualities seems to have broken the prior opposition of elements, as seen in plants. Subsequently, a more perfect life is found in animals, insofar as there is in them a <term>complexion</term><note>The specific balance of bodily humors and qualities.</note> further removed from opposition than in plants. In humans, again, for the same reason, life is more perfect and in a certain way already celestial. Indeed, the human complexion has already approached the celestial temperament, especially in the <term>spirit</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, the 'spiritus' was a subtle vapor that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the soul.</note>, which, beyond the subtlety of its own substance and the temperament of qualities—in which it agrees with the heaven—has also obtained celestial light. Here, moreover, where it is most truly such, it is chiefly celestial, and has divinely obtained a celestial life above all others. And insofar as one makes and preserves oneself as such in every way of life and law of living, to that extent one carries back the singular gifts of the heavens. # MARSILIO FICINO ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

When we speak of the excess of an elementary quality <note>Ficino is discussing the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, we understand that either no such quality exists there at all—but rather the tempered powers that produce those qualities—or if there are any qualities there somewhat similar to ours, they possess an airy temperament. And when we name certain things there as "cold" and "dry," we accept this according to the Platonic reasoning: that is, something is called "cold" because it is the cause of the very least amount of heat. "Dry," indeed, is that which provides us with the minimum of moisture. Thus the astrologer Abraham <note>Likely referring to Abraham Ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note> says that Saturn, in a certain way, leaves our body cold and dry, because it brings less heat and moisture to us than other planets. By the same reasoning, the flesh of the ox and the hare are in themselves warm and moist, yet to us they are cold and dry. 

From this introduction, accept these two corollaries: First, if bodies that are more consistently tempered possess more life, then the heavens—being the most tempered—must live to the highest degree. Indeed, conversely, one may conjecture from the fact that the heaven is most exactly tempered that it possesses within itself the most absolute life; thus, to the extent that other things approach its temperament and life, they obtain a more excellent life. 

The second corollary is that life is a form perfect in itself, perfecting the body and providing the principle of motion. I say an internal principle, both of motion acted upon from within and of motion set free externally through every part. If, therefore, this very thing is life, consider him to be captured by madness <note>original: "mente captum"</note> who does not recognize that such a form exists within the heavens, which is the most excellent of bodies.

<summary>Ficino argues that celestial bodies are not "cold" or "dry" in a literal sense, but rather in relation to their effects on humans, concluding that the heavens must be a living, perfectly tempered entity.</summary>

Nevertheless, the Arabs and Egyptians attribute so much to statues and images manufactured by astronomical and magical art, that they think the spirits of the stars are shut up within them. 

By "spirits of the stars," some understand the wonderful powers of the heavenly bodies, while others mean demons <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, "demons" (daemones) are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, who act as attendants to specific planets.</note> who are the followers of this or that star. They believe, therefore, that the spirits of the stars—whatever they may be—are inserted into statues and images, not unlike the way demons are accustomed sometimes to occupy human bodies, and through them to speak, move, be moved, and perform wonders. They think the spirits of the stars do similar things through images. They believe that demons who dwell in the "world-fire" <note>The elemental fire of the cosmos.</note> insinuate themselves into our bodies through fiery humors or ignited spirits and similar affections. Likewise, they believe the spirits of the stars are inserted into the appropriate materials of images through rays opportunely received, as well as through fumigations, lights, and powerful sounds.

# COMPARISONS. BOOK III.

Just as a gaze sent forth can bewitch, infect, or otherwise affect a neighbor, so much more powerful is the spirit <note>The "spiritus" was viewed as a subtle vapor or fluid that connected the physical body to the immaterial soul</note> flowing forth more abundantly and fervently from the imagination and the heart together. It is so powerful in its motion that it is not at all surprising that certain diseases of the mind and body can sometimes be taken away or inflicted in this manner. This is especially true since a musical spirit of this kind specifically touches and acts upon the spirit that mediates between the body and the soul, affecting both completely with its own disposition. You will concede that there is a marvelous power in the spirit when it is aroused and singing, if you grant to the followers of Pythagoras and Plato that the heaven itself is a spirit, arranging all things by its own motions and tones. 

Remember, however, that all Music proceeds from Apollo. Jupiter is a musician only insofar as he is in harmony with Apollo. Furthermore, Venus and Mercury carry back music due to their proximity to Apollo. Likewise, harmony pertains only to these four; the remaining three <note>The other three "planets" in the ancient system: Saturn, Mars, and the Moon</note> certainly have voices, but not songs. 

Now, we attribute slow, deep, hoarse, and complaining voices to Saturn. To Mars, we attribute the opposite: swift, sharp, harsh, and threatening voices. We give the middle voices to the Moon. To Jupiter, we attribute harmonies that are deep and earnest, yet sweet and joyfully constant. On the other hand, we assign voluptuous songs, full of playfulness and softness, to Venus. Between these two, we attribute the middle ground to the Sun and Mercury. If the songs are venerable, simple, and earnest, along with grace and sweetness, they are judged to be Apolline.

Indeed, that there is a Phoebean <note>associated with Apollo/the Sun</note> and medicinal power in sound—and a specific power at that—is evident from the fact that those in Apulia <note>a region in Southern Italy</note> who are bitten by the Tarantula <note>original: "Phalangio"; referring to the tarantula spider</note> all become stupified and lie half-dead until each hears a certain sound specific to himself. Then he dances fitly to the sound, sweats thereafter, and recovers his health. And if after ten years he hears a similar sound, he is suddenly moved to dance. I conjecture from the evidence that this sound is of the nature of Apollo and Jupiter.

### CHAPTER XXII.

Since the heavens are composed according to harmonic proportion and move harmonically, and since they accomplish all things through harmonic motions and sounds, it is rightly through harmony alone that not only men, but all these lower things, are prepared according to their strength to receive the celestial gifts. We distribute this harmony, which is capable of receiving the higher influences, through seven levels of things in the higher realms. Namely, through images (as they believe) harmonically constructed; through medicinal

...through their own specific, tempered harmony: through vapors and odors prepared with a similar elegance; through musical songs and sounds. To the order and power of these sounds, we wish to relate bodily gestures, dances, and rhythmic movements: through the concepts of the imagination and harmonious motions: through the congruent discourses of reason: and through the tranquil contemplations of the mind. 

For just as we daily expose the body to the light and heat of the Sun through its own harmony—that is, through its posture, habit, and shape—so too we prepare the spirit for the hidden powers of the stars. This is done through a certain similar harmony of its own, compared to images (as some believe) and certainly to medicines and harmonically composed scents. 

And finally, through the spirit thus prepared for the higher powers (as we have often said), we expose the soul and the body to them. I say the "soul," insofar as it is inclined toward the spirit and the body by its affection. Within the soul, we now place the imagination, reason, and mind. 

Certainly, our imagination—either because of the quality and motion of the spirit, or through our own choice, or even through both—can be so disposed, composed, and conformed to Mars <note>The planet associated with courage and heat</note> or the Sun <note>original: "Soli"</note>, that it immediately becomes a proper vessel for the influence of Phoebus <note>A name for the Sun or Apollo, representing light and clarity</note> or Mars. Similarly, reason—either through the imagination and spirit together, or through deliberation, or both—can so prepare itself for Jupiter <note>The planet of justice, law, and benevolence</note> through a certain imitation, that by its own dignity and proximity, it may capture Jupiter and the gifts of Jupiter much more effectively than the imagination can.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

Those whom Socrates describes in the *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue by Plato concerning the soul; Ficino refers here to the description of the "true earth" located above the clouds</note>, dwelling upon the most eminent surface of the earth and higher than the clouds, living quite soberly and content with the fruits of the earth, and devoted to the study of secret wisdom and religion, they taste the happiness of Saturn. They lead a life so prosperous and so long-lived that they are considered not so much mortal men as immortal spirits <note>original: "daemones" – in the Neoplatonic sense, these are intermediary beings between gods and men, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. Many call these beings heroes, a golden race rejoicing in a certain Saturnian age and kingdom.

I think perhaps the Arabian astrologers intended this when they say that beyond the equinoctial line to the south there are certain most refined inhabitants—spirits who seem neither to be born nor to die—and that there Saturn and the Tail of the Dragon <term>Cauda Draconis: the descending lunar node, often associated in astrology with karmic endings or spiritual detachment</term> hold power. Indeed, Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> seems to confirm this in the *Book of Sadar*, saying that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and that the men there are very long-lived, departing only at an extreme old age. He assigns the reason for this to be that Saturn does not harm his own subjects, but only outsiders.

<margin>
The inhabitants of India are long-lived.
</margin>

Do not, however, neglect the power of Saturn. For the Arabs say he is the most powerful of all. Indeed, they say the planets take on the strengths of those they approach; but all planets approach him rather than the other way around, and planets joined to him act according to his nature. For he himself is the head of the widest sphere among the planets. Truly, any planet is the head, heart, and eye of its own sphere. Likewise, Saturn is closest to the innumerable fixed stars, and most similar to the *Primum Mobile* <term>First Movable: the outermost sphere in the Ptolemaic system which moves all others</term>; he completes a long circuit and is the highest of all.

# MARSILIO FICINO: ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and philosophers</note>, Egyptians, and Platonists believe that the decrees of fate can be avoided. Since they do not believe the heavenly bodies to be empty shells, but rather divinely animated and guided by divine minds, they certainly maintain that from those sources proceed not only many things pertaining to the body and spirit, but also many goods that in some way overflow into the soul—not from the physical bodies of the stars into the soul, but from their guiding souls. Furthermore, they believe that even more things of this kind flow from the higher minds that exist above the heavens. Among these matters, if you wish to assign all the reasons that led Moses to command the rest of the Sabbath to the Hebrews, perhaps beyond the more sublime and secret 

<margin>Moses forbade business on the day of Saturn.</margin>

allegory, you will find that the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note> is unsuitable for civil and warlike actions, but apt for contemplations; and on that day, divine protection must be implored against dangers. Abraham, Samuel, and many Hebrew astrologers confess that such protection can indeed be obtained against the threats of Mars and Saturn through the elevation of the mind toward God, and through vows and sacrifices. They confirm that Chaldean precept: namely, that if you raise up a mind burning with the work of piety, you shall also preserve your frail body. It is worth considering that saying of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized ritual and theurgy</note>: that the celestial and worldly divinities possess certain superior powers and some inferior ones. Through the inferior powers, they bind us to the effects of fate, but through the superior ones, they in turn release us from fate, as if they possessed the keys—as Orpheus says—for opening and closing. I say "exposed" not so much by a natural contract, but rather by the choice of free will or by affection. In summary, consider that whoever imitates the beneficence, action, and order of the celestial beings through their vows, study, life, and character—being more like the higher powers—receives more abundant gifts from that source. However, those men who are artificially unlike and discordant with the celestial arrangement are both secretly wretched and, in the end, turn out to be openly unhappy.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

Whoever is born of sound mind and in control of themselves is naturally ordained by the heavens for some honorable work and way of life. Therefore, whoever desires to have the heavens be favorable should, above all, undertake this work and this lifestyle, and pursue it diligently. For the heavens favor their own undertakings. Indeed, you were made by nature for that specific thing which, from your tender years, you first do, speak of, imagine, desire, dream of, and imitate; that which you attempt most frequently and perform most easily; that in which you make the greatest progress and delight in above all others; and that which you leave behind only with reluctance. This is truly that for which the heavens and the Ruler of the heavens <note>Ficino refers here to God as the 'Rector coeli', the governor of the celestial spheres.</note> begot you. To that extent, therefore, the heavens will favor your undertakings and breathe life into your efforts, so long as <margin>The opinion of Plato.</margin> you follow the guidance of your progenitor. This is especially true if that Platonic saying is correct (in which all of antiquity agrees): that for every person at birth, a certain <term>daemon</term> <note>original: "daemonem"; in the Platonic sense, this is not an evil spirit but a personal guardian or guiding spirit, similar to a 'Genius'.</note> is assigned from their own star as a guardian of their life. This spirit assists in the very duty to which the celestial bodies appointed the person at birth. Therefore, whoever examines their own natural character through the evidence we have just mentioned will find their natural work, and at the same time, will find their star and their guardian spirit. By following these beginnings, they will act prosperously and live happily.

<summary>Ficino explains that every individual is born with a specific celestial calling and a guardian spirit (daemon) assigned by their star. Success and happiness depend on identifying this natural inclination early in life and aligning one's profession with it.</summary>

*otherwise he will both experience adverse fortune and feel the heavens to be his enemy. There are, therefore, two types of unfortunate men above all others. The first point is confirmed by the ancient proverb: "The gods help those who act, but are hostile to the idle." For this reason, I believe, Jupiter is beseeched in the Pythagorean poems either to relieve the human race of so many evils himself, or at least to show us which guiding spirit <note>original: "daemone"</note> we should follow. Accordingly, it would be worthwhile to investigate for which region to inhabit and cultivate your star and your spirit have designated you from the beginning: for there they breathe more favorably upon you. That region is truly the one in which your spirit, having first set out, is in a certain way refreshed; where the senses remain more vigorous, where the condition of the body is stronger, where most people are more favorable to you, and where your prayers succeed. Therefore, test these things: choose this region: cultivate it happily. From here, evidently, you would depart unhappy, unless you were both to return and proceed to similar places. But meanwhile, exercise yourself with frequent movements in this region, and perform certain circuits in the likeness of the heavenly bodies. For by such motion and revolution, having been born to similar things, you shall be preserved.*

Furthermore, regarding your place of residence, it will be useful to remember this: just as the countryside supplies the city with the necessary food for life, while the city consumes it, so too is life itself greatly increased by frequent stays in the country—provided you do not succumb to boredom—but it is worn away by both the leisure and the business of the city. But if the profession disagrees with one's natural disposition, then the daemon acquired by our craft is at odds with our natural genius, and life becomes laborious and full of anxiety. # COMPARISONS. BOOK III.

The sign which already takes hold when a human is being born is one thing, but he <note>The author likely refers to a specific authority like Ptolemy or Firmicus Maternus</note> does not think the <term>daemon</term><note>In this context, 'daemon' refers to a guiding spirit or personal genius, not an evil entity</note> should be investigated by the same rule. Indeed, one calculates from the Sun to the Moon in a daytime birth, and conversely from the Moon to the Sun in a nighttime birth. Once the interval between these has been computed, you should traverse an equal distance descending from the degree of the <term>ascendant</term><note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, and take note of the boundary where you stop. For they believe the daemon belongs to whichever star governs that boundary. In summary, they are accustomed to weigh the course of life and fortune together from the lord of the <term>geniture</term><note>The birth chart or moment of birth</note> and the daemon. I have added "fortune" because some compute the <term>Part of Fortune</term> by almost the same method.

The ancients hoped that their own daemon had descended to them from one of the <term>cardinal points</term><note>The four primary angles of the sky: East, West, Zenith, and Nadir</note> of the heavens—namely from the East, the West, or the mid-heaven in either direction—or at least from the eleventh or fifth region. The eleventh region follows the mid-heaven above our heads and is surnamed the **Good Daemon**; it regards the ascending degree from the East in a <term>sextile</term><note>An astrological aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious</note> aspect. The fifth region follows the mid-heaven of the <term>antipodes</term><note>The point directly opposite on the other side of the earth; the lower mid-heaven</note> and is called **Good Fortune**; it gazes upon the ascending degree from a <term>trine</term><note>An astrological aspect where planets are 120 degrees apart, considered very favorable</note> aspect. In the third place, they hoped that if the daemon came from a <term>cadent</term><note>Declining or falling away from the cardinal angles</note> region, it would at least come from the ninth or the third. For the ninth is called **God**, and the third is called **Goddess**. The former regards the ascending degree from a trine, and the latter from a sextile. However, they shuddered at the cadent twelfth and sixth regions. The former they called the **Evil Daemon**, and the latter **Evil Fortune**.

# COMPARISONS. BOOK III.

**Remember** again to enter into friendship with those who are breathed upon by heavenly graces. You shall weigh this by the goods of the mind, the body, and fortune. For just as a scent exhales from musk, so something of the good exhales from a good man onto his neighbor, and often remains infused there. Moreover, a gathering of three fortunate people—or even two—wonderfully overflowing into one another, would be a marvelous thing. Remember, finally, to flee far from the unrestrained, the impudent, the malignant, and the unfortunate. For these, being full of evil demons or rays <note>The author refers to "rays" as the astrological influence or spiritual emissions believed to radiate from a person's soul</note>, are workers of harm; like those with leprosy or the plague, they do damage not only by touch, but even by proximity and sight.

<margin>The proximity of the unfortunate is contagious.</margin>

Indeed, the very proximity of living bodies is considered a form of contact, because of the powerful exhalation of vapors flowing outward from heat, spirit, and emotion. But the friendship of the wicked and the cruel will be especially pestilential, if it be true that after the vegetative life <note>The basic biological life-force</note> is infused in us in the month of Jupiter (that is, the second month of gestation), the sensual soul, enslaved to passions, is then infused in the month of Mars (the third month). For thus, those who are carried away by passion, being full of Mars, infect those near them with a Martial contagion. By the opposite reasoning, frequent association and close dealings with the fortunate and the excellent, as we have said, is accustomed to be wonderfully beneficial. They say that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and miracle-worker from the 1st century AD</note> discovered an old man in Ephesus, under whose form a demon was hiding, who by his presence alone was contaminating the entire city with plague. On the other hand, Xenophon and Plato testify how much Socrates benefited many by his presence alone.

### *By what means men of letters may recognize their own natural disposition, and follow a way of life agreeable to their spirit.* CHAPTER XXIV.

Since I am speaking to those devoted to letters, I wish for each one to remember that he who is captured by the love of learning is, first and foremost, a man of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurialem"; Mercury was the god of communication, intellect, and writing</note>, and furthermore a man of the Sun <note>original: "Solaris"</note> insofar as Mercury himself is Solar. And this is a condition common to all such men. 

But more specifically, beyond the nature of Mercury, whoever excels in the grace of eloquence, in wit, dignity, and charm, should recognize Apollo and Venus within himself. He who is more inclined toward the laws or toward natural and common philosophy should not be unaware that he has Jupiter as his patron. But he who is inwardly driven to investigate the most secret things with greater curiosity should know that he is not only a man of Mercury, but a man of Saturn <note>original: "Saturnium"; Saturn was associated with deep, melancholic, and esoteric study</note>. Under Saturn's lordship also are all those who are diligent to the very end in any study, especially those who are negligent in other matters. 

Finally, if it is true—as some physicians <note>original: "Physici"</note> as well as astronomers <note>original: "Astronomi"</note> hand down—that the soul endowed with intellect descends into the human conception in the month of the Sun (that is, the fourth month), then those who live most fully by the intellect are especially Solar from the beginning and become more so daily. Therefore, the favor of these planets must be sought by these men. Medicines must be forged under their breath <note>original: "spiraculo"; referring to the astrological influence or 'spirit' of the planets</note>. One must dwell within their regions. Most beloved brothers in the love of the Muses <note>The Muses were the nine Greek goddesses of inspiration in the arts and sciences.</note>, those who are far more powerful in intellect than in body surely know that at their birth, the Moon <note>original: "Phœbem"; referring to the lunar influence over physical matter</note> supplied very little material substance, but Apollo <note>original: "phœbeũ"; referring to the solar spirit of light and reason</note> infused a vast amount of spirit. Indeed, every day they transform the greater part of the fluids and nourishment in their bodies into spirit. Each of you, therefore, is almost entirely spirit. You are, I say, a spiritual man masked by this little earthly body, fatiguing the spirit above all others with a certain perpetual labor. Thus, you must diligently refresh the spirit more than others do, and furthermore, in old age—when the spirit commonly becomes thicker—you must recall it back to its proper refinement. You certainly know that a thick body is nourished by the four thick elements <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire</note>. Know, therefore, that the spiritual body is nourished by its own four refined elements.

<margin>Nourishment of the spirit.</margin>
For this spirit, wine stands in place of earth; the very scent of wine takes the place of water; song and sound, in turn, act as air; and light offers the element of fire. By these four, then, the spirit is chiefly nourished: by wine, I say, and its scent, and by song, and likewise by light. We have conversed enough now, brothers, and we have drunk together enough. Therefore, Farewell.

# MARSILIO FICINO ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

In the world familiarly manifest to the senses, there lies hidden within it a certain spiritual body, exceeding the capacity of our frail senses. Within this spirit the soul flourishes, and within the soul the intelligence shines. And just as beneath the Moon air is not mixed with earth except through water, nor fire with water except through air, so in the universe there is a certain fuel <note>original: "esca" or "fomes," meaning bait or tinder</note>, or a kindling for coupling the soul to the body, which is that very thing we call the spirit.

<margin>The soul is the kindling of the spirit</margin>
The soul is also a kind of kindling within the spirit and the body of the world for attaining intelligence from the divine, just as a supreme dryness in wood is prepared for the oil that will penetrate it. The oil soaked into this is the food for the fire—I mean, most closely, for the heat. The heat itself is the vehicle of the light; it is as if this wood were of such a kind that, in the presence of fire, it would shine but not be consumed, such as we have sometimes seen. Now, by this example, we shall see whether either a human being or some other thing beneath the Moon, through certain preparations—partly natural and partly sought through art <term>art: here meaning "alchemy" or "theurgy," the practical application of hidden knowledge</term>—can opportunely receive certain vital and perhaps even intellectual goods from above. Truly, what pertains to religion here we shall discuss elsewhere, where Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired</note> brings these matters forward. But as for what pertains to natural influences <note>original: "influxus," the flowing down of celestial power</note>, of whatever kind they may be coming from above, know that they can only be obtained for us and our materials through art when nature has supplied the kindling for them to us and our things, and when the heavens have conspired more opportunely toward them. Does not the artisan of the fetus itself <note>The "artisan" refers to the formative power of nature or the "World Soul" acting upon the embryo.</note>, when it has shaped and formed the little body in a certain specific way, immediately draw down a spirit from the universe by this very preparation, as if by a kind of bait? # COMPARISONS. BOOK III.

<margin>The constellation of Gemini <note>The Twins</note> signifies the prophets, as they say.</margin>
...and the constellation of Gemini signifies the prophets (as they say). Mars is "combust" by the Sun <note>A term in astrology meaning a planet is so close to the Sun that its power is weakened or hidden</note>, and does not look upon Mercury. The Sun, however, gazes upon the place of that conjunction. Venus meanwhile occupies a certain "angle" <note>A pivotal point in a horoscope, such as the Ascendant or Midheaven</note>; she is in the west and powerful. The Moon gazes upon the ascending degree from a "trine" aspect <note>An auspicious 120-degree angle</note>, as does Saturn. These are their claims.

I, however, first of all hold—following the opinion of the blessed Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note>—that if they truly made statues that speak, it was not the simple influence of the stars that formed the words there, but demons. Furthermore, if it happened that they entered into such statues, I do not believe they were bound there by celestial influence, but rather that they obeyed their worshippers voluntarily, ultimately intending to deceive them. For a superior nature may sometimes be won over by an inferior one, but it cannot be restrained by it. Moreover, that arrangement of the stars described just above perhaps cannot even occur simultaneously.

Although demons are not confined to statues by astronomical calculations <term>astronomica ratione: the use of planetary positions to compel spiritual forces</term>, nevertheless, when they have become present through the worship offered to them, Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says they gave oracles according to astronomical rules. For this reason, the oracles were frequently ambiguous—and rightly so, since Iamblichus <note>A student of Porphyry who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians</note> proves that true and certain prophecy does not belong to evil demons, nor to human arts or nature, but comes from divine inspiration to purified minds. 

But let us return now to Hermes <note>original: "Mercurium," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, or rather to Plotinus. Hermes says that the priests received a power suitable from the nature of the world and mixed it. Following him, Plotinus thinks that this whole soul...

# ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS, BOOK III.

<margin>By what means the higher nature can be reconciled to us.</margin>...can be easily accomplished by the mediation of the World Soul <note>Latin: *anima mundi*; the Neoplatonic concept of a vital force connecting the physical world to the divine</note>, insofar as that Soul generates and moves the forms of natural things through certain "seminal reasons" <note>Latin: *rationes seminales*; the latent "seeds" or blueprints of all things implanted in nature by God</note> divinely instilled within it. Indeed, he calls these reasons "Gods," because they are never severed from the Ideas of the Supreme Mind. Therefore, through such reasons, the World Soul easily applies itself to the materials which it formed from the beginning through those same reasons, whenever a magus <note>A practitioner of natural magic or "wise man"</note> or a priest has applied, at the opportune times, the rightly collected forms of things which specifically pertain to this or that reason. This occurs just as the Magnet attracts iron, Rhubarb draws out bile, Saffron strengthens the heart, Agrimony and Spodium <note>A medicinal powder, often zinc oxide or burnt ivory</note> aid the liver, and Spikenard and Musk benefit the brain. It is truly possible that sometimes, when these reasons are applied to forms in this way, even higher gifts may descend, insofar as the reasons in the World Soul are joined to the intellectual forms of that same Soul, and through them to the Ideas of the Divine Mind. Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and mysteries</note> also approves of this where he discusses sacrifices. We shall discuss this matter more opportunely elsewhere. There it will also become apparent how impure the superstition of the pagan people was; and on the contrary, how pure the Gospel piety has been, which we have already demonstrated for the most part in our book *On the Christian Religion*.

### ->THE END OF THE BOOK ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS.<-

# MARSILIO

### FICINO’S APOLOGY, IN WHICH
### *Medicine, Astrology, the Life of the World, and*

<note>The "Apology" was written in 1489 to defend his work "On Life" (De Vita Libri Tres) against charges of magic and heresy.</note>

Marsilio Ficino of Florence <note>original: "Marsilius Ficinus Florentinus"</note> sends greetings three and four times over to his most beloved brothers in the study of truth: the three Peters—Nero, Guicciardini, and Soderini. Perhaps I should have more correctly said "Triple-Peter" rather than three Peters. For just as where there is one palm, the many fingers upon it do not make many hands, so your three bodies, my friends, seem to offer no obstacle to your single will forming one Peter. Christ, that craftsman of the heavenly fatherland, created so great a rock <note>original: "petram" — a play on the name Petrus (Peter) and the Latin word for rock/stone</note> that this single rock sufficed for the founding of this immense edifice of his Church. I also, by a certain divine fate, have obtained such grand rocks that three of them now suffice for my own building, however arduous it may be. Now, my friends, now—if you do not know it—that citadel of Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena/Pallas, representing wisdom and defensive warfare</note> seems necessary, by which we may ward off the savage assault of the impious giants far from us. For this reason, I have decided to fortify the life of my three "children"—who are coming to the aid of the public life—first with your citadel constructed of three rocks. You know (as I believe) that I have composed a book *On Life*, divided into three small volumes.

# THE WRITINGS OF MARSILIO FICINO

The first of these shall be titled *On Healthy Life*; the second, *On Long Life*; and the third, *On Life from the Heavens*. <note>original: "De Vita sana... De Vita longa... De Vita coelitus"</note> Therefore, the allure of such a sweet title will entice many to taste of it. But in such a great number, many will likely be ignorant, and not a few (I suspect) will be malicious. One man will say: "Is Marsilio not a priest?" Indeed he is. "What then do priests have to do with medicine? What business have they with Astrology?" <term>Astrology: in Ficino's time, this referred to the study of how celestial bodies influence human health and temperament.</term> Another will ask: "What has a Christian to do with magic or images?" Yet another—one truly unworthy of life—will begrudge us a life drawn from heaven. Finally, all those so affected will be utterly ungrateful for our benefit toward them; they will not be ashamed to be cruel toward our charity, through which we provide for the public life and prosperity according to the faculty of our talent.

Therefore, this labor shall be shared among you, but so that it may be somewhat lighter—for there are three of you against three enemies—undertake the struggle in distribution. You shall not refute an invective with an invective (for I know your character), but rather you shall overcome the bitterness of another's gall with the sweetness of your honey (which is your wonderful gentleness). In the beginning, most candid Nerus, respond to the first critics that the most ancient priests were once Physicians and Astronomers alike.

-># APOLOGY<-

Without doubt, that which is most necessary and especially desired by all is to achieve this: that men might have **a sound mind in a sound body.** <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano," a famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> However, we can only provide this if we join <term>medicine</term> to the <term>priesthood</term>. But since medicine without the favor of heaven is more often useless, and often even harmful—as both Hippocrates and Galen <note>Ancient Greek founders of Western medicine.</note> confess, and as we ourselves have experienced—it follows that <term>Astronomy</term> <note>In this context, the study of celestial influences on health.</note> belongs to that same priestly charity to which we said medicine belongs. It is a Physician of this kind, I believe, whom the Holy Scriptures command us to honor, because the Most High created him out of necessity. And Christ himself, the giver of life, who commanded his disciples to heal the sick throughout the whole world, will also command priests that if they are less able to heal by words alone as the disciples once did, they should at least heal with herbs and stones. If these things are not sufficient on their own, he will command the priest to fuse them together with a certain opportune "breath" or influence from heaven and apply them to the sick. For Christ himself, by that same heavenly influence, stirs animals everywhere toward their own specific medicines; to such an extent does he provide most abundantly for the lives of all. Thus, by a heavenly instinct and divine prompting, snakes treat their eyes with fennel <note>original: "marathro"</note> and swallows treat theirs with celandine <note>original: "chelidonia," a flowering plant named after the Greek word for swallow.</note>. Eagles, when troubled by labor, divinely discovered the Eagle-stone <note>original: "Aetitem lapidem," a hollow geode believed in antiquity to assist in childbirth.</note>, by which they might immediately and successfully bring forth their eggs. Therefore, God himself, who through the heavens prompts every animal toward its medicine, certainly permits priests—not for profit, I say, but out of charity—to use medicines strengthened by the heavens.

Arise after this, you too, forceful Guicciardini <note>Piero Guicciardini, a friend and patron of Ficino</note>, and respond to those curious minds: that these matters of magic or images are not indeed "approved" by Marsilio, but are merely recounted while he interprets Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> himself. His writings clearly declare this, if they are read with a fair mind. Not a single word is asserted here concerning that profane magic which relies on the worship of demons. Instead, mention is made of natural magic, which, through natural objects, captures the benefits of the heavens for the prosperous health of our bodies. This faculty should surely be granted to those using their intellects legitimately, just as medicine and agriculture are granted by right—and all the more so, as this industry is more perfect, coupling heavenly things to earthly ones. From this workshop, the Magi, the very first of all men, adored Christ immediately after his birth. Why then, fearful one, do you dread the name of a "Magus"? <note>original: "magi nomen"; referring to the Three Wise Men or Magi</note> It is a name gracious to the Gospel, which signifies not a sorcerer or a poisoner, but a wise man and a priest. What does that first worshiper of Christ, the Magus, actually profess? If you wish to hear: he is like a kind of farmer; indeed, he is a "cultivator of the world" <note>original: "mundicola"</note>. Nor does he worship the world for this reason, any more than a farmer worships the earth. But just as a farmer tempers his field to the air for the sake of human food, so that wise man, that priest, for the sake of human health, tempers the lower things of the world to the higher things; and just as a hen does her eggs, so he opportunely submits earthly things to the heavens to be fostered.

<margin>Two kinds of magic.</margin>
One belongs to those who win over demons <note>original: "dæmonas"; in this context, referring to mediating spirits or supernatural entities</note> to themselves through a certain specific cult; relying on the works of these beings, they often manufacture portents. # EPISTLE

They bark, bite, and tear at others for the sake of mere opinion. Indeed, dogs claim such a large place among philosophers that they have not only inserted themselves into various sects, but even established their own sect at one time under the name of the **Cynics** <note>The "Cynics" (from the Greek word for 'dog-like') were a school of philosophy that emphasized living simply and often criticized social norms with biting wit.</note>. That most brave Giorgio will easily put all wolves to flight, he who once even pierced through a vast dragon. He will relieve me of my anxiety, and at the same time, relieve you of your care.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's philosophical reflections on the nature of the soul and the cosmos, likely following a discussion on the fluidity of spiritual substances.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO

...and unstable. This is the nature of fluid things: if you try to confine them in a narrow space, you lose them instantly. For when forced together, they flow away and quickly escape. If you happen to squeeze a sponge soaked in water, you press the water out and immediately scatter it. If you hold it more loosely, you will retain it; this is even more true for air, fire, and the ether <note>The "ether" was considered the fifth element, the pure substance of the heavens</note>. Hence, in the works of the Poets, those who strive to grasp the vast forms or images of the Gods in their arms struggle in vain. Things that are widest by nature must be received in a very wide manner. Things that are fluid and most ample must be possessed most amply.

Certainly, then, a heavy narrowness oppresses us whenever we reduce the soul itself—and its naturally expansive movement—into a confined space. Whoever weighs their studies and business with excessive precision, and always grinds them down most exactly into every tiny detail, meanwhile miserably wears away their own life—alas, their very life—in secret. Therefore, Pythagoras seems to have commanded rightly: "Take care that you are never by chance confined in a narrow space." Nothing is more ample than the heavens; nothing is more full of life. Conversely, the Earth, being the most narrow, possesses the least amount of life in the world. Finally, if we live by the heavens and by time, the more widely we absorb these, the more and the longer we live.

Live, therefore, expansive and far from narrowness, O my friends. Live joyful. The heavens created you by their own joy, which they declare through a certain laughter—that is, through expansion, movement, and splendor—as if in a gesture of delight. Your own joy will preserve you for the heavens. Therefore, live joyfully in the present every day. For anxiety over present things snatches the present away from you and steals the future in advance. Curiosity for the future...

<margin>
Precepts of this kind exist among the symbols of Pythagoras: "Do not eat your heart" <note>original: Μὴ ἐσθίειν τὴν καρδίαν. A metaphor for avoiding a restricted or constrained life.</note>.

# LETTER.

<margin>Live joyfully</margin>
...quickly carries you away into the past. Therefore, I pray again and again: live joyfully. For the fates allow it, so long as you live free from care. But so that you may truly live without worry, do not take up even this one concern—that you should ever anxiously fret over which specific effort you might use to escape your cares. For this single worry, alas, consumes wretched mortals more than any other care. Therefore, disregard your diligence, and instead, cherish a certain "negligence" <note>The author uses "negligentia" here not as laziness, but as a deliberate "letting go" or ease of mind</note>—and even do this with a sense of ease, as far as it is permitted and proper for you. I command these things to you not so much as a priest advising friends, but as a Physician. For without this one principle, which acts as the very life of all medicines, all other medicines applied to prolong life simply wither away. September 16, 1489.

->In the fields of Careggi.<- <note>Careggi was the site of the Medici villa outside Florence where the Platonic Academy met.</note>

### ANDREAS LEENNIUS SENDS GREETINGS TO STUDENTS OF MEDICINE.

It seemed to us not without purpose to attach to these books *On Life* the same author’s *Antidote to Epidemics* as a sort of finishing touch <note>original: "coronidem"; literally the curved flourish at the end of a book</note>. He had indeed written that work in his own native tongue—that is, Tuscan <note>The Italian dialect of Tuscany, often associated with the literary Renaissance</note>—at the request of his friends. Now, however, this treasure of life has been channeled into a Roman colony <note>original: "in coloniam Romanam deriuatus"; a metaphor for being translated into Latin, the language of Rome</note> by Hieronymus Ricius of Ticino, so that if you measure its usefulness alongside the pleasure it provides, it will not be something to be looked down upon. In this work are handed down not only the definitions of diseases and the causes that bring them about, but also the signs of their onset. Furthermore, it touches upon <term>prophylaxis</term> <note>preventative treatment to ward off disease</note> and the cure for present illness, providing remedies adapted to various and diverse bodies with wonderful brevity and an apparent ease. Relying on these defenses, you may enter into a calculation of life and health; and persuade yourself that, **To a man, to be healthy is the best thing, at least as it seems to me.** <note>original Greek: "Ανδρὶ δὲ ὑγιαίνειν ἄριστον, ὥς γέ μοι δοκεῖ." A common sentiment in classical medical literature.</note>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS

### WHAT THE PLAGUE IS, AND OF WHAT KIND. CHAPTER ONE.

The Plague is a certain poisonous vapor created within the air, which is an enemy to the vital spirit: not because it opposes the spirit through any elementary quality <note>The four elementary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, but by a certain specific property. Just as Treacle <note>original: "Theriaca" — a famous ancient medical compound used as an antidote to poison</note> is indeed a friend to the body, not because it is hot or cold, dry or moist, but because from its entire composition there results a certain form accommodated to the form of the vital spirit. So too, that pestilential vapor is an enemy to nature, not because it is hot, cold, moist, or dry, but because its own proportion is, as it were, diametrically opposed to the proportion in which the vital spirit resides within the heart. 

And just as poisons are continually born in the earth, so a poisonous vapor is frequently born in the air; however, it is not as powerful there because it is more widely dispersed. Nor can it take hold in pure air, as long as such air is conformable to the spirit and to fire, which by the power of its own nature does not receive the mixture of another nature—from which it follows that it undergoes no decay <note>original: "putrefactionem"</note>. Thus, pure air, by receiving no mixture, can by no means decay. Furthermore, a poisonous vapor of this kind attaches itself only to that human body in which there exist humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and temperament</term> prone to fever, namely

<summary>Marsilio Ficino defines the plague as a poisonous airborne vapor that specifically attacks the vital spirit of the heart, noting that it only takes hold in bodies with unbalanced humors.</summary>
<keywords>Marsilio Ficino, plague, vital spirit, Treacle, theriaca, atmospheric vapor, humors, putrefaction, medical theory</keywords>

--- Page 301 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physiological effects of pestilential air and the mechanism by which it turns into poison within the body.</meta>

# ANTIDOTE

...namely those who are disposed toward putrefaction <note>The decomposition of bodily fluids, believed to be the root of many diseases.</note> and inflammation. For if the vital spirit <note>The "spiritus vitalis," a subtle substance believed to carry life and heat from the heart through the arteries.</note> is stronger than the vapor, it drives it far away from itself; but if it is weaker, it flees from it as if from its own contrary work. Therefore, it is useful to correct, purge, and strengthen the air, the humors <note>The four primary bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, and finally the heart. It must be noted (so that you understand correctly) that when I say this vapor is poisonous, you should not believe it to be so according to its form and its entire nature, otherwise everyone would be infected by it. Rather, it is of such a quality that it very easily passes into the nature of a poison. And it properly becomes a poison when, through its influence in the human body, the humors putrefy and boil at a certain stage. This commonly tends to happen on the third day, and sometimes sooner, especially when someone abounds in superfluous humors, particularly blood and yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>. And when it has already taken on the nature of a poison, it receives the quality of lime or Arsenic, the effect of which is to rot, gnaw, and burn, both inside and out. It is therefore of the highest necessity that we resist these three effects, especially internally, with all the industry we can muster.

<margin>The air is not poisonous according to its total form, but its quality.</margin>

### The causes of the origin of the Epidemic, and which bodies are most vulnerable to this evil.

#### CHAPTER II.

A vapor of this kind is created in the air during the entire time of a plague, arising from certain malignant constellations <note>The alignment of stars and planets, then considered a primary cause of disease outbreaks.</note>, especially from the conjunction of Mars with Saturn in the sign—

from the conjunction of human affairs and from eclipses of the luminaries <note>The sun and the moon</note>. Such is the plague in the present year, namely 1479; and such it also was in the year 1408. This type of plague primarily harms human beings. It spreads in those places which have an unfortunate Horoscope or <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The degree of the zodiac rising over the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note> due to the aforementioned aspects of the stars. In more localized pestilences, however, the aforementioned poison is born from winds and the malignant vapors of pits and sewers, and likewise from earthquakes. But whatever the cause of these may be, the plague always reigns most powerfully in thick air, and in marshy, cloudy, and foul-smelling air. When it extends into thin <note>subtle or refined</note> air, it penetrates and kills more swiftly; yet it reigns more quickly, more frequently, and for a longer duration in thick, hot, humid, and stinking air. Some of the Doctors <note>Learned medical authorities</note> assert that pestilential putrefaction exists first in the thin air and afterwards in the thicker air, but that it is much more durable in the thick. I do not know by what discourse of the mind or by what foundation I should adhere to the first part of that argument, since experience shows the contrary. Furthermore, reason dictates to us that since only a mixed element—and not a pure one—can undergo putrefaction, the less mixed an element is (as thin air is known to be), the less fit it is for putrefaction. Therefore, thin air does not receive such corruption except through a constant increase of the pestiferous <term>influence of the stars</term> <note>The belief that celestial bodies emit a physical fluid or force that affects earthly bodies</note>. But just as thicker, mixed, and stagnant water is easily accustomed to rot.

# ANTIDOTE

As is often the case, thick and cloudy air easily undergoes putrefaction <note>The historical theory of "miasma," where rotting or stagnant air was believed to cause disease.</note>. Raymond <note>Likely referring to Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a polymath whose works influenced later medical and alchemical thought.</note> gives this precept: that when the plague is stirred up from below, one must seek higher and thinner air. However, if it arises from above, for the first two months one must flee downward toward air that is somewhat thick, cold, moist, and pure, where illness is usually rare. During the following two months, one should move toward the middle region of the air, and thereafter to a slightly higher region—namely, that which is dry, cold, and thin—always fleeing the hot, moist, and cloudy air. In such air, men are like fish in troubled waters. Furthermore, pestilential air does to men what dark and putrid waters do to fish. 

But what is poison to humans is not necessarily so for other living creatures, due to the diversity of the celestial signs and the species of animals. Hence it arises that I am entirely ignorant of what to say regarding the opinion of those who assert that when the pestilential poison begins in the air, the little birds that usually live on high descend to the depths and inhabit the plains. But when the poison arises in the earth, they say that then the worms and serpents emerge from the bowels of the earth, and the little birds whose custom it is to fly and live near the ground seek the heights and go to the mountains. They add, moreover, that when the poison is ignited first in the air and afterward in the earth, the living creatures sometimes flee from the heights downward, and from there again seek the higher places. This is why it is commonly said...

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a celebrated Florentine philosopher and physician who wrote this manual to help his community survive the plague.</note>

...vultures or kites <note>large birds of prey</note> flee from pestilential air, and that those places inhabited by such kites are not subject to the plague-bearing air. We have quite often heard that this contagion has passed from humans to pigs. This could perhaps happen through some similarity, not indeed of the spirit, but of the flesh. In these most recently passed days, cats and dogs have carried the plague sickness from one house to another once or twice, yet they themselves were in no way harmed by this contagion. Nor should you be seized by any wonder that sometimes a human or a beast may receive the aforementioned vapor without any harm, and yet infect others. For glowing iron consumes flax and straw, yet the iron itself is in no way consumed. This arises from the disposition of the receiving subject, in whom—according to Aristotle, Galen, and Avicenna <note>The three primary authorities of medieval and Renaissance science: a Greek philosopher, a Roman physician, and a Persian polymath</note>—the effect of a thing chiefly consists. Thus, in these recent days, a two-year-old boy in our countryside stayed for a whole day with an infected boy of about seven years of age; he frequently ate food chewed by the mouth of the infected boy, yet he contracted no stain of the disease from him, though others standing quite a distance away were seized by it. Do not have too much confidence in your own disposition, thinking that you are of such health that this contagion is not to be feared by you, but observe this medical rule: That when the matter is highly disposed <note>meaning the body is "ready" or vulnerable to change</note>, then the acting cause, however weak, quickly produces its effect; thus a glowing ember ignites flax and sulfur because of the aptitude of the receiver. And on the contrary:

# THE ANTIDOTE

On the contrary: Whatever cause is most powerful will act even upon matter that is not predisposed to it. Although sulfur receives the action of fire more quickly than wood—and dry wood, cut into small pieces, more easily than other types of wood—nevertheless, a burning furnace immediately seizes even large and green logs into a flame, because the supreme power of the active agent quickly prepares and shapes them. And many times, a pestilential vapor of this kind becomes most powerful by the force of its own causes, and you cannot know exactly when this happens. Even if such a predisposition is not present at one time, it may yet be present in another.

->strikes most swiftly through contagion.<-

### CHAPTER III.

This poisonous vapor <note>original: "Venenosus iste uapor"</note> is often so subtle that it cannot be discerned by sight. Sometimes it is dissipated, but it is easily regenerated from that point as long as the predisposing celestial influence <note>original: "influentia"; referring to the astrological belief that planetary alignments "flowed" into the body to cause disease</note> remains. And now, even if it were tiny at the beginning, it nevertheless expands from place to place with a much faster course than sulfur when it is ignited. It is far more opposed to the vital spirit <term>vital spirit: a refined vapor produced from the blood in the heart, believed in Galenic medicine to sustain life and heat</term> of the heart than sulfur is to the nose. A vapor of this kind is ignited by the infected air only in bodies predisposed to it; but after it has been ignited in those bodies, it spreads everywhere with wonderful speed and ease, just like ignited sulfur, even more than before.

<margin><unclear>...easily... ...contagion.</unclear></margin>
The plague is spread, especially when it has been ignited in a subtle humor <note>In pre-modern medicine, "humors" were the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined health and temperament.</note> and in the thin air of summer; it scatters and leaps from one body into another. It is ignited most powerfully where there is a greater similarity of nature, and in a body full of waste products, with foul vapors both inside and out, and in foods and superfluous humors that are prone to inflammation and decay. It also takes hold where the matter is hot and moist, or where the heart has been weakened by sexual intercourse. Likewise, it strikes a body exhausted by the passions of the soul, or one that is excessively hot, or accustomed to frequent baths, or one whose pores are either too open or greatly obstructed. This indeed was the opinion of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> and Avicenna <note>An influential Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037 AD), author of The Canon of Medicine.</note>.

<margin>**Children and women are most often seized by the plague.**</margin>
Children and women are very susceptible to the plague because their thin and soft substance is more easily transformed, and they are full of humors prone to rotting; furthermore, their way of life is often without moderation or order. For just as wine is disturbed and muddled by a hot and thick wind, so this pestilential vapor infects and forces the spirits <note>The "vital spirits" were believed to be a subtle substance that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> first, and afterwards the humors, toward the heart from all sides; these humors, once putrefied, begin to boil. This boiling is the fever itself, which then spreads through the entire body. It boils or swells more than other fevers because the poisonous matter is so great that nature tries to expel it immediately from the principal organs as much as it can. This vapor can stain every humor, but especially the blood; secondly, the yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>; thirdly, the phlegm; and fourthly, the black bile <note>original: "melancholia"</note>. From this it follows that those subjected to this...

For this reason, the elderly are less liable to the pestilential disease, although the plague of this year has not left even the seniors unassailed. The reason for this was perhaps that, beyond other adverse planetary alignments, **Saturn** in retrograde was the ruler of the year. It is a marvel to say that although almost the entire population fled from our city of **Florence**, nevertheless about one hundred and fifty people died every day.

### Chapter IV. On the signs and indications of the plague.

As for which signs indicate a pestilential fever, so that it may be easily and clearly detected, no one can show this quite so easily because of the great diversity and deceptiveness of the symptoms. Indeed, the entire assembly of Doctors testifies to this, especially **Avenzoar** <note>An influential 12th-century Andalusian physician</note> and **Rhazes** <note>A Persian polymath and famous physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note>. For sometimes the urine will be clear, because the humors do not reach the liver; a moderate fever will appear, because the poison is not in a hot humor and therefore does not spread outward, and thus the patient will die suddenly. Sometimes the patient will seem restored, because nature at the first onset drove the poison away from the heart, yet a little later he will be deprived of breath, because nature will not be strong enough for a second onset of repelling it. From which...

For this reason, in these times it is by no means appropriate to delay by examining the signs of the disease, because you will be deceived, nor will nature wait for you unless you hurry in administering remedies. Therefore, for this reason, when you see a fever present in these times, presuppose that the plague is present, or could soon be, and administer the care for a pestilential fever; especially because as long as the poisonous influence of the air <note>Ficino refers to the "miasma" or astrological influence believed to corrupt the atmosphere</note> lasts, every superfluous humor <term>humor: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that govern health</term> is easily infected. Whence it commonly happens that in this diseased time, no sickness appears except the plague. But if other and indeed manifold sicknesses appear, then the plague is abating and ceasing.

### Prophylactic care through diet and the method of nourishment 
### during a pestilential state. CHAPTER V.

During a pestilential time, one must abstain from things that cause inflammation and those that are overly aperitive <note>Aperitives are substances used to "open" the pores or digestive pathways, which Ficino feared would allow miasma to enter the body more easily.</note>, because they dispose the body to receive the poison more readily. Specifically, one must guard against solar heat from without, and likewise from the heat of fire and heavy clothing; and from within, one must avoid salt, spices, and hot medicines. Similarly, avoid herbs of intense heat and the frequent use of pungent things—except for onion and chicory, or radish with vinegar, because these oppose the poison. Likewise, avoid wine that is too smoky <note>original: "vinum fumosum," likely referring to heavy, heady wines that were thought to cloud the senses and overheat the blood.</note>, exercise after eating (especially in hot weather), and sweating, because it alters the humors. In infected air, one should not expose oneself much to the atmosphere, nor engage in excessive exercise under the open sky, because by heating the body and opening the pores, it immediately takes in a great deal of the infected air. Likewise, one must abstain from things that cause blockages <term>oppilationem: a medical term for the clogging of internal organs or vessels</term> and putrefaction, because these provide the material for a pestilential fever; such things are viscous, cold, and moist, especially when they take on some accidental or external heat. Also avoid things that are viscous, hot, and moist, where the moisture predominates over the heat and is poorly digested; to speak briefly, moisture is the mother of putrefaction. And those things which are difficult to preserve outside of us are also not easily preserved within us

<summary>Marsilio Ficino provides dietary and lifestyle guidelines to prevent plague infection, advising against heat, moisture, and "opening" the body's pores to the infected air. He emphasizes avoiding foods that lead to internal putrefaction, which he identifies as the root cause of pestilential fevers.</summary>

Therefore, fish should be avoided as much as possible; in this category, small little fish are less harmful, specifically those from a clear, rocky, and flowing river, fried in oil with salt and dipped in staphisagria <note>likely a reference to a pickling herb or larkspur, used here as a condiment</note> or vinegar, or orange juice with salt and a little pepper or cinnamon. One must also avoid milk and all recooked foods <note>original: "recocta," likely referring to dairy byproducts like whey or twice-cooked cheeses</note>: but if you wish to use it, let it be the first among other foods and in a small quantity with a little sugar. All fruits are to be avoided, except for almonds, sour cherries, pears, apricots <note>original: "chrysomelis," literally "gold-apples"</note>, peaches, quinces, hazelnuts, dried plums, sloe berries, medlars, and cornelian cherries, Apius apples <note>a specific variety of dessert apple</note>, pomegranates, and "malatestis" <note>likely a specific regional variety of apple or citrus</note>. Truly, do not use other fruits at all, or do so rarely, or very rarely. However, you may use fruits and herbs that are cold, dry, and acidic, or somewhat bitter, for a longer period. But when using hot and moist fruits, such as figs, grapes, blackberries, and sweet cherries, ensure they are taken in small amounts, and immediately afterward eat an orange with salt. Furthermore, if you use cold and moist things, such as melons, soft and tender fish, or fatty plums, take a little fennel and orange with salt shortly after, drinking a little good and fragrant wine on top of it. You must also avoid mushrooms and moist herbs, purslane, gourd, and all moisture, as well as anything that is prone to easy putrefaction. You shall also beware of fruits and things that are excessively sweet and moist herbs: I permit you lettuce, provided it is mixed with mint.

or with cinnamon. You may also correct the same with <term>basilicon</term><note>A royal ointment or preparation, likely containing basil or similar aromatic herbs</note>, and with very finely ground cloves that tend toward a certain redness and possess the scent of cloves; for this is most pleasing to the heart. Therefore, be cautious not to take such liberty in regions that are not similar to Egypt.

It must be noted furthermore that substances which are vinegary, harsh, and sharp are to be administered in a preventative regimen just as much as in a curative one. This is because the greatest danger looms in heat and moisture, and in the putrefaction depending therefrom, in the weakening of the spirits, and in the approach of poison to the heart. Therefore, things of the aforementioned flavor resist all the evils already spoken of, because they cool, dry out, preserve, comfort, restrict, and unify. It is worthwhile to remember here that things which are too sharp—where a tightness of the chest or weakness of the stomach is feared—must be tempered with sugar, salt, almond milk, cinnamon, pepper, fennel, saffron, eggs, and a small amount of fat. I highly recommend bread made of spelt or barley, and dishes prepared from these. Likewise, biscuits, rice, and raisins tending toward tartness, and bread of the best grain, sufficiently baked.

Use eggs with verjuice <note>original: "agresta"; the tart juice of unripened grapes</note>, vinegar, and bitter oranges <note>original: "pomis anarantijs"</note>. Let your meats be light and dry, well-cooked: chickens, small birds, castrated kids <note>young goats</note>, young pigeons <note>original: "pipiones"</note>, turtle doves, and wild birds. If you use moist meats, let them be roasted, but see to it that they are well-filled throughout the inside with sharp and sour seasonings, with a little pepper, cinnamon <note>original: "cinnamomo"</note>, coriander, and salt. Cloudy wines are entirely harmful, and especially unfermented grape must. Be more sparing than usual in food and drink; let the food be somewhat more plentiful than the drink. Yet I do not wish for you to endure excessive thirst or hunger. Take care not to allow the stomach to become disgusted, but preserve it with moderation in food and drink, with exercise and fasting, and with appropriate evacuations <note>referring to the therapeutic clearing of the bowels or humors</note>. Abstain from sexual intercourse <note>original: "coitu"</note> and excessive passions of the soul, unless perhaps you find yourself completely burdened by the abstinence from intercourse...

In short, at all times beware of things that generate blood that is either excessive, watery, thick, or turbid, and likewise anything that harms the stomach. This is the rule for food and drink. In my judgment, it is useful for everyone to sprinkle the following composition of spices over their meals.
