### ->Preservative treatment for the Epidemic. On preservative pills and powders.<-

### ->CHAPTER VI.<-

<margin>Signs of a proper Theriac.</margin>
Twice a week we have need of that queen of all compositions, the heaven-sent Theriac <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium</note>. So that you may recognize a true Theriac, it preserves its flavor in the mouth for a long time and brings a binding quality to the stomach; it ought to be between four and twelve years of age, and it should be tested beforehand on venomous animals. A choice Theriac, according to the opinions of Galen, Avicenna, and Averroes <note>Ficino cites the primary Greek and Arabic authorities of medieval medicine</note>, renders a person secure from every poison and venomous disease. It is even admitted during the pestilential fever itself. Galen said he found that Theriac, more than all other things, was divine in preserving and curing. Moses the Egyptian <note>original: "Moses Aegyptius" referring to Maimonides</note> said that a wonderful experiment was performed with it during the plague of Antioch. # ANTIDOTE

<margin>Seven principal herbs against poison.</margin>
There are seven principal herbs which are said to be most powerful against poison. The first of these is the herb **St. John’s Wort** <note>original: "hypericon"</note>, also known by the name **Perforata** <note>so named because the leaves appear to have tiny punctures or "perforations" when held to the light</note>. The second is the herb called **Tame-poison** <note>original: "vincetoxicon," likely White Swallow-wort</note>; the third is **Elecampane** <note>original: "enula"</note>; the fourth is **Radish**; the fifth is **Dittany**; the sixth is **Birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochia"</note>; and the seventh is **Sow-thistle** <note>original: "lactucella"</note>. To these, **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** and **Raymond Lully** <note>two influential medieval alchemists and physicians</note> add the herb **Pink** <note>original: "tunici," likely Dianthus</note>. Nor should we overlook **Agrimony**, **Wood Sorrel**, **Chicory**, **Horehound**, **Hyssop**, **Scabious**, **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "pentaphyllon," meaning five-leaved</note>, **Capers**, **Lemons**, **Watermelons**, and **Oranges**—which we call "Golden Apples." Generally, all things that are acidic or share a certain sharp astringency <term>ponticity: a quality of being both sour and astringent, often associated with unripe fruit</term> are useful. 

Know also that the small flowers of the **Grapevine** contribute much to health if you make a habit of using them in food, drink, and medicinal pastes <term>electuaries: medicinal powders mixed with honey or syrup</term>. Likewise, the water of **Scabious** and **Lemon Balm** <note>original: "melissæ"</note> is wonderful in all these preparations administered to both the healthy and the sick, because it dries out poisonous humors. 

In cases where much cooling is needed during the drying process, one should instead use the waters of **Endive**, **Roses**, and **Plantain**; rose-infused vinegar; or the water or juice of **Wood Sorrel**, **Lemon**, **Citron**, **Orange**, **Chicory**, **Burnet** <note>original: "pimpinellæ"</note>, and **Fumitory** <note>original: "fumi terræ," literally "smoke of the earth"</note>. However, when it is necessary to use temperate remedies, take the water of **Borage** and **Bugloss**, and in each decoction include **Damson Plums**, **Myrobalans** <note>a dried plum-like fruit used in Ayurvedic and medieval medicine</note>, and **Tamarinds**.

If it becomes necessary to act with some speed, you shall administer the appropriate remedies in a thin and liquid form, or give those things we mentioned previously to be drunk. Raymond <note>Likely referring to Ramon Lull, a medieval polymath often cited in medical and alchemical texts</note> says that if the matter can be delayed long enough for the aforementioned pills to be composed, it is better for the pills to be administered than the powders. This is partly because a composition of this kind is better fermented, and through this fermentation, it acquires a specific virtue <note>A "specific virtue" refers to a medicinal power that goes beyond simple elemental qualities like heat or moisture</note> beyond its basic temperament; and partly because by remaining in the stomach longer, it preserves, strengthens, and comforts more effectively, and travels better to the remote parts of the body, provided a small amount of some liquid substance is drunk afterward and much abstinence is practiced. However, we do not wish for the pills to be very dry or hardened; indeed, if they are such, they ought to be softened again. For those of a sanguine temperament, phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term> is appropriate—that is, to extract blood so that they may be preserved—provided they do not otherwise have a natural flow of blood from themselves.

<margin>Sanguine individuals.</margin> By sanguine individuals, I mean those who are decently fleshy, red in color, hairy, and robust, who have large veins and who eat foods of great nourishment. From these, I say, blood should be extracted from the right basilic vein <note>original: "basilica dextra"; the basilic vein is a large vein in the arm</note>, and then after a space of two months, a small cutting should be made again from the left basilic vein. Do not exceed the weight of a pound in a single instance. Let this also be done during temperate times of the year, and while the moon is in a good and fortunate aspect <note>A reference to medical astrology, where the position of the moon determined the safety of surgery</note>. Pure blood is reduced at sunrise, choleric blood at noon, melancholic at sunset, and phlegmatic in the middle of the night. Regarding the four types of blood previously enumerated, one should observe those four specific hours when extracting it. These types are recognized first by their specific signs, and then according to the four ages of life in which they dominate, following the aforementioned order. Where there does not appear to be a great abundance of blood, the author <note>Likely referring to a specific authority like Galen or Avicenna</note> wishes that no bloodletting <term>minutio: a technical term for bloodletting or "diminishing" the blood</term> be performed at all, neither for the sake of preservation nor for a cure. 

And when you wish to extract blood, take care that on the preceding day a clyster <note>an enema</note> is administered, and some non-laxative medicine is given. Nor do I think it should be overlooked that where the blood declines significantly toward other humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, evacuation should be avoided. Remember that Galen and Avicenna <note>Galen (129–216 AD) and Avicenna (980–1037 AD) were the primary authorities on medicine in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>, the more they practiced the art of healing, the more timid they always became toward phlebotomy <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term>. This is because phlebotomy draws more from the natural and good substance and from the spirits than medicine itself does; furthermore, it allows less time to discern the bad blood from the good.

For infants and children, those things which are effective against worms are beneficial, as the danger of these is especially imminent during these times. Administer to them in a drink once a week one drachm <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of dittany <note>original: "dictami"</note> with a somewhat styptic <note>astringent</note> wine, or with a wine made from a decoction of wormwood <note>original: "absynthij"</note> and black cumin <note>original: "nigellæ"</note>, or "holy seed" <note>original: "seminis sancti," likely Santonica or wormseed</note>. <meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's medical discourse on the causes of plague, specifically focusing on the interaction of heat and moisture and the dangers of the autumn season. Catchword: 'simpli' refers to 'simplicia' (simple medicines) on the following page.</meta>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS

Bodies are weakened and filled with corruptible substances, which provide moist matter to the heat of the air, leading to putrefaction <note>Ficino follows the Galenic theory that plague is caused by "putrefaction" of the bodily humors triggered by corrupted air</note>. Indeed, if this heat were accompanied by dryness both internally and externally, it would do little harm; likewise, moisture joined with coldness—whether in the air or in one's temperament—is not very damaging. However, it is extremely dangerous when heat is mixed with moisture, whether outside or inside the body. We have learned through experience that a long period of dryness in a warm season diminishes the plague, but in a cold season, it stirs it up and brings it on. Finally, in autumn, the over-fullness caused by eating fruits increases, as does the weakness of bodies. The air is thin due to the preceding summer and easily receives vapors, which it cannot disperse because of the decrease in heat; consequently, the air becomes foggy and variable. Frequently, a thick and moist wind is present, heat exceeds moisture and arrives often, and the blockage <term>oppilatio: a medical term for the clogging of the body's pores or channels</term> of the pores increases because the air frequently turns cold after the preceding heat. It must also be known that when the pores are tightly blocked, they compress the putrefiable matter within. Conversely, when they are opened more than is proper, they suddenly take in too much poisonous air, so that sometimes (especially after sweating or sexual intercourse) it kills in a few hours, like a sword.

# THE ANTIDOTE

<note>original: "Antidotus"</note>

Avoid using simple aperients <note>medicines used to open the pores or bowels</note>, because they provide an entrance for the poison to reach the heart and open a path for the exhalation of the spirits. Instead, so that inflammation and putrefaction <note>the decay of bodily humors</note> may be prevented, immediately use those things which are slightly cooling and greatly drying. For these strengthen the heart and close the pathways leading toward it, lest the poison reach that organ. Furthermore, the humor <note>the bodily fluids, such as blood or bile</note> must be well purged in part, and the spirits must be frequently restored with nourishment; continually administer those things which are effective against poison, for poison by its very nature seeks the heart. But if you delay until the poison has arrived there, it may perhaps happen that the parts of the heart become greatly constricted; to open them again might then be more harmful or dangerous than beneficial.

Therefore, as soon as anyone perceives a heaviness in the head and all the limbs together with an accompanying fever, see to it that you do not put your faith in deceptive or ambiguous signs, nor delay until an inflation or a bleb <note>original: "bulla"; a blister or pustule often associated with the plague</note> appears. But when these do emerge, as quickly as you are able, immediately anoint with oil of scorpions and theriac <note>a famous ancient herbal jam used as a universal antidote</note> the pulses of the temples, the hands, and the feet, as well as the nostrils, the back of the head, the throat, the chest, and the area around the blister and the

# ANTIDOTE

<margin>307</margin>

Regarding indigestion and the onset of poison: indeed, when nature is oppressed, it works harder than it ought to. Therefore, after a suitable time for sweating has passed, you should either reduce the blood if it is in excess <note>A reference to bloodletting, a common practice to balance the "humors" or bodily fluids</note>, or, if it is not in excess, you shall administer a purgative, using substances that do not disturb the stomach. For a violent bout of vomiting, by dilating the passages of the chest, causes the poison to run toward the heart and draws it toward the brain. For this reason, those who administer goat’s rue <note>original: "capraginem"; Galega officinalis, once thought to be a remedy but here criticized for its harshness</note> and similar emetic and poisonous things are in error; for nature can scarcely resist a single poison.

Perhaps someone might oppose us by asking why physicians <note>original: "physici"; referring to natural philosophers or medical doctors</note> are accustomed to lead those who are poisoned to vomit? I say that the condition of poisons is not equal: for other types have more physical matter and are more suited to be drawn out through vomiting, and they remain in the stomach; but this [pestilential poison] is a certain poisonous vapor located in the regions of the chest. Therefore, let no medicine be present that can violently produce vomiting, nor should one condemn that which produces it with no violence at all. It is, however, more approved that the diversion [of the poison] be made through the lower parts <note>i.e., through the bowels rather than the mouth</note>.

Let the medicine you give be dissolved in white wine and the waters of scabious, endive, roses, plantain, bugloss, and lemon balm, or in rose vinegar, in which a decoction has been made of Damson plums, myrobalans <note>A dried plum-like fruit from India used as a laxative</note>, and tamarinds. If, however, the disease attacks someone with a full stomach, what then must be done according to the order of the moderns? See to it that after anointing with oil of scorpions and theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made of many ingredients</note>, he vomits easily with warm water, vinegar, oil, and juice...

It should be noted that if the fever clings to thin and hot humors, there will appear a vehement thirst, dryness of the throat, blackness of the tongue, acute headache, <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "phrenesis"; delirium or mental agitation</note>, or similar horrific symptoms. If, however, it clings to thicker and less furious humors, the fever will seem slow, and the aforementioned symptoms will be milder. Consider signs of this kind, and know that in whatever humor it occurs, <term>trisera with agaric</term> <note>an electuary containing larch fungus, used as a purgative</note> is suitable, as are the aggregate pills, either alone or with the pills of fumitory. Also, the laxative syrup which we shall describe below—if it be in "furious" matter—is suitable, as is <term>diasenna</term> <note>a senna-based compound</note> with <term>electuary of hamech</term> <note>a bitter purgative used to treat melancholy</note> or juice of roses. It pleases me exceedingly for persons who are not extremely weak and who do not have a very loose stomach. It should be taken once a week by both the healthy and the sick.

Note that after the operation of medicine, or after bloodletting <note>term: phlebotomy (the surgical opening of a vein to balance the humors)</note>, if you have not administered medicine on the following day, one drachm of theriac <note>term: theriaca (an ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh)</note> should be offered with one ounce of rose water and a small amount of rose vinegar. Do not fear the heat of the theriac, since such a small portion can provide little heat, because its elemental quality—such as heat and the like—[is balanced].

# ANTIDOTE

<note>original: "Antidotus"</note>

...since they are highly material in nature, they do not achieve much unless administered in large quantities. However, a <term>specific virtue</term> <note>A "specific virtue" refers to a hidden, almost magical property of a substance that works directly on a disease, rather than just balancing the body's heat or moisture.</note>, being a celestial and, as it were, spiritual gift, achieves much even in small amounts according to Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note>. Furthermore, **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium.</note> works against poison by its specific property; beyond this, it barely reaches the second degree of heat. Therefore, it is far more powerful at expelling poison than it is at heating the body. Likewise, a pestilential fever is much more poisonous than it is hot; yet, Theriac should be administered with rose water, and in other treatments, care must be taken to lean toward a certain coolness so that you may be able to use this remedy. **Mithridatum** <note>Another complex ancient antidote, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> can also be given in place of Theriac, but much more powerful results have been seen from Theriac through experience.

For this reason, **Moses the Egyptian** <note>Referring to Maimonides (1138–1204), the famous Jewish philosopher and physician.</note> says it was told to him by a certain wise physician that while he was practicing medicine in **Antioch** during a time of plague, he discovered the truth of the matter: all other remedies were weak, but those who took Theriac upon his advice escaped safe and surviving, while the others did not. Even those who used it after the onset of the disease were liberated, while others exchanged life for death. By this, what Galen says in his short book *On Theriac, addressed to Caesar* is confirmed: that it is opposed to all poisons and will be powerful where other things fail and are weak. Moreover, it possesses this through a certain miraculous power. There are also those who administer urine as a drink, or lye, and likewise the juice of white onions...

Some practitioners administer spurge <note>original: "euphorbium"; a caustic plant resin used as a drastic purgative.</note> with mastic and gum elemi. This is indeed a dangerous medicine, and is not suited for anyone except the strongest individuals, and then only at the very beginning of the illness. Some assert that gum elemi is the resin of the cedar tree.

It must be understood that in this case, a "weak" medicine—that is, one that produces a meager effect—should not be administered, because if the first medicine does not work well, nature itself will not wait for a second attempt. And yet, one should not purge with excessive force, for by this the spirits <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle substances that carried life and sensation through the body.</note> would be dissolved; this evil consists more in a certain poisonous quality than in the quantity of the matter. Gentilis of Foligno <note>A famous 14th-century Italian physician known for his commentaries on Avicenna and his work during the Black Death.</note> says that he has experienced much with the aforementioned powder; from the beginning, he administered it thus: Take half a drachm of spurge and one drachm of mastic; from these he gave [several] scruples...

### On the Feeding and Regimen of the Sick.
### CHAPTER X.

Food ought to be (according to Rhazes and Avicenna <note>Rhazes (865–925) and Avicenna (980–1037) were influential Persian physicians whose works formed the basis of European medical study.</note> in the fourth book of the *Canon*) frequent, moderate, light, boiled, and of much and moist nourishment, seasoned with sour and cold things, such as endive, sorrel, vinegar, verjuice <note>The tart juice of unripe grapes.</note>, pomegranates, oranges, lemons, sour cherries, and plums. The substance of the food should be chicken, partridge, pheasant, crushed meats, consommés, distillations, fresh eggs; I also do not forbid the meat of young goats. In short, let the patient be nourished with liquid, moist things of high nutritional value. However, they must be nourished in such a way that nature can tolerate it and the fevers do not multiply: for in this case, much more than in others, there is need for more abundant food. Avicenna says in the fourth book of the *Canon* that the filling of the veins through nourishment prevents the passage of the poisonous vapor of the air and humor, and that those are more frequently delivered from the disease who are fearlessly aided by nourishment. Note that once the loosening clyster <note>An enema used to purge the bowels.</note> has been administered, which we mentioned above, if there is need for further restoration, let the patient take something by mouth; you shall perform the loosening either with an enema or a suppository, and then after four hours you shall administer some of the nourishment we discussed a little earlier. The wine should be white, thin, and fragrant

A certain countryman of ours, a robust man, as soon as this disease attacked him, immersed himself in cold waters and stayed there for two hours; upon exiting, he was cured. Nevertheless, this is a most deceptive experiment <note>Ficino warns that while this "cold shock" worked for one strong man, it is a dangerous and unreliable treatment for most</note>.

# THE ANTIDOTE

Perhaps it would be safer to sit in lukewarm waters that do not reach the chest, since these parts must not be opened <note>The author refers to the "pores" or "passages" of the chest, fearing that heat might draw toxins toward the heart.</note>, nor should the humors <term>Humors: the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to govern health.</term> be drawn toward them. Among these people, a certain physician <note>original: "physicus"</note> had been cured. It seems to me, however, to be a very dangerous matter.

### On treatment through the art of surgery. CHAPTER XI.

In this case, one must not wait until an inflation or a blister appears; rather, once the purging or <term>Phlebotomy: the practice of bloodletting to balance the humors.</term> has been performed, be swift and ready to extract the poison. This is done by creating a <term>Ruptory: a caustic substance used to break the skin and create an artificial sore or blister.</term> using leaven and <term>Cantharides: "Spanish Fly" beetles, used topically to cause blistering.</term>, or another of those methods which we shall describe below. You should apply it to the muscle of the right arm below the inner elbow, or where the pulse is usually felt, though not directly upon the pulse itself. Similarly, you shall do this above the ankle of the right foot, four fingers inward, so that a blister forms; open this blister and keep it open. If the usual sign appears, and the discomfort or the shortness of time prevents the standard order from being followed, let the bloodletting and purging be done immediately. Once these are finished, or at least the bloodletting, you shall make a ruptory and apply it to the same side at a distance of six fingers below the sign <note>Likely referring to the site of a bubo or swelling.</note>. There are those who do not trust the variability of the timing, but regardless of the order, both before and after, and simultaneously as best they can, they apply reme—

But if it should be on the back part in that same place, it ought not to be applied on the front, but rather below the location of the sign. 

And so you shall allow the ruptory to remain there until it has created a blister, which you should open and place butter and cabbage leaves upon. Likewise, apply a sponge soaked in this decoction: Take chamomile, bristanica <note>likely Great Water Dock or a similar astringent herb</note>, melilot <note>sweet clover</note>, and scabious, one handful of each; let them boil in half a pound of water until half is consumed. Because this draws out the poison, keep it renewed and hold it there often until the end of the cure.

<note>original: "accidens apoftematis"</note> occurring with an abscess. On the other hand, it is different when it comes after a fever. For this abscess is of two types: one is a blister and is named **anthrax** <note>a severe, ulcerating sore</note> and **carbuncle**. The other is a swelling and is called a **bubo** <note>an inflamed lymph node</note> and **glandule**. The blister commonly emerges through the <term>emunctories<note>the body's natural drainage points or cleansing organs</note></term>, and the further it is from the principal organs, the less dangerous it is. The **black** variety is the worst of all; the **green** is in second place and is a little less evil; the **gray-blue** is third, and the **red** is fourth. And the drier it is, the worse it is. Swelling commonly tends to occur in the emunctories, that is, in the 

<margin>The three emunctories of the principal organs.</margin>
purgatories of the principal organs, which are three: namely, in the places behind the ears, under the arms, and in the groin. The **brain** sends down poison through the emunctories behind the ears, as well as into the neck. The **heart** sends it under the arms. The **liver** sends it to or around the groin. For this reason, the swelling is worse than the blister, since it shows that much of the poison has flowed toward the principal organs. And the closer the swelling is to the heart, the more dangerous it truly is. The cure for both—namely the blister and the swelling—is essentially the same. There are those who, when an abscess appears before the fever and far from the heart, suddenly apply ligatures <note>tight bandages</note> between the site of pain and the heart, and they place cold, dry things on top for the sake of <term>repelling<note>original: "repercutiendi"; a medical technique to drive fluids away from a site</note></term> the infection. But upon the site of the pain itself, they place hot and moist <term>resolutives<note>substances intended to dissolve or scatter the swelling</note></term>. Others, as soon as the abscess begins to appear, place <term>cupping glasses<note>original: "uentofas"</note></term> both directly on top and to the side, as we have said, as well as <term>ruptories<note>substances used to break the skin or "ripen" an abscess</note></term>, immediately administering this medicine.

Take half a <term>drachm</term> <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> each of prepared black hellebore, senna, and cinnamon; half a <term>scruple</term> <note>A small weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of <term>diagridium</term> <note>A preparation of scammony juice purified with quince</note>. ### Rules and methods for applying caustic remedies. CHAPTER XIV.

When it is not appropriate for blood to be drawn with <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "uentosis"</note> or leeches, nor for a <term>cautery mark</term> <note>original: "signum"; a brand or burn made with a hot iron</note> to be burned, <term>caustics</term> <note>original: "ruptoriorum"; substances used to break or erode the skin</note> should be placed below or above, or in both places at once, using the compositions mentioned and those I shall describe in the following sections. You should administer the aforementioned if the opportunity of time seems right, after the blood has been drawn.

The blood has settled and the patient has rested a little, or at least after the taking of the medicine and its completed operation; and if there is no surgeon present to work with his hands <note>original: "qui manu operetur" - referring to a barber-surgeon who performed manual procedures like lancing</note>, give the powder, which if you do not have, administer the medicine. Take care that you do not place things so cold and binding <term>sypticas: styptic or astringent substances that constrict tissues</term> upon the mark that they drive the poison back inward. Nor should you fear pain much, since it draws the poison to the abscess <term>apostema: a swelling or large boil filled with purulent matter</term>. However, I do not wish you to tolerate excess pain, since it would add strength to the poison, likewise increase the fevers, and weary nature too much. I do not want you to completely heal the site of the corrosive application by medical art until three months have elapsed; and when you do this, repeat the purgation. A certain fellow Florentine of ours had a boil lanced <note>original: "incidit bullam"</note> this Spring; although he was so liberated from this disease that he was no different from the healthy, not long after he first closed the wound—and after forty days had passed—he was again infected by the disease.

He died within the space of two days, primarily because he had closed the wound without a proper purging <note>original: "purgatione"; the process of draining or cleansing the body of corrupt fluids</note>. For you should know this: whoever dies after the seventh day, it happens more through poor care than through the natural course of this disease. Know that after the poison <note>original: "venenum"</note> has flowed so far into the abscess <note>original: "apostema"; a swelling or boil typical of the plague</note> that the vital organs are relieved by it, unless you draw it out, rectify it, and purge it thoroughly and continuously, the internal poison of the abscess becomes more aggravated; by contracting, it sends vapors inward and kills. Therefore, continually strengthen the heart itself by constricting its passages from within and without; evacuate the humors <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health</note> frequently, and rectify and purge the poison of the wound. Do not hope for anything certain based on those who have an irrational hope for health; indeed, do not cease from remedies for a moment because of this, especially if the seventh day has not yet passed.

### Compound ruptories and certain strong plasters. CHAPTER XV.

There are many kinds of compound ruptories <note>term: ruptoria; medicines designed to break the skin or open an abscess</note> that are strong in drawing the poison outward. We shall describe many, so that you may conveniently use the help of whichever is appropriate to the occasion. Take figs, iris <note>original: "ireos"</note>, and crushed grains of wheat in equal parts; this ripens the swelling quickly and breaks it open. Also, leaven with oil and salt. Also, pitch with raisins and honey. Also, sparrow dung with hog's lard <note>original: "axungia porci"</note>. Also, powdered glass with turpentine. Also, unless it should be considered loathsome, human dung is very effective both before and after the rupture, by placing hot bread crumbs on top.

### On the method of cleansing the wound. Chapter 20.

### On the cure according to the custom of the Spaniards and Catalans. CHAPTER XXV.

We have spoken in the preceding sections concerning the cure of this kind of disease according to the intentions of the Greeks, the Latins, and also the Barbarians <note>Ficino uses "Barbarians" here to refer to Arabic medical authorities like Avicenna</note>, but especially according to the practice of the Italians. At present, we shall consider these medications according to the custom of the Spaniards as well as the Catalans. Therefore, according to them, a clyster <note>an enema</note> is administered immediately; afterwards, if blood is in excess, phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note> is performed. If not, medicine is administered according to the quality of the offending humor. From the beginning they apply an epithem <note>a topical liquid poultice or compress</note>, then, after some evacuation has been performed—at least with a clyster—they proceed to the treatment of the abscess <note>original: "apostematis"; a swelling or bubo characteristic of the plague</note>. Also according to their custom, nothing of an inflammatory or burning nature should be placed over the abscess, because such things induce spasms, kindle fevers, and render the poison more malignant, especially if the abscess is located in the emunctories <note>the lymph nodes or "cleansing" areas of the body, such as the armpits or groin</note>. They likewise say that at the beginning, substances that are overly ripening or softening should not be applied, since they clog, obstruct, cause putrefaction, make the infection boil over, and drive the poison inward. Nor do they say that cold applications should be administered, nor anything with a sponge (because it dries), nor with a cloth, because it traps the vapors inside and constricts them. ### *On the preservation of bystanders who govern the sick.* CHAPTER XXIV.

Finally, I would have you know this: that the poison remains in persons for a period of two months. Walls, iron tools, and things constructed of wood—unless they are corrected with washings, fumigations, and fires—will perhaps retain their poisonous quality for a year or more. Likewise, woolen garments and that sort of thing, unless they are aired out, washed, and frequently fumigated, or placed by a fire, in the wind, or in the sun, remain infected for three years and beyond. Similarly, the scent of musk remains for a long time in the same cotton where it first resided. Indeed, just as oil is to fire, so wool is the nourishment of this poison; and truly, this wool so nourishes the poison that it not only preserves it, but increases and strengthens it at the same time. One must not use the vessels of those who are infected for the preparation of food or drink, nor should anything that has touched them be handled. During those indeed heavy pestilences (which had occurred in Athens), the philosopher Socrates preserved himself unharmed. For this reason, Aristotle and Galen say that there is such a disposition in pure bodies that they almost never feel the plague, or if they are infected, they at least do not perish. Behold, I now hand over to you two singular methods so that you may preserve yourself. Prepare an **emerald** <note>original: "smaragdum"</note> so that it can be drunk <note>likely as a powder dissolved in liquid</note>, touched, held in the mouth, or suspended from the neck; its power against poisons is so great that, according to the testimony of Rhazes, Avenzoar, and Serapion <note>famous Persian and Arabic physicians whose works were central to Medieval and Renaissance medicine</note>, the eyes of vipers and serpents <note>original: "tyris et bubonibus," referring to specific venomous snakes</note> immediately fall out of their own accord just by the sight of it. 

To the poor, I am accustomed to give **wild radish**, a little at a time so that it does not inflame the blood; for it has such great efficacy against poison that it causes a scorpion to burst by its mere touch. And Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist</note> says that if the hands are washed with its seed crushed in vinegar, serpents can do no harm at all when touched. 

The **Bezoar stone** <note>a mass found in the digestive tract of certain animals, highly prized as a universal antidote</note> (if anyone is able to obtain it) prevails above all things against poisons; for although in the Persian language <note>original: "Persico idiomate"</note> everything was customarily called "bezoar" by the ancients if its property and virtue was the repelling of poisons, nevertheless, according to Serapion and Rhazes, the name "bezoar" is principally given to a certain stone that resists all poisons—whether hot or cold—as well as bites and all poisonous ulcers by its own power. It is beneficial whether it is taken by mouth, held in the mouth, suspended from the neck, or finally applied in any way to the exterior of the body. It originates in Syria, in India, and in parts of the East, and it is of various kinds and of three different colors.

->*Flee quickly, go far away, and return slowly.*<-

### C H A P T E R  X X V.

It has seemed appropriate to reserve for the end of the book the explanation of the principal rules regarding this matter. Flee as much as you are able from the company of men, and especially when you are fasting. Always remain distant from a companion by at least the space of two cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters; two cubits is approximately 3 feet.</note>, and in a free, open place. When speaking with an infected person, remain even further away, by an interval of at least six cubits <note>Approximately 9 feet or 2.7 meters.</note>, and stay under the open sky or in a well-ventilated place. Take care that the blowing of the winds does not breathe from him toward you. Between you and him let there be sun, fire, odors, or a wind blowing toward him; for narrow places and a crowd of people together are exceedingly dangerous. I also mention this: that the morbid contagion is multiplied by the enclosure of walls and the touching and continuity of houses. Above all, I persuade you to flee quickly and far from those places where the plague is imminent, and return slowly. I said "quickly," that is, as soon as the signs of the approaching plague appear. These signs are indeed when the air of that place is seen to be outside its natural disposition, declining toward heat and humidity; when it appears foggy with dense clouds and is dusty; when the winds are thick and lukewarm; and also when the waters and fields smoke and smell. Likewise, the fish are of bad flavor and odor. When many animals born from putrefaction <note>The theory of spontaneous generation, where small creatures were thought to arise from decaying matter.</note> appear upon the earth, along with an abundance of mushrooms and rotten herbs, the fruits of the earth and animals are tasteless and are poorly preserved, and they become turbid...

# THE ANTIDOTE

...wines are spoiled, many creatures of the earth and air flee from that place, and unusual fevers arise—hidden, raging, continuous, and deceptive—accompanied by anxiety in the chest, a collapsing pulse, delirium <note>original: "phrenesis," a term used for inflammation of the brain or severe mental confusion</note>, turbulent urine, the stripping of the skin from the palate and intestines, redness of the eyes, worms, measles <note>original: "morbilli," which could refer to measles or any similar eruptive skin disease</note>, many disturbances among women, rabid anger, brawls, dire wars, monsters of nature, and wondrous signs sent either by nature or by God, which are much hated and rare. For these things which we have mentioned are the omens of a nearing plague; flee, therefore, before you become one of the twelve thousand marked for death. 

This can happen in two ways: either because you will have already been caught by the contagion of the infected, or because you have already taken in the grim quality of the infected air, so that the air gradually becomes familiar to you. In that case, neither your nature resists the air, nor does the air resist your nature; but if you suddenly seek a foreign breeze, the first air will depart and nature will resist it, and from this conflict of natures arises the origin of the plague. 

I also advise that you flee far away, namely that you betake yourself to those places where neither things, nor persons, nor sounds, noises, or rumors of any kind from the infected place can reach you. Be so remote that high mountains stand between you, by which the approach of vapors may be blocked, lest they reach you by the blowing of the winds or the spreading of the air. Consider the disposition and site of the place to which you run, namely that it be not similar in any way to the pestilential air—whether in heat, cold, moisture, dryness, clouds, rains, or winds—and finally, be established in such a place...

<keywords>plague symptoms, contagion, miasma, public health advice, omens, pestilence, environmental health</keywords>

# MARSILIO FICINO ON EPIDEMICS

so that winds, clouds, and rains are by no means able to breathe, expand, or move from that place toward you. Nor should it escape your notice that the horoscope or *Ascendant* <note>The point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment, believed by Ficino to influence the "health" of a city.</note> of any infected city or castle often spreads the plague to all those locations which were subject to that city or castle from its beginning, and which have some degree of conformity with that *Ascendant*. 

Thirdly, we say that you should be slow to return, since a very tiny remaining infection of a past disease is powerful enough to very suddenly stain all those who began their flight even at a timely hour. This is because those who frequent an infected place after they have previously fled are in greater danger than those who always remained in the same spot (provided they stayed with caution), since nature tolerates sudden and new occurrences poorly. 

Furthermore, these qualities remain for a very long time (as we have said before) in walls, timberwork, clothes, all kinds of cloths, and other such things. As far as the disposition of the air alone is concerned, one *angaria* <note>original: "angaria"; likely referring here to a specific period of time or a "shift" of quarantine, roughly forty days or a season.</note> is sufficient, so that when all people whatsoever have remained immune from this disease for three months, it can be judged that the air is now purged. 

But be most cautious in approaching and touching those things which retain the poison more than the air does. The enclosures of furnaces in walls preserve poisonous warmth longer than wood does; however, they are purified (as we have often said) namely with fires, washings, ventilation, fumigations, odors, and the rest. Men are commonly purified in the space of fourteen days.

# PAUL OF AEGINA ON

->*The useful method of diet for any*<-
->*season of the year.*<-

It would be most excellent to also consider the seasons of the year in one's method of diet <note>Latin: "uictus ratione"; referring to the broader lifestyle including food, drink, and exercise</note>. In **Winter**, one should employ both more vigorous exercise and more abundant food, especially if the weather is North-windy <note>Aquilonia: referring to the cold, dry North wind</note>. If, however, the wind is from the South, one ought to exercise similarly but subtract something from food and drink; and throughout a humid period, one should make the body entirely dry; during a cold period, however, make it warmer, and then eat warmer meats and vegetables, and drink wine more undiluted.

As **Spring** approaches, one person may be purged by vomiting, another by the bowels, and another may let blood by cutting a vein <note>Phlebotomy or bloodletting was a standard preventative measure in ancient medicine to balance the humors</note>, according to each person's custom or readiness of mind. In **Summer**, rest is beneficial, along with more relaxed exercise and a small amount of food, which indeed ought to be selected from the colder variety; then, however, one should add to the drink and employ whatever is able to cool and moisten. Throughout **Autumn**, there is need for greater caution, since it is everywhere both unequal and disordered, and brings on many-shaped diseases. Therefore, one must take care lest any mistake be made regarding cooling; one must also abstain from sexual intercourse and cold drinks. Nor should anyone trust themselves to the air, either during the morning chill or during the midday heat. To be filled with fruit is harmful, not only because of the ease of eating it, but also because faulty humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient doctors believed governed health</note> are born from it, and they also excite wind <note>Flatulence</note>, since indeed

<summary>This page outlines the seasonal health regimen prescribed by Paul of Aegina, detailing how diet, exercise, and medical treatments like bloodletting should be adjusted to balance the body's humors against the environment.</summary>
<keywords>Paul of Aegina, seasonal diet, humoral theory, ancient medicine, bloodletting, hygiene, exercise, winter health, autumn diseases</keywords>

--- Page 395 ---
<meta>This page concludes the discussion on seasonal dietary regimens, specifically addressing the transition from autumn to winter.</meta>

Of all fruits, figs and grapes are the best; however, they both produce gas <note>original: "flatum"</note> and spoil other nutrients unless they are eaten before other foods. If they are taken beforehand, they neither cause bloating nor interfere with digestion. When the air begins to grow cold, it is necessary to warm the body in proportion to the chill, and to do everything as one would when winter has already progressed. It would not be out of place, once the equinox <note>The autumnal equinox, marking the start of the colder season.</note> has returned, to purge the body using one of the methods we have previously mentioned. This ensures that any "redundancy" <note>An excess of bodily humors or waste products.</note> retained through the winter does not cause distress.
